lead: This week the Great Fast walks with Abram. Today God calls him to leave everything on the strength of a promise, and in John a man who has waited thirty-eight years is told to stand up. The second reading shows the opposite of that trust, Achan’s hidden theft and its bitter end in the Valley of Achor. In the epistle Paul grieves for his own people and insists that God’s word has not failed. Both main readings begin with a word from God to someone who has nothing to offer in return.

set: Genesis 1–11 tells of a world spreading away from God, and it closes with Babel, where people said, “let us make a name for ourselves” (11:4). Now God says to one man that he will make his name great (12:2). Abram’s father Terah had left Ur for Canaan and stopped at Haran (11:31), and Abram is called from there. He has no child, for Sarai is barren (11:30). That makes the promise of a great nation seem impossible from its first word.
str: vv. 1–3: the call and the promise: a land, a people, a name, a blessing.
vv. 4–5: Abram goes, with Sarai, Lot and all they have.
vv. 6–9: through the land: Shechem, then between Bethel and Ai, with an altar at each of the first two stops, and on toward the Negeb.
kw: Two short Hebrew words open the story of Israel. The second adds force and is hard to translate: “go, you yourself”. Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator, took it to mean “go for your own good”.
The root “bless” comes five times in vv. 2–3. In Genesis, blessing means life, fruitfulness and peace given by God. Abram receives it so that it may pass through him to others.
Abram owns none of this land, and yet he builds altars in it (vv. 7–8). His first act in the promised land is worship.
vv: Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
The list moves inward: country, clan, home. Each step costs more than the last. God does not name the land yet: he says only, “that I will show you”.
in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
This is the widest line in the chapter. The call of one man is for the sake of all the families scattered at Babel. St Paul reads it as “the gospel beforehand”, and quotes it in Galatians 3:8.
So Abram went, as the Lord had told him;
Abram asks nothing and says nothing. The next thing we learn is his age, seventy-five, which tells us that this call does not come too late for anyone.
ch: The Catechism sees in this call the beginning of God’s answer to a scattered humanity: God calls Abram “in order to gather together scattered humanity” (CCC 59), and his descendants are the trustees of the promise (CCC 60). Abraham is its great example of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–146), as in Hebrews 11:8: he set out, “not knowing where he was going”. Nostra Aetate 4 recalls that the beginnings of the Church’s faith are already found among the patriarchs, Moses and the prophets.

r.h: Do you want to be made well?
set: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for a festival John does not name. The pool lay near the Sheep Gate, north of the Temple. Excavations near the Church of St Anne have uncovered a large double pool of the right period, which fits John’s description well.

The oldest manuscripts have no explanation of the moving water. A later addition, found in some copies, says that an angel stirred it, and many Bibles omit this as v. 4; the verse numbers of the NRSV and the POC differ here. John’s story depends only on what the sick man says in v. 7.
str: vv. 1–5: the place and the man, ill for thirty-eight years.
vv. 6–9a: the question and the word: he stands and walks.
vv. 9b–13: it is the sabbath: questions about the mat.
vv. 14–15: Jesus finds him in the Temple.
vv. 16–18: “My Father is still working”, and the dispute deepens.
kw: The word comes again and again in the passage (vv. 6, 9, 11, 14, 15). It means sound and healthy. The whole story turns on it.
A poor person’s pallet. Mark uses the same word for the paralysed man let down through the roof (Mark 2:4). What once carried this man he now carries.
The verb of v. 17. Jesus answers the charge of working on the sabbath by speaking about the work of his Father.
vv: Do you want to be made well?

Jesus speaks first; the man has asked for nothing. The question is not a foolish one. After thirty-eight years a person can stop hoping. The man does not answer yes. He explains why it has never happened: “I have no one” (v. 7). The Lord then becomes that someone.
See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to you.
Jesus looks for him a second time, because the bodily cure is not the whole gift. See the question below on sickness and sin.
My Father is still working, and I also am working.

Jewish teachers of that age also reflected that God keeps the world in being even on the sabbath. Jesus places his own work beside the Father’s. That is why John says the claim went further than the sabbath: he was “making himself equal to God” (v. 18).
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, and that he gives its true meaning (CCC 2173; see also 582). John’s phrase “the Jews” in vv. 10–18 means here the authorities in Jerusalem who opposed him, not a whole people: the man, the disciples and Jesus himself are Jews, and the Church firmly rejects any blame laid on the Jewish people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). St Augustine took the five porticoes as a figure of the five books of Moses, which show us our sickness and lead us to the healer (Tractates on John 17; in substance).

qa: Does this mean that sickness is a punishment for sin?

No. In John 9:3 Jesus says of the man born blind, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned”. The word in 5:14 is addressed to this one man and warns of something worse than illness: to lose what God has given. The Church does not teach that each illness comes from a person’s own sin (see CCC 1502–1505).
study: What has God asked me to leave behind in this Great Fast, and have I gone “as the Lord had told” me?
Is there a place in my life where I have stopped hoping? How would I answer if Jesus asked, “Do you want to be made well?”

lead: Yesterday Abram set out in great faith. Today, at the first hard test, he goes down to Egypt and gives way to fear, and God keeps the promise even so. The second reading sends Joshua back to Ai after his defeat, with the word “Do not fear”. Paul in the epistle teaches that everything rests on the God who shows mercy. In John, Jesus says that all he does comes from the Father. Taken together, the readings point away from our own strength: what God has begun depends on him, and on what the Son receives from the Father.

set: Abram has only just reached the land when a famine drives him out of it. Famine sent people from Canaan down to Egypt, whose food came from the yearly flood of the Nile. Genesis tells a like story twice more, of Abraham in Gerar (Genesis 20) and of Isaac (Genesis 26).

Many readers notice that this story runs ahead of the Exodus: famine, a going down to Egypt, danger to the family, plagues on Pharaoh, and a departure with great wealth. What will happen to the people happens first to their father.
str: vv. 9–10: from the Negeb to Egypt, because of famine.
vv. 11–13: Abram’s plan: “Say you are my sister”.
vv. 14–16: Sarai is taken to Pharaoh’s house, and Abram grows rich.
v. 17: the Lord acts.
vv. 18–20: Pharaoh’s rebuke, and Abram is sent away.
kw: The word of v. 10. Abram goes as a foreigner without rights. He knows what it is to be a migrant in someone else’s land, and Israel’s law later remembers that experience (Exodus 22:21).
The half-truth of the story. Genesis 20:12 will say that Sarah was the daughter of Abraham’s father by another mother. Even so, the words here are meant to deceive.
Literally “blows” or “strokes”. Exodus 11:1 uses the same word for the last plague on Egypt.
vv: Now there was a famine in the land.
The land of promise greets Abram with hunger. Following God’s call does not remove trouble, and a true call can lead straight into difficulty.
Say you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you,

Yesterday’s man of faith is afraid for his life and puts his wife in danger. Abram did not ask God before he made this plan. The Bible does not hide the faults of its great figures, and that is one reason why it can be trusted.
What is this you have done to me?
The sharpest words in the passage come from a pagan king, who speaks the question of conscience to the man of promise. Abram has no answer, and the narrator gives him not a word.
ch: The promise stands because God keeps it, not because Abram is perfect. It is God who acts in v. 17 to protect Sarai, the mother of the promise. St Augustine, answering critics in Against Faustus 22, argued that Abraham concealed the truth rather than told a lie, since Sarah was his close kinswoman (in substance). The Catechism’s own teaching on lying is clear (CCC 2482–2486), and we need not defend every act of the patriarchs in order to honour their faith.

r.h: The Son does what he sees the Father doing
set: This is the start of Jesus’ reply to the charge that he made himself equal to God (5:18). The discourse runs to the end of the chapter. It does not deny the charge, but it explains it: the Son’s equality with the Father is a total dependence and communion. These verses are one of the clearest places in the Gospels for the relation of Father and Son.
str: v. 19: the principle: the Son does nothing on his own, and whatever the Father does, the Son does.
v. 20: the reason: love, and “greater works”.
vv. 21–22: two works that belong to God alone: giving life and judging.
v. 23: the purpose: the same honour for the Son.
kw: A double amen, found only in John. Jesus uses it to open a solemn teaching, and he speaks it on his own authority.
In Jewish faith, to raise the dead belongs to God. Jesus says that the Son shares this work.
The word used for the honour given to God. In v. 23 the same honour is asked for the Son.
vv: the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing;

This does not mean that the Son is lesser. Only one who shares the Father’s life can do “whatever the Father does”. The image of a son learning his father’s trade may stand behind the verse, but the claim goes far beyond it.
just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.
The healing of the man at the pool was a sign of this. The “greater works” of v. 20 begin here and reach their end at the empty tomb.
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
No one can honour God rightly and put the Son aside: the verse says plainly that the two honours are one.
ch: The Church confesses the Son as “one in being with the Father” at the Council of Nicaea. St Augustine, preaching on this passage, taught that Father and Son do not do different works but the same works inseparably (Tractates on John 20; in substance). The Catechism teaches that the whole divine economy is the common work of the three divine persons (CCC 258), and that the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (CCC 679, quoting John 5:22).

qa: If “the Son can do nothing on his own”, how can he be equal to the Father?

The verse speaks of origin, not of rank. All that the Son has he receives from the Father, from eternity, and he receives all of it. Because of that he does “whatever the Father does” (5:19). This is what the Church means in the Creed by “God from God, Light from Light”.
study: When has fear made me plan as though God were not there? What did it cost those near me?
Jesus lives by looking at the Father. What daily practice in this Great Fast helps me to look at him?

lead: The Great Fast reaches its midpoint today, and the readings ask what we are choosing. Abram lets his nephew choose first, and Lot goes by what looks good to his eyes. In John, many disciples walk away from a hard teaching, and Peter answers for those who stay. Between these stand the capture of Ai in the second reading, a hard page of ancient war to be read in the light of Christ, and Paul’s word that salvation is for all who call on the Lord. At the middle of the road the question is simple: to whom shall we go?

set: Abram has come back from Egypt rich, and Lot has flocks of his own. The land cannot support them both, and their herders quarrel (13:5–7). The chapter says that the Canaanites and Perizzites were then living in the land, so this family quarrel takes place in full view of the neighbours.
The “Plain” is the region of the lower Jordan, which looks green from the hills near Bethel. The narrator adds a warning: all this was before Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed.
str: vv. 8–9: Abram’s proposal, and the choice given to Lot.
vv. 10–13: Lot looks, chooses and moves toward Sodom.
vv. 14–17: God tells Abram to look, and renews the promise.
v. 18: Abram moves to Mamre and builds an altar.
kw: A quarrel, sometimes a case at law. Exodus 17:7 uses the same word as a place name, Meribah, where the people quarrelled with God.
Literally “brothers”, though Lot is Abram’s nephew. Hebrew uses this word for close relatives. Abram’s argument is short: we are family.
The great trees near Hebron where Abraham will later receive three visitors (Genesis 18:1). Abram’s new home will be the place of that visit.
vv: Is not the whole land before you?
Abram is the elder and the one who received the promise, and he could have chosen first. He gives up that right because he knows that the land is God’s to give.
Lot looked about him, and saw that the plain of the Jordan was well watered everywhere like the garden of the Lord,

The words recall Eden, but the next phrase names Sodom. What looks like paradise may be the road to ruin. Lot does not sin in choosing, but he chooses only by what he sees, and soon he has moved “as far as Sodom” (v. 12).
Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are,
Lot raised his eyes for himself. Abram, having given way, is told by God to raise his. The one who let go of the choice is given more than he could have chosen.
ch: St John Chrysostom, preaching on Genesis, admires the humility of the elder who gives the choice to the younger (in substance). The passage prepares for the Lord’s word, “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), and “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9). The Catechism teaches that respect for persons and for the bonds between them belongs to the peace that the fifth commandment protects (CCC 2304).

set: Jesus has fed the five thousand and taught in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:59) that he is the bread of life: “the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh” (6:51), and “my flesh is true food” (6:55). The earlier listeners in the chapter were the crowd. Now it is his own disciples who find this too hard. John does not narrate the institution of the Eucharist at the Last Supper; this chapter does that work, and this is how it ends.
str: vv. 60–61: the disciples complain.
vv. 62–65: Jesus answers: the Son of Man’s ascent, spirit and flesh, the Father’s gift.
v. 66: many turn back.
vv. 67–69: the question to the Twelve, and Peter’s confession.
kw: Literally “hard”, like dry, rough ground. The word here means not that the teaching is hard to understand but that it is hard to accept.
To make someone stumble, from skandalon, a stumbling block.
Peter’s title for Jesus. The only other place the Gospels use it is on the lips of a demon (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34). It names the one set apart by God and belonging wholly to him.
vv: It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless.

This does not take back what Jesus has said about his flesh. “Flesh” here is human nature left to itself: human reasoning alone cannot receive this teaching. The Malayalam POC has “body” at this point. St Augustine explains that the flesh would be of no use if it were understood as meat sold in a market, but joined to the Spirit it gives life (Tractates on John 27; in substance).
Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.
Jesus does not run after them to soften his words. The reason John gives for their leaving is the teaching about the bread of life.
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
Peter does not say that he understands. He says that there is nowhere else to go. Sometimes that is what faith looks like at the midpoint of the road, and he says “we”, speaking for the Twelve.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage directly: the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them; the Eucharist and the Cross are stumbling blocks, and the Lord’s question, “Do you also wish to go away?”, sounds through the ages as an invitation to discover that only he has the words of eternal life (CCC 1336). Every reception of Holy Qurbana is an answer to it.

qa: Does “the flesh is useless” mean that the Eucharist is only a symbol?

No. Jesus has just said “my flesh is true food” (6:55), and the disciples leave because they understood him to mean it. Verse 63 contrasts “flesh”, human nature on its own, with the Spirit who gives life. The Church believes that Christ is truly, really and substantially present in the Eucharist (CCC 1374), and only the Spirit opens us to this faith.
rite: The midpoint of the Great Fast is marked in the calendar of the Syro-Malabar Church, and in some parishes the Cross is honoured today with special prayers, according to local custom. Today’s Gospel fits the day: halfway along the road, the Lord asks those who remain whether they too wish to go.
study: Where in my family or parish could I, like Abram, give up the first choice for the sake of peace?
Which teaching of Christ do I find hard? What would it mean to say, with Peter, “to whom can we go?”

lead: Family ties run through today’s two main readings. Abram gathers his household and goes to rescue Lot, the nephew who chose the better land for himself and has been carried off as a prisoner. In John, Jesus’ own “brothers” do not believe in him and urge him to show himself at the festival. Between them, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and reads the whole law to the people, and Paul asks, “has God rejected his people?”, and answers, “By no means!” God does not give up on those who are his, and neither does Abram.

set: Genesis 14 is unlike the chapters around it. It reads like an old war record: four kings from the east against five kings of the cities of the Plain. The rulers named have not been securely identified in other ancient sources, and scholars differ about the date of the chapter. Lot, who “settled among the cities of the Plain” (13:12), now lives in Sodom (14:12), and so he is caught up in its defeat.
The reading stops just before the best-known part of the chapter, when Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram (14:18–20).
str: vv. 8–10: the battle in the Valley of Siddim, and the flight.
vv. 11–12: Sodom is plundered, and Lot is taken.
v. 13: the news comes to “Abram the Hebrew”.
vv. 14–16: the pursuit by night, the victory, and everyone is brought back.
kw: This is the first use of the word in the Bible (14:13). Its origin is uncertain. In this story it marks Abram as an outsider in the land.
A word found only here in the Hebrew Bible. These are not a royal army but servants born in his household.

In vv. 14 and 16 the Hebrew calls Lot Abram’s “brother”, although v. 12 has told us that he is his brother’s son. The NRSV rightly says “nephew”. The POC has “brother” in v. 14 and “kinsman” in v. 16. See the question below.
vv: they also took Lot, the son of Abram’s brother, who lived in Sodom,
The narrator reminds us of the family bond and of the place. Lot’s choice in the last chapter has brought him to this.
When Abram heard that his nephew had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house,

Abram does not say that Lot deserves what has happened. He gave up the better land without a quarrel, and now he risks his life for the man who took it. The Epistle of Barnabas (9) saw a sign of Jesus and the Cross in the number of these men, 318, written in Greek letters (in substance); this is the kind of symbolic reading some early writers loved, and not the plain sense of the text.
and also brought back his nephew Lot with his goods,
Everything comes back, “the women and the people” as well. Abram takes nothing for himself, as he will tell the king of Sodom (14:22–23).
ch: The next verses of the chapter give the Church one of her oldest images of the Eucharist. The Catechism names Melchizedek as a figure of Christ’s priesthood (CCC 58), and sees in his offering of bread and wine a prefiguring of the Church’s own offering (CCC 1333; see also 1544). So the road of Abram’s rescue ends at a meal of bread and wine, which is a good thought for those who keep the Great Fast on the way to the Holy Qurbana of Easter.

r.h: My time has not yet come
set: The Festival of Booths (Hebrew Sukkot; Leviticus 23:33–43) was a joyful autumn pilgrimage. For seven days the people lived in shelters of branches, remembering the desert, and an eighth day closed the feast. Chapters 7–8 of John take place at this festival.

In v. 1 and v. 13 John’s “the Jews” cannot mean the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his brothers and the crowd are all Jews, and people go in fear of “the Jews” (v. 13). John means the authorities in Jerusalem who were hostile to him (see CCC 597).
str: vv. 1–2: Galilee, the danger in Judea, the festival near.
vv. 3–5: his brothers’ advice: “show yourself to the world”.
vv. 6–9: his reply: “My time has not yet come”.
vv. 10–13: he goes up in secret; the crowds are divided and afraid.
kw: Literally “the setting up of tents”. This is its only use in the New Testament.
The right moment. In vv. 6 and 8 Jesus uses this word, which elsewhere in John gives way to “hour” (hōra). The Malayalam POC has one word, samayam, for both.
A low muttering. It recalls the murmuring of Israel in the desert, the same setting that the festival remembers. Here the POC speaks of people saying many things in secret.
vv: (For not even his brothers believed in him.)
A sad note from the evangelist. Living close to Jesus does not by itself bring faith. On the word “brothers”, see the question below.
My time has not yet come,
His brothers are thinking of publicity, but Jesus lives by the Father’s timetable. “Your time is always here” means that they have nothing they must wait for from God.
Yet no one would speak openly about him for fear of the Jews.

The people are afraid of their leaders, not of their own people. On v. 8, “I am not going to this festival”, many ancient manuscripts have “not yet going”. The NRSV and the POC follow the shorter text. Either way, Jesus refuses to go at his brothers’ urging and for their purpose, and goes later at the Father’s time, “not publicly” (v. 10).
ch: St John’s Gospel keeps asking when and how Jesus will be shown to the world. The Catechism teaches that his “hour” comes at the Passion, when he gives the Spirit (CCC 729–730). For all the opposition reported here, the Church reads these chapters with care: there were believers and doubters among the leaders and among the people, and there was long-standing dispute about him (CCC 595–597).

qa: If Jesus had “brothers”, how can Mary be ever-virgin?

Hebrew and Aramaic have no separate common word for “cousin” or “kinsman”, and “brother” covers them. Today’s first reading is the clearest example: Lot is Abram’s nephew, and the Hebrew calls him his “brother” (14:14, 16). The Catechism cites this very passage when it explains that those called the brothers of Jesus are close relations (CCC 500, citing Genesis 13:8; 14:16). St Jerome made the same argument against Helvidius (in substance).
study: Is there a “Lot” in my family, someone who chose badly and needs my help, not my judgement?
What do I do when God’s timing is not the time I would like?

lead: At the centre of today’s readings stands one question: can God be trusted? Abram, still childless, is taken outside to look at the stars, and he believes. In John, the crowds argue about where Jesus comes from, and he tells them that he comes from the one who sent him. Beside these, the Gibeonites deceive Joshua in the second reading because the leaders “did not ask direction from the Lord”, and Paul ends his long reflection on Israel with praise, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable”. It is also a First Friday, when many families turn to the Heart of Jesus, in whom God’s faithfulness has a human face.

set: Years have passed since the first promise, and Abram has no child. By the custom of the time, a childless man’s heir might be a servant of his household, and Abram names Eliezer of Damascus (15:2). This is the first time in the story that Abram answers God, and his first words are a complaint. Many scholars think that the chapter joins two scenes: the promise of an heir (vv. 1–6) and the promise of the land (vv. 7–21).

The reading ends at v. 15, just before the climax, when a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch pass between the divided animals (15:17). Jeremiah 34:18 shows the meaning of such a rite: those who pass between the pieces accept the fate of the animals if they break their word.
str: v. 1: the vision: “Do not be afraid”.
vv. 2–3: Abram’s complaint.
vv. 4–5: the stars.
v. 6: Abram believes.
vv. 7–11: the land, and the animals prepared.
vv. 12–15: a deep sleep, and a word about slavery and return.
kw: From the same root as “amen”. It means to lean on, to hold firm. Abram rests his whole weight on God’s word.
To count, to credit as to an account. God treats this trust as the right relationship with him.
In the Old Testament this is faithfulness to a relationship. The POC has nīthīkaraṇam, “justification”, which already points to St Paul’s use of the verse.
vv: Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield;
The chapter opens with the words God so often speaks to those he calls. Abram has just come back from a war, and God himself will be his shield.
Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
God brings an old man out of his tent and gives him the night sky. Nothing has changed in Abram’s house, and nothing will for many years. The promise is all he has.
And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.

One of the great verses of the Bible. St Paul builds on it in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6. St James quotes it too, and adds that Abraham’s “faith was active along with his works” (James 2:22–23). Abraham’s faith is God’s gift, and by grace it bears fruit in obedience.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham thus fulfils the definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1 (CCC 146), and calls him the father of all who believe. Justification comes from God’s grace, and it is given to those who believe, and calls us to cooperate by faith and works of charity (CCC 1987–2005). Nostra Aetate 4 and CCC 839 remember that Israel is still loved by God for the sake of the patriarchs, as today’s epistle says.

set: Jesus has gone up in the middle of the festival and is teaching openly in the Temple (7:14). People from the city are surprised that the authorities do nothing. Their question shows a real belief of some Jews of the time, found in writings outside the Bible: that the Messiah would stay hidden until the moment of his appearing. Others held a different view, as later in the chapter some say that he must come from Bethlehem (7:42; Micah 5:2).
str: vv. 25–27: the people of Jerusalem wonder, and raise an objection.
vv. 28–29: Jesus cries out: “I have not come on my own”.
v. 30: an attempted arrest fails: his hour has not yet come.
v. 31: many believe.
kw: A loud, public cry, used also in 7:37 and 12:44. In John it marks a solemn word from Jesus.
In John this is the hour of the Cross and glory (see 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). Until it comes, no one can touch him.
John’s word for the miracles, which point beyond themselves to who Jesus is.
vv: Yet we know where this man is from; but when the Messiah comes, no one will know where he is from.
John loves this kind of irony. They know Nazareth, and they think that settles the matter. They do not know where he is really from. The reader, who has read John 1:1–18, does know.
I have not come on my own. But the one who sent me is true, and you do not know him.
This is what the discussion has been missing. The question is not his home town but the one who sent him.
but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.
His life is not in the hands of his enemies. He will give it when the time comes (see John 10:18). Only God sets that hour.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Son came down from heaven to do the will of the Father who sent him (CCC 606), and that the hour of Jesus is the hour when he passes to the Father and gives the Spirit (CCC 729–730). The Creed answers the question of the crowd: he is “God from God, begotten, not made”, and also a man of Nazareth, of the Virgin Mary.

study: What promise of God have I waited for so long that I have nearly stopped believing it? What would it mean to look at the stars again?
Do I think I know Jesus so well that I have stopped asking who he is?

lead: Saturday brings two readings about authority. Paul tells the Christians of Rome that governing authority comes from God and that good citizens obey it in conscience. In John, the temple police return without their prisoner, saying, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”, and the leaders argue among themselves. Read together, they set human authority in its place. It has real dignity, it answers to God, and it must itself listen before it judges, as Nicodemus reminds his colleagues.

set: Paul writes around AD 57 to a Church in the capital of the Empire, under the emperor Nero, before the persecution of AD 64. Some years earlier, Jews had been expelled from Rome under Claudius, Aquila and Priscilla among them (Acts 18:2). Many scholars think that Paul wants these Christians to live quietly and to give no reason for further trouble. Some also connect v. 7 with public anger over taxes at about this time.

This passage does not stand alone. Just before it Paul says “Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (12:17), and straight after it he says “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (13:8). It is part of what the life of love looks like in public.
str: vv. 1–2: the principle: authority comes from God.
vv. 3–4: the purpose: to reward good and to punish wrong.
v. 5: the motive: not only fear, but conscience.
vv. 6–7: the practical result: taxes, respect, honour.
kw: Literally to place oneself under, within an order. It is not the same as blind obedience. Paul uses it of keeping one’s place in an order God has given.
The right to act. In the Gospels Jesus has this authority from the Father, and he tells Pilate that Pilate’s authority was “given you from above” (John 19:11).
The word in v. 6, from which “liturgy” comes. Paul calls even the authorities who collect taxes ministers in God’s service, a striking way to set them under God.
vv: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities;
Paul speaks of “every person”, not only Christians. He rejects the idea that being in Christ puts believers above the law of the land.
for it is God’s servant for your good.

The authority is a servant, and its purpose is the common good. This sets a measure by which every government can be judged. The next phrase, about the sword, describes the Rome of Paul’s day. The Church today teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible (CCC 2267).
Therefore one must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.
Conscience is the deciding word. A person who obeys from conscience is able also to refuse when an order is evil, which is what Peter and the apostles did (Acts 5:29).
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches that authority is required by the moral order and comes from God (CCC 1897–1904, esp. 1899). It also draws from v. 7 the duty of citizens to pay taxes and to share in public life (CCC 2238–2240). And it adds the other side: a citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow orders contrary to the moral order, for “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29; CCC 2242). St Clement of Rome, in a time of danger, prayed for rulers that God would give them health and peace (1 Clement 61).

r.h: Never has anyone spoken like this
set: The police were sent to arrest Jesus during the festival (7:32), and he has just spoken of living water (7:37–39). They now return to the chief priests and Pharisees with empty hands. The scene shows division among those in authority. Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2), speaks up for a fair hearing here, and he will bring myrrh and aloes for Jesus’ burial (19:39).

Verse 53 begins the story of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the earliest manuscripts of John do not have. The Church receives the story as inspired Scripture, and the NRSV prints it in brackets.
str: vv. 45–46: the police return and explain.
vv. 47–49: the Pharisees’ angry reply.
vv. 50–51: Nicodemus appeals to the law.
v. 52: the retort about Galilee.
v. 53: each goes home.
kw: Temple attendants who worked under the chief priests. These men had authority to arrest, yet a few words left them unable to do it.
To lead astray. The same charge was heard in the crowd earlier (7:12). The irony is that the men sent to arrest him are accused of being fooled.
In v. 51, literally, “unless it first hears from him”. The law requires a hearing (see Deuteronomy 1:16–17). Those who will not listen cannot judge.
vv: Never has anyone spoken like this!
The police are not theologians and they offer no argument. They just report what they heard. The words of Jesus have done what weapons could not.
“Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing to find out what they are doing, does it?”

Nicodemus says “our law”. He speaks as a loyal Pharisee and uses the law to defend Jesus. He is not yet openly a disciple, but he has taken one brave step. That he is one of them shows that no group here can be judged all together.
Surely you are not also from Galilee, are you?

An insult, not an answer. The claim that no prophet comes from Galilee is what these speakers say in anger. Yet 2 Kings 14:25 says that Jonah came from Gath-hepher, a town in Galilee, and an early papyrus of John here reads “the prophet”, which would mean the one foretold by Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15).
ch: The Catechism draws from this passage the honest picture of the leaders of that time. Among the religious authorities of Jerusalem, the Pharisee Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were secret disciples of Jesus, and there was long-standing dissension about him (CCC 595). That is why the Church refuses to lay the responsibility for his death on the Jews as a people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). These harsh words about the crowd come from a few men in a moment of anger and are not the voice of Israel.

qa: Does Romans 13 mean that Christians must obey any government, whatever it does?

No. Paul describes authority as “God’s servant for your good” (13:4). Its right to be obeyed depends on that purpose. When a command goes against God’s law, the Christian must follow God first (Acts 5:29; CCC 2242). Revelation 13 shows the other face of an empire that demands what belongs only to God.
study: How do I speak of those who govern us? Do I pray for them, as well as criticize them?
Am I like Nicodemus, ready to ask for a fair hearing when others have already decided against someone?

lead: Water runs through this Sunday’s readings, and with it the question of who is seen and who is given a place. A runaway slave woman is found by a spring in the wilderness, and she gives God a name: the God who sees. The Gibeonites, spared because of an oath, become “drawers of water” at the altar of the Lord. Paul asks us to offer our whole lives as a living sacrifice, in one body where each has a gift. And on the great day of the festival, in a Temple bright with water and light, Jesus cries out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me”, and says, “I am the light of the world.” In the middle of the Great Fast, those who are thirsty and those on the margins are the ones to whom God comes first. The key words are seeing, serving and thirst.

r.h: Hagar and the God who sees
set: Ten years have passed in the land, and Sarai still has no child (16:3). She gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram, following a custom known in the ancient Near East, by which a slave’s child could count as her mistress’s. Hagar conceives and looks on Sarai with contempt (16:4), and Sarai turns on Abram (16:5). Our reading starts at the moment Abram hands the matter back.
The irony is sharp. An Egyptian slave is now oppressed by the family of Abram. Generations later, Hebrew slaves will be oppressed in Egypt, and God will hear them too.
str: v. 6: Abram yields; Sarai deals harshly; Hagar flees.
vv. 7–8: the angel finds her and asks two questions.
vv. 9–12: the command and the promises: many descendants, and a son named Ishmael.
vv. 13–14: Hagar names God, and the well is named.
vv. 15–16: the birth of Ishmael.
kw: The verb of v. 6, also used for the Egyptians’ oppression of Israel (Exodus 1:11–12). The related noun in v. 11 is translated “affliction”. God has noticed exactly what has been done to her.

This is the first time that the Bible mentions the angel of the Lord, and he comes to a slave. In v. 13 Hagar understands that it is the Lord himself who has spoken with her: in such passages the angel of the Lord and the Lord are very closely joined.

Usually taken to mean “God who sees” or “God of seeing”. The Hebrew of v. 13 is difficult, but Hagar’s amazement is clear. She is often noted as the only person in the Old Testament who gives God a name of her own.
“God hears.” The child’s name will be a lasting reminder that God heard a slave’s pain.
vv: Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she ran away from her.
Genesis does not hide this. The father and mother of the promise fail badly here, and Abram’s “do to her as you please” is a shameful word from the man of faith.
Hagar, slave-girl of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?

No one in this story has yet spoken to her or used her name. Abram and Sarai said only “my slave-girl” and “your slave-girl”. The angel calls her by name. The two questions are the questions of every person in the Great Fast.
for the Lord has given heed to your affliction.
God hears the prayer that was never spoken: the text gives no word of prayer from her. The POC has “your cry”, which brings out the same sense.
So she named the Lord who spoke to her, “You are El-roi”;
She has been treated as property, as someone not seen. Now she says: he sees me. The well is called Beer-lahai-roi, “the well of the Living One who sees me” (NRSV note).
ch: The Catechism counts the rescue of Hagar and her child among the works of the angels (CCC 332). It also teaches that the cry of the oppressed, of the foreigner, the widow and the orphan, is a cry that reaches heaven (CCC 1867), and that the Church’s love for the poor and the oppressed has a special place (CCC 2448). Slavery is condemned by the seventh commandment (CCC 2414). St Paul uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory in Galatians 4:21–31, about life under the law and life in Christ; he is making a point about the Christian life, not passing judgment on a people. Genesis itself shows God’s care for Ishmael, and the Church regards with esteem Muslims, who link their own faith to Abraham (Nostra Aetate 3).

set: Friday’s reading told how the people of Gibeon, a city only a few miles from Jerusalem, came in worn-out clothes with dry bread and pretended to be from far away. The leaders took them at their word and “did not ask direction from the Lord” (9:14). Deuteronomy 20:10–18 had distinguished between far cities and the cities of the land, and so they had every reason to lie.

Now the truth is out. Many scholars think that this story took shape, in part, to explain how a non-Israelite people came to live within Israel and to serve at its sanctuary. Whatever its history, it is a story about an oath that holds.
str: vv. 16–17: three days later the truth comes out, and the Israelites reach their cities.
vv. 18–21: the people grumble, and the leaders stand by the oath.
vv. 22–23: Joshua confronts the Gibeonites.
vv. 24–25: their answer: we were afraid.
vv. 26–27: they are saved, and they serve at the altar.
kw: The oath in the name of the Lord is what controls the whole passage. The word comes again and again in vv. 18–20.
Literally “one lifted up”, a chief of the congregation. These leaders made a mistake, and they now bear the anger of the people without breaking their word.
hewers of wood and drawers of water
Humble work, done also by aliens in Israel’s camp (Deuteronomy 29:11). Here it is given a new place: “for the altar of the Lord” (v. 27).
vv: But the Israelites did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the Lord, the God of Israel.

The oath was obtained by a trick, and the people want to break it. The leaders refuse. God’s name, once called on, cannot be used and then thrown away. Long afterwards, Saul’s violence against the Gibeonites was remembered as a great sin that brought famine (2 Samuel 21:1–2).
so we were in great fear for our lives because of you,
The Gibeonites speak with honesty at last, and their fear is that of ordinary people caught in a war. Like Rahab (Joshua 2:9–11), they have heard what God has done, and they want to live.
hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the Lord,

The harsh sentence has a strange result. The people under a curse are placed beside the altar, the holiest place. They stay close to God’s worship “to this day”. We should not defend what was unjust in the arrangement, but we can see God’s mercy working through it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that promises made to others in God’s name engage the divine honour, and that they must be respected in justice (CCC 2147, 2150). Psalm 15:4 praises those “who stand by their oath even to their hurt”. Origen, preaching on this chapter, took the Gibeonites as a warning to those who come into the Church and are content with minor tasks, and he urged his hearers to go further (Homilies on Joshua 10; in substance). For those who keep the Great Fast, the page has a gentler message too: whoever comes in fear and honesty to the house of God will find a place in it.

set: For eleven chapters Paul has spoken of what God has done: sin, grace, faith, the Spirit, the mystery of Israel. Chapter 11 ended in praise. Now comes “therefore” (12:1), and the letter turns to how we live. The moral life flows out of God’s mercies. Paul writes to a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles, and the call to one body in vv. 4–5 speaks directly to it.
str: vv. 1–2: the foundation: our whole life is worship, and our minds are renewed.
v. 3: sober judgement about oneself.
vv. 4–5: one body, many members.
vv. 6–8: different gifts.
vv. 9–11: love without pretence.
kw: Paul’s appeal is made “by the mercies of God”: he does not command by fear but appeals to what we have received.
The Temple’s sacrifices were put to death. Here the offering stays alive and goes on giving itself each day. “Bodies” means the whole person, in concrete daily life.
Logikē can mean reasonable or spiritual, and latreia means worship. It is the worship that fits people endowed with reason, who offer themselves willingly and knowingly.
The same verb used for the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2; Mark 9:2). The form means an ongoing change that God brings about in us.
From charis, grace. A gift in the Church is a share of grace, given for others.
vv: to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God,
Fasting belongs here: the body takes part in worship. Paul’s words about sacrifice do not take the place of the Church’s offering at the altar. They flow from it and return to it.
but be transformed by the renewing of your minds,
Change begins in the way we think, not only in what we do. Without this we simply take the shape of the age around us.
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another.
Not only members of Christ, but members of each other. No one in the Church can say that the others do not concern him.
Let love be genuine;
The Greek says “without hypocrisy”, without a mask. After speaking of gifts, Paul goes straight to love, as he does in 1 Corinthians 12–13.
ch: The Catechism quotes this very verse when it teaches that the moral life is spiritual worship, nourished in the liturgy and the sacraments (CCC 2031). Romans 12–15 is among the great moral catechesis of the apostles (CCC 1971). The Second Vatican Council quotes v. 1 when speaking of the common priesthood of all the baptized (Lumen Gentium 10). St Augustine, in The City of God 10.6, draws together this chapter and the altar: the whole redeemed community is offered to God as one sacrifice through Christ, and this is what the Church celebrates in the Sacrament of the altar (in substance). In the Eucharist the lives of the faithful are joined to Christ’s one offering (CCC 1368).

r.h: Living water and the light of the world
set: John has been following Jesus at the Festival of Booths. The Mishnah, a later collection of Jewish tradition, describes two rites of the feast. Each morning a priest brought water in procession from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar. And in the Court of the Women great lamps were lit, so that the whole city was bright (Sukkah 4–5). Zechariah 14 had joined the feast of Booths to living waters and a day without night (14:7–8, 16). Jesus speaks into that setting.
“The treasury” (8:20) was in the Court of the Women, near where those lamps stood. The reading skips 7:40–8:11, including the story of the woman taken in adultery, and joins the two sayings directly.
str: 7:37–38: the cry on the great day: come and drink.
7:39: John’s explanation: this is about the Spirit.
8:12: “I am the light of the world”.
8:13–18: the dispute about testimony.
8:19–20: “Where is your Father?”, and the hour that has not yet come.
kw: In ordinary speech this means running water, from a spring, not from a cistern. The same phrase means water that gives life. John likes such double meanings (see John 4:10).
The form of the great sayings of Jesus in John. It echoes the name God reveals in Exodus 3:14 and God’s own speech in Isaiah.
A theme of John from the first page (1:4–5; 3:19). The “pillar of fire” also led Israel at night in the desert (Exodus 13:21), and the feast remembers that journey.
Legal language runs through the passage: witness, judgment, validity. Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two witnesses. Jesus names his two: himself and the Father.
vv: Let anyone who is thirsty come to me,
Jesus stands up, though teachers usually sat, and he cries out at the height of the festival. He does not offer the crowd a new rite: he offers himself.
Out of the believer’s heart shall flow rivers of living water.

No one verse of the Old Testament says exactly this; compare Isaiah 12:3, Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8. The Greek says “out of his inner being” (literally “belly”) without saying whose, and the ancient texts had no punctuation to settle it. Many Greek Fathers, with the NRSV and the POC, read it as the believer. Some Western writers read it as Christ, whose heart is the source. Both are true: the water comes from him and through him flows to others.
Now he said this about the Spirit, which believers in him were to receive;
John says that the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified. He is not saying that the Spirit did not exist. The promise is kept at the Cross and at Easter (19:34; 20:22).
I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.
“Follows” is the word for discipleship and also for walking behind the pillar in the desert. The lamps of the feast shone only for its few nights; this light does not go out.
If you knew me, you would know my Father also.

The argument about witnesses ends here. To know the Son is the way to the Father. This is said to those Jesus is debating with, within a discussion among Jews about the law they all honour. His “your law” (8:17) does not mean that he stands outside it: he is showing what they themselves accept.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Spirit is “the living water” welling up from Christ crucified as its source and from him springing up in us for eternal life (CCC 694; see 1137). It names Jesus as the light of the world in whom the whole of God’s truth is made known (CCC 2466). Vatican II opens its great Constitution on the Church with the same image: Christ is the light of the nations (Lumen Gentium 1). St Augustine preached on these verses at length, and he taught that the Spirit was to be given in a new way after Christ’s glorification, not that he was absent before (Tractates on John 32; in substance).

qa: Why does the angel send Hagar back to a mistress who has mistreated her?

This is a hard verse, and we should not hide it. The text does not approve of slavery, and the Church teaches that enslaving human beings is a grave wrong (CCC 2414). Within the story, returning means that her child will be born in Abram’s house and so will be recognized as his son (16:15). The promise given to her is her own, and it comes directly from God. Later God will care for Hagar and Ishmael again, in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17–20).
Does God accept an oath that was gained by a lie?

Joshua 9 is not a lesson in the law of contracts. It shows ancient Israel’s deep respect for a promise made in God’s name. Today the Church would ask whether a promise obtained by fraud binds at all. The lasting point is that God’s name must never be used lightly (CCC 2147–2150).
What does “there was no Spirit” mean, when the Spirit is already in the Old Testament?

The Holy Spirit is eternal God and was at work in creation and in the prophets (CCC 702). John means that the outpouring on all believers, which the prophets promised, was not yet given. It comes when Jesus is glorified (CCC 729–730).
rite: The Syro-Malabar faithful fast through these weeks of the East Syriac year and gather on Sunday for the Holy Qurbana, on the road toward the Pasch. Hagar’s spring, the altar of Joshua 9, Paul’s living sacrifice and the rivers of John 7 all meet there: the thirsty come, those on the edge find a place, and our lives are offered with Christ’s one offering. Water, oil and light in the sacraments of the Church also speak of the same gift of the Spirit that Jesus promised at the festival.
study: Hagar says, “You are El-roi”. Who in my parish or neighbourhood feels unseen? What can I do so that they know God sees them?
The Gibeonites served near the altar. How do I look on the small, hidden tasks in the Church? Do I do them with love?
Romans 12:1 speaks of a living sacrifice. What part of my body or my daily time have I not yet offered to God in this Great Fast?
What am I thirsty for? What would it mean this week to come to Christ and drink?

lead: Both readings ask what we are really holding on to. Colossians warns against people who make food, festivals and visions the measure of a believer, and it answers that all these are a shadow, while the substance belongs to Christ. In Luke a good man has kept the commandments from his youth and still lacks one thing, because his wealth holds him. For the Great Fast the lesson is close to home: the fast is not the goal. It clears the hands so that they can hold on to Christ.

set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13). The community heard the Gospel from Epaphras (1:7), and the letter suggests that Paul had not met them in person (2:1). Teachers there were pressing rules about food and holy days, with talk of visions and angels (2:8, 16–23). Exactly what they taught is still discussed, since we know it only from this letter. The letter names Paul as its author. Many scholars think that a close disciple wrote it in his name, while others hold to Paul himself. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case.
str: v. 16: the warning: let no one condemn you over food and holy days.
v. 17: the reason: shadow and substance.
v. 18: the rival teachers: self-abasement, angels, visions.
v. 19: what they have lost: the head, from whom the whole body grows.
kw: A shadow is real, and it is cast by something. The Letter to the Hebrews uses the same word for the law (Hebrews 10:1). The word does not sneer at Israel’s feasts. It says that they point beyond themselves.

The NRSV has “substance”. The Greek word is “body”, and in the ancient world shadow and body were a natural pair. It may also carry a second sense here, since two verses later the Church is called the body whose head is Christ.
The source of the body’s life and growth. The rival teachers looked up to angels and left aside the one to whom everything belongs.
vv: Therefore do not let anyone condemn you in matters of food and drink or of observing festivals, new moons, or sabbaths.
This verse does not forbid fasting or feasts, which the Church herself keeps. It refuses to let anyone make these things the test of whether a person truly belongs to Christ.
These are only a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
The feasts of Israel were God’s gift, and they prepared for what was to come. In Christ the reality has arrived. Our own fasting is of the same kind: a good and needed practice that serves him.
and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows with a growth that is from God.
The picture is taken from the human body. Growth in holiness does not come from private visions. It comes from staying joined to Christ together with the rest of his body, the Church.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the head of the Church and that he provides for the growth of his body (CCC 792–794). It also says that Sunday fulfils the spiritual truth of the Jewish sabbath (CCC 2175). The Church has not stopped fasting because of this reading: Scripture and the Fathers insist on fasting, prayer and almsgiving as forms of inner conversion (CCC 1434). Their value lies in the turning of the heart.

set: Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem (9:51). Just before this he has said that the kingdom must be received like a little child (18:15–17). Now a man of standing comes with a good question. Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell the story: Matthew calls him young (Matthew 19:20), Mark adds that Jesus looked at him and “loved him” (Mark 10:21), and only Luke calls him a ruler. Just after our reading, the listeners ask who then can be saved, and Jesus replies, “What is impossible for mortals is possible for God” (18:27).
str: v. 18: the question about eternal life.
v. 19: “No one is good but God alone.”
vv. 20–21: the commandments, and the man’s honest answer.
v. 22: the one thing lacking: sell, give, come, follow.
v. 23: his sadness.
vv. 24–25: the saying about the rich and the camel.
kw: A person with authority or high standing. Luke does not say over what. Position, goodness and wealth are all in his hands, and still he asks.
Jesus does not deny the man’s obedience. What is lacking is not one more rule. It is the step of leaving his security to follow a person.
The man does not get angry and does not argue. He is grieved, because he is hearing the truth about himself.
vv: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?

Pope St John Paul II builds the first chapter of Veritatis Splendor on this story (in Matthew’s form) and sees in this man everyone who asks about the meaning of life (Veritatis Splendor 7, in substance).
No one is good but God alone.

Jesus is not denying his own goodness. He is turning the man’s eyes to the source of all goodness. To ask about the good is finally to turn toward God (Veritatis Splendor 9, in substance). The reader who knows who Jesus is sees more in this sentence than the man could.
There is still one thing lacking. Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.
Luke’s wording has “all”. The poor gain from this, but the point of the verse is its last word: follow. The giving clears the way for the following.
it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle

This is a deliberate overstatement: the largest animal in the land and one of the smallest openings. A story about a small gate in Jerusalem called the “Needle’s Eye” is often told, but it has no support in ancient sources. The saying is meant to sound impossible, and that is why the next verses speak of what God can do.
ch: The Catechism says that this second call does not cancel the first: following Christ includes keeping the commandments (CCC 2053), and Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544). Hearing the same call in Matthew’s words, St Antony of Egypt gave away his land and went into the desert (St Athanasius, Life of Antony 2). Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole work on this passage, Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, arguing that what must go above all is the grip of possessions on the soul (in substance).

qa: Must every Christian sell everything?

Not everyone in the same outward way. The Church sees in this call the root of the evangelical counsels, which some are called to live literally (CCC 915), and teaches that all the faithful are called to perfection of charity, each in their own state (CCC 2013). But no one is excused from the question. All are to direct their hearts so that attachment to riches does not get in the way of love (CCC 2545), and love for the poor is a duty for all (CCC 2443–2447).
study: What holds me back from following most closely: a possession, a position, or a good reputation?
Which of my religious habits have I begun to treat as the goal rather than as a way to Christ?

lead: Today the Great Fast turns to its other hand, almsgiving. Paul tells the Corinthians that their gift for the poor of Jerusalem is a sowing that God himself will multiply, a service that ends in thanksgiving. In Luke a Samaritan stops on the road, and at his own cost he cares for a wounded stranger. The two readings together say that mercy is not an extra. It comes from God’s own giving, and it becomes praise of him.

r.h: A service that ends in thanksgiving
set: Chapters 8–9 of this letter concern the collection Paul was gathering among his Gentile communities for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (see Galatians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; Romans 15:25–28). To him it was more than relief. It was a sign that Jewish and Gentile believers belong to one Church. He writes from Macedonia (2:13; 7:5), probably about AD 55–56, and he urges the Corinthians to complete what they began a year earlier (8:10). Our verses close the appeal.
str: v. 10: God gives the seed, and he multiplies the harvest.
v. 11: generosity produces thanksgiving.
vv. 12–13: the service meets needs and also glorifies God.
v. 14: those who receive will pray for those who give.
v. 15: the cry of thanks for God’s own gift.
kw: The word of v. 12, from which “liturgy” comes. In Greek cities it meant a public service carried out at one’s own expense, and in the Greek Old Testament it was used for the worship of the Temple. Paul uses it here for a collection of money.
The word of v. 13, and the same word used for communion in the body and blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16). Sharing money and sharing the altar are not two separate matters for Paul.
Found only here in the New Testament. It means what cannot be fully told. Many commentators take the gift of v. 15 to be Christ himself, or the grace given in him.
vv: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
Paul’s words echo Isaiah 55:10 and Hosea 10:12. The giver is not losing anything of his own. He is passing on seed that God supplied, and God remains the farmer.
for the rendering of this ministry not only supplies the needs of the saints but also overflows with many thanksgivings to God.
This is the movement of the whole passage: gift, relief, thanks. Almsgiving does not stop with the person who is helped. It goes on and comes home to God.
Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

Paul has been speaking of what the Corinthians will give, and he ends with what God has given. Earlier he said why: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (8:9). All Christian giving is a reply.
ch: The Catechism says that from the very beginning Christians brought, together with the bread and wine for the Eucharist, gifts to share with those in need, and it links this custom to the example of Christ who became poor to make us rich (CCC 1351). Giving alms to the poor is one of the chief witnesses of fraternal love and is also a work of justice pleasing to God (CCC 2447).

set: The reading is the second half of a parable. A lawyer has asked, “And who is my neighbor?” (10:29). Jesus tells of a man robbed and left half dead on the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho, a steep and lonely way. A priest and a Levite pass by. The parable gives no reason, and it is no attack on Judaism or on the law: both the question and the commandment of love come from Israel’s own Scripture (Leviticus 19:18). Then the surprise comes. Relations between Jews and Samaritans were bitter (John 4:9), and a Samaritan village has just refused Jesus (Luke 9:52–53). The hero of the story is a man the listeners would not have expected.
str: v. 33: the Samaritan comes, sees and is moved.
vv. 34–35: what he does: a chain of plain actions, and a promise to pay more.
v. 36: Jesus’ question, which turns the lawyer’s question around.
v. 37: the lawyer’s answer, and the command.
kw: Literally to be moved in one’s inner parts. Luke uses this verb also of Jesus before the widow of Nain (7:13) and of the father who sees his son returning (15:20). The Samaritan feels what God feels.
Literally “one who is near”. The lawyer asks whom he must count as near. Jesus asks who came near.
The word in the lawyer’s reply. It is mercy that acts, and the word Greek-speaking Jews used for God’s covenant love in the Psalms.
vv: But a Samaritan while traveling came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with pity.
The priest and the Levite also saw (10:31–32). Seeing is the same in all three. The difference comes in what happens inside, and then in the feet.
The next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper,
One denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). He does not simply offer first aid. He stays, he pays, and he promises to come back. Mercy takes time and costs money.
Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?
The lawyer wanted a limit: who counts as my neighbour? Jesus changes the question: whose neighbour can I become?
Go and do likewise.
The lawyer began by asking what he must do to inherit eternal life (10:25). Here is the answer, and it is a command for the road.
ch: Origen (Homilies on Luke 34) and St Augustine read the parable as the story of salvation: the wounded man is Adam, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the Church (in substance). This reading does not replace the plain command. Together they show that we can show mercy because we were shown mercy first. The Catechism draws from it the duty to make ourselves neighbours to others (CCC 1932). Pope Benedict XVI calls the parable a standard that requires universal love toward the needy we meet “by chance” (Deus Caritas Est 25), and Pope Francis gives it a whole chapter in Fratelli Tutti (chapter 2).

qa: Is it enough to give money, or must I also go myself?

The Samaritan does both, and each fits its time. He uses his own hands first, and then pays the innkeeper to continue the care he cannot give himself. The Church needs both the personal act and the organized work of charity (Deus Caritas Est 20, 31). Money sent is true help. A gift that never lets us see the wounded person, however, can leave the heart unchanged.
study: What has been my almsgiving in this Great Fast? Whom has it reached, and has it ended in thanks?
Whom do I pass on the other side of the road? Whose neighbour could I become this week?

lead: Today’s two readings stand side by side like hard and tender hands, and they meet at one point: judgment belongs to God. Jude uses fierce images against false teachers, yet he recalls that even the archangel Michael would not pronounce sentence, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” In John a crowd of accusers holds stones, and Jesus, the one person with the right to condemn, does not condemn, and sends the woman away to sin no more. Neither reading makes sin small. Both take the verdict out of our hands.

set: This short letter calls its author “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). Many identify him with the Jude named among the Lord’s relatives (Mark 6:3), while other scholars think that a later disciple wrote in his name. Its date is uncertain. The letter warns against intruders who “pervert the grace of our God into licentiousness” (v. 4). Jude writes as a Jewish Christian steeped in Scripture and in Jewish tradition, and he even quotes the book of Enoch (vv. 14–15). Many scholars think that 2 Peter 2 draws on this passage.
str: v. 8: three charges: they defile the flesh, reject authority, slander the glorious ones.
v. 9: the contrast: even Michael would not slander.
v. 10: they slander what they do not understand.
v. 11: three examples from Scripture: Cain, Balaam, Korah.
vv. 12–13: pictures from nature: clouds, trees, waves, stars.
kw: People who appeal to their own dreams or visions as authority. This may also suggest that they are living in a kind of sleep, cut off from reality.
The word of vv. 8–10. It is the chief charge in this passage. The “glorious ones” of v. 8 are most probably angels.

The NRSV of v. 12 has “blemishes”. The Greek word can also mean rocks hidden under the water, on which a ship is wrecked. Either sense fits. Such people spoil the love-feast, or they wreck those sitting beside them.
vv: But when the archangel Michael contended with the devil and disputed about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a condemnation of slander against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!”

This dispute is not told in the Old Testament. Early Christian writers such as Origen traced it to a Jewish writing about the end of Moses’ life, whose relevant part is now lost. The words themselves come from Zechariah 3:2. Even the prince of the angels leaves the sentence to God.
Woe to them! For they go the way of Cain, and abandon themselves to Balaam’s error for the sake of gain, and perish in Korah’s rebellion.
Three old warnings: Cain the murderer (Genesis 4), Balaam who, in Jewish tradition, was led by gain (Numbers 22; see 31:16), and Korah who rose against those God had set in authority (Numbers 16).
They are waterless clouds carried along by the winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted;

Clouds that promise rain and bring none, trees with nothing on them at harvest time. The danger is the appearance of life without its fruit. A season of fasting asks whether our religion gives what it promises. The Malayalam POC does not have the phrase “twice dead”.
ch: Jude’s anger is a pastor’s anger for a flock in danger, and the letter also says, “have mercy on some who are wavering” (v. 22). The Catechism names rash judgment, detraction and calumny as sins against the truth (CCC 2477), and it asks us to take our neighbour’s words and deeds in a good sense as far as we can (CCC 2478). In the first letter to the Corinthians Paul also speaks of abuses at the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17–22): the table of love can be damaged from the inside.

set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple. Those who bring the woman are “the scribes and the Pharisees” (v. 3): a particular group on a particular morning, and not the Jewish people. They are using her to trap him. If he says to let her go, he sets aside the law of Moses. If he says to stone her, he gives up his mercy and perhaps offends the Roman power, which many scholars think had kept the death penalty to itself (see John 18:31). The law they quote names both the man and the woman (Deuteronomy 22:22). The man is not there.

A note on the text. This passage is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts of John and from the earliest Syriac versions, and some later manuscripts place it elsewhere, one group after Luke 21:38. Many scholars therefore think that it was a very old story that entered the Gospel later. The Catholic Church receives it as inspired Scripture: St Jerome kept it in the Vulgate, and the Council of Trent received the sacred books “with all their parts”.
str: vv. 1–2: dawn in the Temple, and Jesus teaching.
vv. 3–6a: the woman, the law, the trap.
vv. 6b–8: he writes, he speaks one sentence, he writes again.
v. 9: the accusers leave, beginning with the elders.
vv. 10–11: Jesus and the woman alone.
kw: The same word the Gospels use for the devil’s temptation of Jesus. The question is a trap, and the woman is only the bait.
Found only here in the New Testament. Jesus does not repeal the law. He asks who is fit to carry out its sentence.
It occurs twice at the end of the passage. No one has condemned her, and the only sinless person present will not either.
vv: Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.

The Gospel does not say what he wrote, and we should not claim to know. St Jerome reports the view that he wrote the sins of the accusers (Against the Pelagians 2.17, in substance). Others recall Jeremiah 17:13, where the Hebrew says that those who turn away from the Lord are written in the earth, or the finger of God writing the law (Exodus 31:18). The action itself turns the eyes of the crowd away from the woman.
Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.

Under the law the witnesses threw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). This sentence turns the accusers’ attention to their own lives. Jesus does not call the adultery a small thing. He does not let anyone else’s sin become a place to hide from one’s own.
Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.
Both halves belong together. Mercy comes first, and the call to change is its fruit. Jesus does not say that she did nothing wrong. He says that she has a future.
ch: St Augustine sums up the scene: when the others had left, two remained, “the wretched woman and Mercy” (Tractates on John 33, in substance). Pope Francis took those words as the title of his letter Misericordia et Misera (2016), which opens with this scene. The Catechism says that the Gospel is the revelation in Jesus Christ of God’s mercy to sinners (CCC 1846). It also teaches that adultery is a grave wrong against the marriage covenant (CCC 2380–2381). Both are true in this passage, and both are true in the sacrament of Reconciliation.

qa: If this passage was not in the oldest manuscripts, is it truly the word of God?

Yes. A passage’s place in the canon does not depend on its being in the earliest copies we happen to have, and the Church received this story as Scripture long ago. A note about manuscripts tells us something about how the text came to us, and the story has every mark of the mercy of Jesus. That is why NRSV prints it in double brackets, and why the Church goes on proclaiming it.
study: When did I last pick up a stone against someone, in speech or in my thoughts? What would it mean to put it down?
“From now on do not sin again.” What particular change is the Lord asking of me in my next confession?

lead: Today’s readings speak of training and of the road. 1 Timothy tells a young pastor that training in godliness is worth more than any athlete’s effort, and that we toil because our hope is set on the living God. In Luke, Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them plainly what waits in Jerusalem, and they understand nothing. The Great Fast is a training for that road. We are close enough now to Hosanna Sunday to hear the words again and to ask whether we understand them.

set: The First Letter to Timothy is one of the three Pastoral Letters, addressed to a co-worker of Paul who is leading a community at Ephesus (1:3). The letter names Paul as its author. Many scholars think that a disciple wrote it some time after his death, while others hold to Paul himself or to Paul working through a secretary. It is inspired Scripture in either case.

Just before our reading the author warns against teachers who “forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods” (4:3), since “everything created by God is good” (4:4). That explains the balance here. The Christian discipline he praises is not contempt for the body or for God’s creation.
str: v. 6: what makes a good servant of Christ: being nourished on sound teaching.
v. 7: what to avoid and what to pursue.
v. 8: bodily training and godliness compared.
vv. 9–10: a sure saying, and the reason for all the toil.
kw: The word gives us “gymnasium”, a place every Greek town knew. Paul’s letters use athletic pictures (1 Corinthians 9:24–27). Holiness needs daily practice.
A favourite word of the Pastoral Letters. It means a whole way of life marked by reverence for God. The Malayalam POC renders it “ദൈവഭക്തി” and “ആത്മീയത”.
A formula found five times in the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). It marks a saying that the community already holds firmly.
vv: Have nothing to do with profane myths and old wives’ tales.

“Old wives’ tales” was a common Greek phrase of the time for foolish stories. The author means empty speculation, and his target is not older women, whom he honours (5:2). Those who feed the community need to know what they are feeding it.
for, while physical training is of some value, godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for both the present life and the life to come.
He does not despise the body’s training: it has some value. Our fasting also trains the body, and it does so for a further purpose. Godliness reaches beyond the grave.
For to this end we toil and struggle, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.

The whole effort stands on hope, and that hope is in a living God. “All people” agrees with 2:4: God “desires everyone to be saved”. Believers know this and have already received it in a special way. The verse does not say that all will be saved without conversion.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross, and that spiritual progress entails ascesis and mortification (CCC 2015). It also quotes 1 Timothy 2:4 to ground the Church’s mission (CCC 851). For pastors, the Second Vatican Council names proclaiming the Gospel as the first duty of priests (Presbyterorum Ordinis 4), which is what this reading means by being “nourished on the words of the faith”.

r.h: We are going up to Jerusalem
set: Luke’s long journey to Jerusalem began at 9:51. This is the third of his main announcements of the Passion (see 9:22; 9:44), and Matthew and Mark give it also (Matthew 20:17–19; Mark 10:32–34). Luke makes two additions of his own: all that the prophets wrote will be fulfilled, and the Twelve fail to understand. Next comes the blind man near Jericho, who sees (18:35–43). The placing is surely deliberate.
str: v. 31: the Twelve taken aside: Jerusalem, and what the prophets wrote.
v. 32: handed over; mocked, insulted, spat upon.
v. 33: flogged, killed, and on the third day raised.
v. 34: three statements that they did not understand.
kw: to accomplish, to bring to its end
The word of v. 31. The Passion is not a sudden disaster. It brings God’s plan to its goal. Jesus will say from the Cross in John’s Gospel, “It is finished”, from the same root (John 19:30).

A word that keeps returning in the Passion story. Humans do the handing over, and behind it stands the plan of God. Luke speaks here only of the Gentiles and does not lay this on any people as a whole.
The saying “was hidden from them” (v. 34). It does not say by whom. The veil is lifted only by the risen Lord (24:25–27, 44–46).
vv: See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.

One may think here of the Servant who did not hide his face “from insult and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). The same point is made on Easter day: “Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things and then enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26).
and on the third day he will rise again.
Every announcement ends here. The Passion is never told apart from the Resurrection, and the Great Fast should not be either.
But they understood nothing about all these things; in fact, what he said was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.

Luke says it three ways. Peter has already confessed him as Messiah (9:20), and still a suffering Messiah makes no sense to them. They walk on with him anyway. That is an encouragement for anyone who follows without understanding everything.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem knowing that he would die there (CCC 557). The Church remains faithful to the reading of “all the Scriptures” that Jesus himself gave, before and after his Passover (CCC 572), and the Resurrection fulfils both the promises of the Old Testament and those of Jesus himself (CCC 652). The Catechism also forbids laying the Passion on the Jewish people as a whole: all sinners were its authors (CCC 597–598).

study: Where in my life do I keep walking with the Lord without yet understanding?
What is my daily training in godliness? What in this Great Fast has really become a habit?

lead: Four readings on this Friday of the Fast, and the thread that runs through them is God’s promise and those who live by it. At Mamre the Lord comes as a guest and promises a son to Abraham and Sarah in their old age. Caleb at eighty-five asks for the hill country God promised him forty-five years before. Paul tells us that the night is far gone, so we are to put on Christ. And in the Temple Jesus says that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and then: “before Abraham was, I am.” The one who promised and the one who was promised meet in that sentence.

set: God has promised Abraham descendants (Genesis 12; 15; 17), and years have passed. Abraham is an old man and Sarah is past the age of bearing. Abraham has settled by the oaks of Mamre, near Hebron (13:18). Hospitality to a passing stranger was a sacred duty among the peoples of the desert and is still honoured there today. The narrator tells us at once that it is the Lord who appears, but Abraham sees only three men.
str: vv. 1–2: the Lord appears; three men; Abraham runs.
vv. 3–8: the invitation and the meal: “a little bread” becomes a feast.
vv. 9–10: the promise: a son.
vv. 11–12: Sarah laughs.
vv. 13–14: “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?”
kw: The root of the name Isaac (yiṣḥāq, “he laughs”). Sarah’s laugh of doubt here will become a laugh of joy (Genesis 21:6). The child’s name carries both.
