The word of v. 14. It means something beyond human power, and the same root describes God’s wonders in the Exodus. The Malayalam POC gives the sense: is there anything the Lord cannot do?
An appointed time, as in “tent of meeting”. God keeps his own calendar, and he keeps it faithfully.
vv: He looked up and saw three men standing near him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent entrance to meet them, and bowed down to the ground.

An old man, in the heat of the day, runs. Again and again in these verses he runs or hastens (vv. 2, 6, 7). He offers “a little bread” (v. 5), and then gives three measures of the best flour, a calf, curds and milk. His guests receive far more than he said.
So Sarah laughed to herself,
She is not condemned for her laugh, though the Lord asks about it. God’s promise has met her long disappointment. Anyone who has stopped hoping will understand her.
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
The angel gives the same answer to Mary: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). The story of the Bible’s old mother prepares for the story of its young one.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham’s remarkable hospitality at Mamre foreshadows the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571). The Letter to the Hebrews has this scene in mind: “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). The Fathers read the three guests in various ways. St Justin saw the Word of God in one of them (Dialogue with Trypho 56, in substance), and St Augustine saw a hint of the equality of the Trinity, since Abraham addresses three as one (On the Trinity 2, in substance). This reading of it is best known from the icon of St Andrei Rublev.

set: The land is being divided among the tribes (Joshua 13–21). Forty-five years before, at Kadesh-barnea, twelve men went to spy out the land. Ten discouraged the people, and only Caleb and Joshua urged them on (Numbers 13–14). God then said: “my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me wholeheartedly” will enter the land (Numbers 14:24). Caleb is called a Kenizzite (14:6), of a clan linked with Edom (Genesis 36:11), yet he stands among the leaders of Judah. Many scholars think that the book took shape long after the events and has a religious purpose in telling them; these matters remain under discussion.
str: v. 5: the land is allotted as commanded.
v. 6: Caleb comes to Joshua and recalls God’s word.
vv. 7–9: the story of Kadesh, and Moses’ oath.
vv. 10–11: forty-five years later, still strong.
v. 12: his request: the hard country, where the Anakim live.
kw: Literally “filled after the Lord”. It comes in vv. 8 and 9, and again in v. 14, like a title for Caleb’s life.
A share that comes as a gift and stays in the family. The land is never simply taken: it is received.
The word of v. 12. Caleb does not presume on God. An old soldier who has trusted for decades can say “perhaps” and still march.
vv: yet I wholeheartedly followed the Lord my God.
He says this without boasting, since he is claiming a word already given by God. Everyone else’s fear did not become his.
I am still as strong today as I was on the day that Moses sent me;

Scripture sees this as the Lord’s gift: “The Lord gave Caleb strength, which remained with him in his old age” (Sirach 46:9). It is a word for older people in our parishes, whose faith often carries everyone else.
So now give me this hill country

At eighty-five he does not ask for the easy valley. He asks for the place that frightened the others forty-five years earlier. For the Church’s reading, this is about the courage of faith. The conquest itself belongs to a violent age and is read in the light of Christ (see Dei Verbum 15).
ch: Sirach praises Caleb so that “all the Israelites might see how good it is to follow the Lord” (Sirach 46:10), and 1 Maccabees 2:56 recalls that he received his inheritance because he testified in the assembly. The Church finds in him the virtue of perseverance: the Catechism teaches that hope sustains us in the time of waiting and keeps us from discouragement (CCC 1818).

set: Paul writes to Rome, probably from Corinth, around AD 57. From chapter 12 he has been drawing out how the mercies of God shape daily life. Just before this he has said to pay to all what is due, taxes included (13:7). That gives him the word for the next verse: owe no one anything, except love. Then he lifts his eyes from the debt to the clock: what time is it?
str: vv. 8–10: the one debt that is never paid off: love fulfils the law.
vv. 11–12a: the time: wake up, for the day is near.
vv. 12b–13: take off the deeds of the night, and walk as in the day.
v. 14: put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
kw: Love is the fullness of the law (v. 10). It does not cancel the commandments he has just listed. It is what they were always for.
Not time by the clock, but the time of decision. Paul’s word to all who feel that there is always tomorrow.

The word for putting on clothes. Paul uses it of baptism: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27). The “armor” of v. 12 is the same act, for the same day.
vv: Owe no one anything, except to love one another;

Other debts can be cleared. This one grows the more it is paid. St Paul’s line of thought does not abolish the law: the commandments he cites come from Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, and their summary from Leviticus 19:18.
the night is far gone, the day is near.
The picture is of the hour before dawn, when the sky begins to change. Christians have this hour as their home: already awake, and not yet in full day.
Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

These are the words that St Augustine read in the garden at Milan in 386, after hearing a child’s voice say “take and read”. He tells us in the Confessions (8.12) that he needed to read no further. “Flesh” in Paul is the self closed against God, and not the body as such.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 9–10 to say that the Ten Commandments must be understood in the light of the twofold commandment of love, which is the fullness of the law (CCC 2055). This does not make the commandments optional: love does no wrong to a neighbour, so the commandments show what love looks like. For the Great Fast, these verses are an invitation to do today what we keep putting off.

set: Jesus is in the Temple around the feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 14). The argument of chapter 8 has been growing sharper since v. 31, when he spoke to those “who had believed in him”. In John, “the Jews” in scenes like this means those who are opposing him in this dispute, and above all the authorities. It does not mean a whole people: Jesus, his mother and his disciples are all Jews. The harsh language on both sides was familiar in disputes within one family of faith at that time, and the Church firmly teaches that no blame may be laid on the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4). Today’s first reading stands behind this one: Abraham has received the promise and rejoiced.
str: vv. 49–50: Jesus does not seek his own glory.
v. 51: “will never see death”.
vv. 52–53: “Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died?”
vv. 54–56: the Father glorifies him; Abraham rejoiced.
vv. 57–58: “before Abraham was, I am”.
v. 59: stones; he hides and leaves.
kw: A simple phrase in Greek, but used here with no complement and set against “was”. It recalls God’s name in Exodus 3:14 and God’s words in Isaiah (see Isaiah 43:10, in the Greek).
Keeping his word means holding it as treasure and living by it. Jesus says he himself keeps the Father’s word (v. 55).
Strong and open joy, the same word as Mary’s “my spirit rejoices” (Luke 1:47). St Irenaeus says that Abraham by the Spirit saw and desired the Lord’s day (Against Heresies 4.5, in substance).
vv: Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.
His hearers take this as physical death, and they are right that Abraham died. He means the death that separates from God. His claim is that his word gives what only God can give.
Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.
John does not say when. Interpreters have proposed the birth of Isaac, the promise itself, or a vision given by God. What is certain is the claim: the whole hope of Israel was moving toward this day.
Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.

Not “I was”. St Augustine draws out the difference: Abraham came to be, as a creature; the Lord says “I am”, as God (Tractates on John 43, in substance). His hearers understand the claim, and they pick up stones because they take it as blasphemy (see Leviticus 24:16).
ch: The Catechism lists this saying among those that only the divine identity of Jesus can explain (CCC 590). It also teaches that the Jewish people as a whole may not be held responsible for his death (CCC 597), and Christians are warned to look first at their own sins (CCC 598). As Hosanna Sunday draws near, the question of the reading is ours as well: “Who do you claim to be?”

qa: Did Abraham really see Jesus?

The Gospel does not explain how. The Church reads the whole Old Testament as moving toward Christ (CCC 128–130). Abraham’s faith looked forward to what God had promised. Hebrews says of the patriarchs that “they saw and greeted” the promises “from a distance” (Hebrews 11:13). Jesus’ point is that the hope of Abraham has its goal in him, and that he is not simply one more figure in the line of Abraham.
study: Which of God’s promises have I, like Sarah, stopped expecting?
What “hill country” am I still avoiding at this stage of my life?
What is it that I keep putting off in this Great Fast, knowing that “the day is near”?

lead: Two readings on love that lasts. Paul’s great chapter tells a divided community that without love every spiritual gift is empty noise, and that love alone will never end. In Mark, Jesus is asked about divorce, and he goes behind the concession of Moses to the beginning of creation: “what God has joined together, let no one separate.” One reading describes what love is, and the other shows it as a covenant. Both are demanding, and neither is possible without grace.

set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8) in the mid 50s to a gifted and quarrelsome community. Chapters 12–14 concern the spiritual gifts, especially tongues and prophecy, which some were treating as marks of rank. Chapter 13 stands in the middle of that argument. People often hear it at weddings, and it does suit them, but its first hearers were a divided parish. Paul is correcting them.
str: vv. 1–3: without love, every gift and sacrifice is nothing.
vv. 4–7: what love does and does not do, in fifteen short verbs.
vv. 8–12: gifts pass away; we now see in part.
v. 13: faith, hope and love; the greatest is love.
kw: Paul’s word for the love that seeks the good of another. It is not mainly a feeling, as vv. 4–7 show, since every word there describes conduct. In this chapter Paul nowhere gives a definition: he gives a portrait.

The NRSV has “dimly”, and the Greek literally reads “in a riddle”. It echoes Numbers 12:8 in the Greek, where God speaks to Moses “face to face”, not “in riddles”. Ancient mirrors were of polished metal and gave an imperfect image.
What is whole and has reached its goal. Most interpreters take it to be the full vision of God at the end. The gifts are for the journey.
vv: If I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ by one Greek letter in the key verb. Some of the oldest read “so that I may boast”, which the NRSV follows. Many others read “to be burned”, which the Malayalam POC follows. Either way, even heroic giving is empty without love: a sobering word for a season of fasting and alms.
Love is patient; love is kind;

Paul begins with patience, the slow-to-anger of God in the Old Testament, and kindness. The Corinthians’ faults stand behind the list: envy, boasting, rudeness, insisting on one’s own way. It is said that one may test the passage by putting one’s own name in the place of “love”. Better still, put Christ’s.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then we will see face to face.

This is the Church’s language for heaven (CCC 1023). What we know of God now is true, and it is only partial. The verse ends with something greater than our knowing: we have “been fully known”, and we are known by God now.
And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.
These are the three theological virtues. Love is greatest because it does not pass into something else: in the end, faith gives way to sight and hope to possession, and love remains.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 4–7 and vv. 1–3 when it teaches on charity, the form of all the virtues (CCC 1825–1827). Pope Benedict XVI calls this hymn “the Magna Carta of all ecclesial service” (Deus Caritas Est 34). St Thérèse of Lisieux, searching these chapters for her own vocation, wrote that in the heart of the Church her mother she would be love (Story of a Soul, Manuscript B). It is a page that speaks to every vocation.

set: Jesus has left Galilee and is moving toward Jerusalem, through “the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan”. Some Pharisees come “to test him”. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 presupposed that a husband might write a certificate of dismissal. Later Jewish sources record a debate among teachers about what grounds for it were sufficient, so the question was a live one. The land beyond the Jordan was also ruled by Herod Antipas, who had put to death John the Baptist, the man who challenged his marriage (Mark 6:17–18), so it was also a dangerous question.
str: v. 1: journey and teaching.
v. 2: the question.
vv. 3–5: Moses’ permission and the reason for it.
vv. 6–9: back to the beginning: Genesis 1:27 and 2:24.
vv. 10–12: in the house: the teaching for the disciples.
kw: Used in the Greek Old Testament of Israel’s stubbornness (Deuteronomy 10:16). The permission tells us the state of the human heart, and it does not express what God wants for marriage.
The word in the Pharisees’ question and in v. 11. Their question speaks of the husband’s act, which is how the custom they knew worked.
Literally to yoke together. It has God as its subject. Marriage is more than a contract between two people, since God himself joins them.
vv: Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this commandment for you.
Jesus does not attack Moses or Israel’s law. He distinguishes what the law allowed for a broken situation from what God wanted in the beginning, using the Torah itself to do so.
Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
Here is the heart of the reading. The new thing is that the Kingdom has come, and with it a grace that can heal the hard heart. Jesus’ word protects the wife as well as the husband.
and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.

Only Mark has this verse. Roman law allowed a wife to divorce, and many scholars think that Mark is applying Jesus’ word to his Gentile readers. The rule is the same for both, and that itself was a protection for women.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus unequivocally taught the original meaning of marriage, and that the permission of Moses was a concession to hard hearts (CCC 1614). It adds that he gives strength and grace to live marriage in the new dimension of the Reign of God (CCC 1615). The bond of a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved (CCC 1640).

qa: What does the Church say to those whose marriages have broken down?

She holds to the Lord’s word and also to his mercy. Separation is allowed where living together has become practically impossible, for instance when there is danger, while the bond remains (CCC 1649). A Church tribunal can examine whether a valid marriage ever existed (CCC 1629). Those who have divorced and entered a new civil union have not been cut off: the Catechism asks for attentive care for them (CCC 1651), and Pope Francis asks that they be made to feel part of the Church (Amoris Laetitia 243). A priest can guide each person through what is possible in their situation.
study: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 slowly with one person in mind. Which single word is the Lord asking me to practise toward that person this week?
How can our parish support married couples, and those whose marriages have been wounded, with both truth and mercy?

lead: This is the last Sunday before Hosanna Sunday, and the four readings ask whose hand we are holding as the Great Fast comes near its end. In Genesis, angels take a lingering man by the hand and pull him out of a doomed city. In Joshua the promises of God stand fulfilled, and the people are told to hold fast to him. Paul asks the strong to give up what they have every right to, for the sake of a brother or sister “for whom Christ died”. And in John the Good Shepherd lays down his life of his own accord, for sheep he knows by name. The line runs from God’s mercy on Lot to the shepherd who will go up to Jerusalem next week. Its key words are mercy, faithfulness and laying down.

set: The chapter follows Abraham’s bold prayer for the city (18:23–32). Two angels have come to Sodom, Lot has taken them in, and a crowd has surrounded the house to do violence to the guests (19:1–11). Lot himself cuts a poor figure in that scene (19:8), and yet the New Testament can call him “a righteous man” (2 Peter 2:7). Now the angels tell him to leave. The site of Sodom has never been established with certainty. The tradition of the Bible places it in the Dead Sea plain, a land of salt and sulfur, where salt formations still stand.
str: v. 15: dawn, and the angels’ urging.
v. 16: Lot lingers; he is seized by the hand.
v. 17: the command: flee, do not look back, do not stop.
vv. 18–22: Lot bargains for a little town, and God gives way.
vv. 23–25: the sun rises, and the cities are overthrown.
v. 26: Lot’s wife.
kw: The Hebrew form suggests hesitation drawn out. It is a small word about a large human habit.
The Lord’s compassion in v. 16: a pity that spares. The rescue is explained by this word. Lot’s courage has no part in it. Verse 29 adds another reason: “God remembered Abraham”.
Lot says twice in v. 20 that the town is “a little one”. The name Zoar is explained by this play on words (v. 22). Lot wants a small compromise rather than the hills.
A standing pillar. The verb “look back” in v. 26 is the same as in the command of v. 17. It means more than a glance: it is a look that dwells.
vv: But he lingered; so the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the Lord being merciful to him,
This is one of the most human sentences in the Bible. Lot knows the danger, and he still does not move. God does not wait for him to be brave. The hand that holds him is the mercy of God.
Flee for your life; do not look back or stop anywhere in the Plain;
Three commands in short bursts. Conversion has an urgency, and it also has a direction: it means leaving behind the place where one is standing.
Look, that city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one.
Even on the road to safety, Lot argues. And God grants it (19:21). Grace works with weak people and meets them where they are, without calling their weakness strength.
But Lot’s wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.

She had come out of the city, but the text suggests that her heart had not. Genesis does not explain her thoughts. Wisdom calls the pillar “a monument to an unbelieving soul” (Wisdom 10:7), and Jesus gives us the shortest of warnings: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32).
ch: St Clement of Rome says that Lot was saved for his hospitality and piety, and that his wife became a sign to the double-minded (1 Clement 11, in substance). The Catechism says that interior conversion is a radical reorientation of the whole life, a turning away from evil (CCC 1431). And because “God remembered Abraham” (19:29), the Church sees here the power of intercession: since Abraham, asking on behalf of another has marked a heart in tune with God’s mercy (CCC 2635).

set: This reading stands at a turning point. The long division of the land is finished (Joshua 13–21). Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh had received land east of the Jordan from Moses on condition that their fighters would cross and stand with the other tribes until all had rest (Numbers 32; Joshua 1:12–18). Now they are sent home.

Many scholars think that this book took its final form long after the events, perhaps around the time of the Exile, when a people who had lost the land needed to hear that God keeps his word. The book itself knows that things were not finished: “very much of the land still remains to be possessed” (13:1). Its summary here is a confession of faith about God.
str: 21:43–45: the summary: land, rest, every promise kept.
22:1–3: Joshua praises the tribes who stayed faithful.
22:4: rest has been given, so they may go home.
22:5: the charge: five verbs of faithfulness.
kw: More than a pause in war. It is the settled life God promises to his people (Deuteronomy 12:9–10). Hebrews will take this word further.
the good word, the good promise
Literally “the good word”. Every word God has spoken for his people’s good has come to pass.
The word of 22:5, the same word used in Genesis 2:24 for a man clinging to his wife. It is the language of a bond, not of a duty alone.
vv: Not one of all the good promises that the Lord had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.

This sentence is the summit of the book. A people that has often failed is told that God has not. It can be said honestly only after a long road, and it is said here so that later generations can hold on to it in the dark.
you have not forsaken your kindred these many days,

These tribes already had their land, and they could have stayed at home. Faith here means staying in the fight until the rest have received what you have. This is a rule of love that Paul will echo today.
to love the Lord your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, and to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.
The language is that of Deuteronomy (see Deuteronomy 6:5; 10:12). Five verbs, and love comes first. Having received the land, they now need to keep the giver.
ch: The Catechism says that God’s words are true and that his promises always come true (CCC 215). Paul says, “in him every one of God’s promises is a ‘Yes’” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The Letter to the Hebrews reads the rest given through Joshua as pointing further: “a sabbath rest still remains for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). This does not take away the gift given to Israel, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). Passages about conquest belong to a harsh age and are read in the light of Christ (Dei Verbum 15).

set: Paul writes to Rome, probably from Corinth, around AD 57. The Roman believers were divided over food and holy days (14:1–6). Paul speaks of the “weak” and the “strong” without naming groups. Many scholars think that the weak were mainly Jewish Christians who kept the food laws or feared impure meat, and that the strong were mainly Gentile believers. This remains a reconstruction. Paul counts himself among the strong (15:1), and yet it is the strong whom he asks to yield. He has no contempt for anyone’s fidelity to conscience.
str: v. 13: stop judging, and resolve not to trip another.
v. 14: Paul’s own conviction: nothing is unclean in itself.
vv. 15–16: if your food harms a brother or sister, you are not walking in love.
vv. 17–18: what the kingdom is.
vv. 19–21: build up, do not tear down.
vv. 22–23: conscience and faith.
kw: Paul plays on the word in v. 13: let us no longer judge one another; judge this instead, that you will not trip anyone.
An obstacle in the path and a trap. “Scandal” in the Church’s moral language comes from this second word: leading another into wrongdoing.
A builder’s word (v. 19). The test of a Christian’s freedom is whether the house of the community stands more firmly because of it.
vv: Do not let what you eat cause the ruin of one for whom Christ died.

The price of the other person is the blood of Christ. Anyone who sets a dish against that has lost all sense of proportion. Chrysostom makes this point sharply in his homilies on Romans (in substance).
For the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

This does not cancel the Fast. It tells us what the Fast is for. Food is neither the way in nor the barrier. The gifts of the Spirit are the signs of the kingdom. The Catechism quotes this verse in explaining the prayer for the coming of the kingdom (CCC 2819).
it is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that makes your brother or sister stumble.

The Catechism quotes this among the rules of conscience (CCC 1789). Paul makes the same choice in Corinth (1 Corinthians 8:13). It does not mean that one must follow every scruple of the loudest person. It means that love is prepared to give up a right.
for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.

In this context “faith” means the settled conviction before God about what one is doing. To act against one’s own conscience is wrong, even when the thing itself is allowed (CCC 1790). See the question below.
ch: The Catechism treats scandal as a grave offence against a brother or sister, especially against the weak (CCC 2284–2287). It also says that charity always proceeds by way of respect for one’s neighbour and his conscience (CCC 1789). Paul’s own words sum it up: “Let us then pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding” (14:19).

r.h: The good shepherd lays down his life
set: Chapter 9 ended with the healing of a man born blind and a dispute with some Pharisees who said, “We see” (9:41). The sayings of chapter 10 continue that dispute without a break. Israel’s Scripture lies behind them: “The Lord is my shepherd” (Psalm 23:1), the God who says “I myself will search for my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:11), and Ezekiel’s complaint against leaders who feed themselves (Ezekiel 34:2). Jesus speaks to some leaders of his day, and his words test leaders of every age, in the Church above all.

A shepherd in that land lived with his flock, led it from the front, knew each animal and defended it against wolves, which were a real danger then. The sheep were often brought at night into a walled fold.
str: v. 11: “I am the good shepherd”; he lays down his life.
vv. 12–13: the hired hand and the wolf.
vv. 14–15: mutual knowledge, and the Father’s knowledge of the Son.
v. 16: other sheep: one flock, one shepherd.
vv. 17–18: laid down of his own accord, taken up again; the Father’s command.
kw: Not simply “good” in the sense of kind. It suggests what is excellent and beautiful in its kind: the real shepherd, as a shepherd ought to be.
It comes five times in this short reading (vv. 11, 15, 17, and twice in v. 18). John uses the same verb at the Supper, when Jesus lays aside his garments (13:4).
The fault lies not in being paid but in what the sheep are to him. The sheep do not belong to him, and so he does not care for them (v. 13).
Verse 16 distinguishes the “fold” (aulē) from the “flock”. St Jerome’s Latin reads “one fold” here, but the Greek says “one flock”. Unity is first of all a matter of hearing the one shepherd.
vv: The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

This is unheard of in ordinary farming: a shepherd who dies leaves his flock to the wolf. Here the death is what saves them. The Malayalam POC says “ജീവൻ അർപ്പിക്കുന്നു”, a word for offering, which gives the verse its priestly tone.
The hired hand runs away because a hired hand does not care for the sheep.

St Gregory the Great says that a hireling can run away without moving, when he sees sin and stays silent out of love for his own comfort (Homilies on the Gospels 14, in substance). St Augustine’s Sermon 46, on pastors, is a long meditation on Ezekiel 34.
I know my own and my own know me,

In the Bible, to know is to be in a bond, not simply to have information. The next verse sets the measure: “just as the Father knows me and I know the Father”. The life of the Trinity is the pattern for how Christ knows you.
So there will be one flock, one shepherd.

John later explains: Jesus would die “to gather into one the dispersed children of God” (11:52). The Second Vatican Council names the restoration of unity among all Christians as one of its chief concerns (Unitatis Redintegratio 1).
No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.

The Catechism quotes these words to show the sovereign freedom of the Son going to his death (CCC 609). It also quotes them on the Resurrection, which is the work of the Father, the Son and the Spirit together, the Son rising by his divine power (CCC 648–649). The arrest and the Cross are not something that overpowered him.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church is a sheepfold whose one gate is Christ, and a flock whose shepherd is God himself (CCC 754). The image of the Good Shepherd is one of the oldest in Christian art, already painted in the catacombs of Rome, carrying the sheep on his shoulders. The Second Vatican Council asks each bishop to keep the example of the Good Shepherd before his eyes, who came to serve and to give his life (Lumen Gentium 27). Holy Qurbana is where this reading is fulfilled for us: he who said “I lay down my life” gives that life to his sheep.

qa: What was the sin of Sodom?

Scripture names more than one thing. Genesis shows a crowd ready to do violence to strangers under Lot’s roof (19:4–9). Ezekiel says: “she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). Jude speaks of sexual immorality (Jude 7). The Catechism refers to this chapter when it teaches that homosexual acts are contrary to the natural law (CCC 2357), and it immediately requires that persons with this inclination be treated with “respect, compassion, and sensitivity” (CCC 2358). No one may use this story as a stone to throw. It calls all of us to conversion.
“Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin”: does this mean that everything non-Christians do is sin?

No. Paul is speaking here about one Christian’s conscience about a question of food. The Church has rejected the idea that all works done without faith are sins (Council of Trent, Session 6, canon 7). The Second Vatican Council says that those who seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, moved by grace, can attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16).
Who are the “other sheep”?

Most of the Fathers and most modern interpreters take them to be the Gentiles, who would come to Christ alongside the believers from Israel (see 11:52). Readers have also rightly heard here a call to all who have not yet heard his voice, and a call to work for Christian unity. The promise is the Lord’s, and he is the one who brings them: “I must bring them also.”
rite: This is the Sixth Sunday of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Next Friday is the Fortieth Friday (Nalpatham Velli), and the Sunday after this one is Hosanna. Many of our families keep this Fast with care, leaving aside meat and fish and other foods as our ancestors did. Romans 14 is a good page to read in our homes this week: it asks us to keep our own fast faithfully without measuring a neighbour’s plate, and it reminds us why we fast. John 10 turns our minds to our shepherds. At every Holy Qurbana we pray for the Pope, for our Major Archbishop and for the bishop of our eparchy. This week let us also pray for our priests, and let each parent, teacher and catechist ask who has been entrusted to their care.
study: Lot lingered and had to be taken by the hand. What am I lingering over, this close to Hosanna Sunday? Who has taken me by the hand?
Where have I seen God keep a promise in my life, so that I could say, as Joshua says, “all came to pass”?
What right of mine, however legitimate, am I being asked to give up for the sake of someone weaker?
If the Lord knows me as the Father knows him, how should that change my prayer this week?

lead: Both readings are about being sent and about what depends on it. Paul had to leave the young Church of Thessalonica in a hurry, sent Timothy back to see how it stood, and now hears that the believers have held firm. In John, Jesus speaks his last public words: he has been sent by the Father as light, to save and not to condemn. An apostle lives for those to whom he is sent, because the Son lives wholly for the One who sent him.

set: This letter is very probably the oldest writing in the New Testament, sent from Corinth around AD 50 or 51. Acts tells how Paul’s preaching in Thessalonica stirred up trouble and how the believers sent him away by night (Acts 17:1–10). He had been with them for only a short time. From Athens he sent Timothy back, because he could no longer bear not knowing how they were (3:1–5). Today’s passage is his answer to the news Timothy brought when he rejoined him (compare Acts 18:5).
str: vv. 6–8: Timothy’s report, and Paul’s relief.
vv. 9–10: thanksgiving, and his prayer night and day to see them.
vv. 11–13: a prayer in the form of a blessing: for the journey, for growth in love, for holiness at the Lord’s coming.
kw: The verb Paul almost always keeps for the gospel of Christ. Here he uses it for Timothy’s report about their faith and love. For Paul, a Church that stands firm is itself good news.
Used in v. 8. It is the stance of someone who keeps his ground under pressure. They were suffering for the faith (2:14), and standing was the victory.
The verb in v. 10, “restore whatever is lacking”. The same word describes the fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). A good faith may still have holes that need a patient teacher.
vv: For we now live, if you continue to stand firm in the Lord.

A short and surprising sentence. Paul is suffering “distress and persecution” (v. 7), and yet his life depends on theirs. This is how a pastor, a catechist or a parent feels about those in their care.
Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and restore whatever is lacking in your faith.
Even this praised Church lacks something. Paul’s joy does not make him careless. The letter he is writing is itself part of the mending, since he cannot yet come in person.
And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, just as we abound in love for you.
Love is asked for as a gift from the Lord. It grows. It also reaches outward: “for one another” and then “for all”, including those who were making life hard for them.
ch: The Catechism points to Paul’s prayer for his Churches as a model of intercession in the first Christian communities: he shares his ministry with them and intercedes for them (CCC 2636). Verse 13 looks to the Lord’s coming “with all his saints”, a phrase that echoes Zechariah 14:5; it may mean the angels, the faithful, or both. In the Great Fast, the passage asks whose faith we carry in our prayer night and day.

r.h: The last public words of Jesus
set: In John’s Gospel Jesus has already left the crowds: “he departed and hid from them” (12:36). The evangelist then reflects on those who did not believe (12:37–43). These verses follow with no place or audience named. They gather up the main themes of his public teaching, and many scholars read them as the evangelist’s summary. From chapter 13 Jesus speaks only with his disciples.
str: vv. 44–45: to believe in me and see me is to believe in and see the One who sent me.
v. 46: I have come as light.
vv. 47–48: I came to save, and the word itself will judge.
vv. 49–50: the word comes from the Father, and his commandment is life.
kw: The verb of v. 44, used for solemn proclamation in John (7:28, 37). This is public, urgent speech, a last call.
A favourite phrase of Jesus in John. A later Jewish saying holds that one who is sent stands for the sender. Jesus goes much further: he is one with the Father who sent him (10:30).
John plays on this word. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), and yet no one who meets him stays neutral. Refusing the light is its own verdict (3:19).
vv: And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.
This looks ahead to the supper: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:9). Everything Jesus says and does shows us who the Father is.
I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
The purpose is stated plainly. The light does not come to expose people for their shame, but so that they need not stay in the dark.
for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
Then v. 48 adds that the word he has spoken will serve as judge on the last day. Both are true. The offer is salvation, and a person remains able to refuse it.
ch: The Catechism says that the Son did not come to judge but to save, and that by rejecting grace in this life one already judges oneself (CCC 679). It also teaches that Christ’s whole life reveals the Father (CCC 516). Preaching on this passage, St Augustine explains that when Jesus says the word will judge, he means himself, since he is the Word (in substance).

qa: If Jesus did not come to judge, why do we say in the Creed that he will come to judge?

Both belong together. His first coming was for salvation, and that offer is open to all. The judgment on the last day will reveal the response each person has made to that offer. The judge is the same Lord who died for us (CCC 679).
study: Whose faith do I carry in my prayer, as Paul carried the Thessalonians? What am I doing for them?
“Should not remain in the darkness.” Where do I still prefer the dark to the light of Christ in this Great Fast?

lead: Today’s readings set two faces of God side by side. In 2 Peter the Lord judges sin but knows how to rescue the godly, as he rescued Noah and Lot. In Luke Jesus, walking toward his death, speaks of Jerusalem with the tenderness of a hen gathering her chicks. The judge and the one who longs to gather are one Lord. He is patient, and he can be refused.

r.h: The Lord knows how to rescue
set: 2 Peter takes the form of a last testament of the apostle, warning against false teachers (2:1) who deny the Lord’s coming (3:3–4) and live as they please. The Church received it as Scripture under the name of Peter; many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name after his death, while others hold a closer link with the apostle. Either way it is the inspired word of God. Its argument in this passage is a long single “if” sentence in Greek: if God acted so in the past, then he will act now.
str: v. 4: the angels who sinned.
v. 5: the flood, and Noah saved.
vv. 6–8: Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot rescued.
vv. 9–10: the conclusion: the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgment.
kw: A word found only here in the New Testament, formed from Tartarus, the Greek name for the deepest place of punishment. The author borrows it from the language of his readers to speak of the angels’ fall (compare Jude 6).
Genesis calls Noah righteous (Genesis 6:9). 2 Peter adds that he proclaimed that righteousness. The Malayalam POC has “forerunner of righteousness”.
Used of Lot (v. 7) and in the conclusion (v. 9). It is the verb of the Lord’s Prayer: “rescue us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13).
vv: and if he rescued Lot, a righteous man greatly distressed by the licentiousness of the lawless

Genesis shows Lot as a weak and hesitating man, yet Abraham’s plea for the righteous and Wisdom 10:6 stand behind this word for him. What mattered was that evil still hurt him. He had not grown used to it, as the next verse says: he was “tormented in his righteous soul”.
then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment
The letter’s readers felt surrounded and outnumbered. Noah was one family, and Lot one household. God can see the few, and numbers do not limit him.
ch: The Catechism cites this passage when it speaks of the sin of the angels, whose choice was radical and irrevocable (CCC 391–393). It also teaches that God predestines no one to hell, and quotes the same letter: God is “not wanting any to perish” (CCC 1037; 2 Peter 3:9). The warnings of this chapter should be read together with that patience.

r.h: As a hen gathers her brood
set: Since 9:51 Jesus has been walking steadily toward Jerusalem. He is probably still in the territory of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee and Perea, who had already killed John the Baptist (9:9). Some Pharisees warn him. Luke does not say that they meant harm, and in his Gospel Pharisees also invite Jesus to their table (7:36; 14:1). Jesus answers with a message for Herod and then turns to speak to the city itself.
str: v. 31: the warning.
vv. 32–33: the answer: his work will go on, and his road leads to Jerusalem.
v. 34: the lament.
v. 35: a word about the house, and a promise of a greeting to come.
kw: In Jewish and Greek speech a fox could suggest cunning, and also a small creature compared with a lion. Jesus is not frightened by this ruler. His life is in his Father’s hands.
Literally “I am brought to completion”. The same family of words appears when he dies in John (“It is finished”, John 19:30). “The third day” also points the Christian reader to Easter.
The prophets used the picture of God gathering the scattered. The image of wings comes from the Psalms (Psalm 36:7; 91:4) and from Deuteronomy 32:11. Jesus speaks as God speaks in Israel’s Scripture.
vv: Go and tell that fox for me,
Jesus will not change his route because of a threat, nor hurry because of a warning. “Today and tomorrow” he goes on healing. His timetable is the Father’s.
because it is impossible for a prophet to be killed outside of Jerusalem.
A grim piece of irony. Not every prophet died there, as John’s death shows. Jesus means that the holy city, where God’s word should be most welcome, is where the prophet’s road ends.
How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!

This is the centre of the passage: a tender picture of a hen, who shields her young with her own body. God’s love is never forced. It can be refused, and the sorrow in this verse shows what that refusal costs him.
you will not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’

The words are from Psalm 118:26. “Your house is left to you” echoes Jeremiah 22:5. The saying ends with a greeting. Luke will soon let the disciples cry out this very psalm at the entry into the city (19:38), and many read here a hope for the future as well.
ch: The Catechism quotes this lament when it describes Jesus going up to Jerusalem: he recalls the martyrdom of the prophets, yet goes on asking the city to gather around him, and he weeps over her (CCC 558). The words are those of a Jew grieving for his own city, in the line of Jeremiah. They give no ground for any blame of the Jewish people (CCC 597–598, 839). St Augustine often returns to this picture of the hen to speak of Christ’s humble love, which weakens itself to shelter us (in substance).

qa: Does 2 Peter teach that God is harsh?

It teaches that God takes evil seriously, and that the godly are not forgotten. The same letter explains the delay of judgment as patience: God does not want anyone to perish, but all to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Today’s Gospel shows how much that love longs to gather.
study: Lot was “tormented” by what he saw. Have I grown used to any evil around me that once hurt me?
Jesus wanted to gather and was refused. What in my life keeps me from coming under his wings during the coming Week of the Passion?

lead: Today’s readings look at life inside the community of believers. John says that nobody can claim to be in the light while hating a brother or sister. Matthew gives Jesus’ patient steps for winning back one who has sinned, and promises his presence where two or three gather in his name. Love in the Church is not a mood. It has a practice, and the Lord himself stands in the middle of it.

r.h: The old commandment that is new
set: 1 John has no greeting and names no author; tradition links it with the apostle John, and it clearly comes from the same world as the Fourth Gospel. Many scholars date it to the end of the first century. A group has left the community (2:19), and the writer gives his readers tests of true faith: do you keep his commandments, and do you love one another? Just before this passage he says that whoever claims to abide in Christ “ought to walk just as he walked” (2:6).
str: v. 7: an old commandment, the one you have heard from the beginning.
v. 8: yet it is new, because the true light is already shining.
vv. 9–11: the test: hating means darkness, and loving means light.
kw: The one Jesus gave at the supper: “love one another” (John 13:34). It is old because it was heard from the beginning, and new because Christ has lived it to the end.
The same verb returns in 2:17: “the world and its desire are passing away”. Darkness is still around, but its time is ending. The present tense gives hope.
The word used in v. 10. It first meant a trap or something that trips a person. One who loves does not trip over his own feet, and he does not trip others.
vv: because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
It is a picture of early dawn. The writer does not claim that all is bright. He says which way the day is moving.
Whoever says, “I am in the light,” while hating a brother or sister, is still in the darkness.

Fine words about faith cannot cover hatred. The NRSV’s “brother or sister” represents the Greek “brother”, a member of the Christian family, and the Gospel of the same tradition shows God’s love reaching the whole world (John 3:16).
Whoever loves a brother or sister lives in the light, and in such a person there is no cause for stumbling.
The verb is “abides”, a key word of this letter. Love is more than an act. It is where a person lives.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, and that by loving his own to the end he shows the Father’s love (CCC 1823). St Augustine preached ten homilies on this letter, and for him its one subject is charity (in substance). In the Great Fast the question is direct: is there someone I will not speak to? My fast and my prayer should begin there.

r.h: Where two or three are gathered
set: Chapter 18 is the fourth of the five great discourses in Matthew, on life in the community. Just before this, the shepherd goes after one lost sheep (18:12–14). Just after, Peter asks how often he must forgive, and Jesus tells the parable of the unforgiving servant (18:21–35). The steps of today’s passage stand between mercy and mercy, and must be read in that light.
str: v. 15: go alone.
v. 16: take one or two others.
v. 17: tell the Church, and the last step if all is refused.
v. 18: binding and loosing.
vv. 19–20: prayer in agreement, and the Lord’s presence.
kw: In the Gospels this word appears only here and in Matthew 16:18. It is the Greek word used in the Greek Old Testament for the assembly of Israel.
“You have regained that one.” It is a merchant’s word: a brother is treasure. The whole aim of correction is to win him back, not to win the argument.
The Greek behind our word “symphony” (v. 19). It means more than a shared opinion. Voices are joined in one request.
vv: If another member of the church sins against you, go and point out the fault when the two of you are alone.

The first step asks for two things: courage and discretion. It is easier to tell others than to tell the person. A note on the text: some important old manuscripts lack “against you” (the NRSV notes this), and the POC follows that shorter wording.
let such a one be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.

This is the last step, and it should be read with care. In Matthew Jesus eats with tax collectors (9:10–11) and calls one of them to be an apostle (9:9). It marks a real break, and it also says where the Church must begin again: with a call to come back.
Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

“Bind” and “loose” were terms used by Jewish teachers for forbidding and permitting, and for imposing or lifting a ban. Here “you” is plural. The authority given to Peter (16:19) is also given to the apostles with him.
For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.

Matthew’s Gospel is framed by this promise: “God is with us” (1:23) and “I am with you always” (28:20). A Jewish saying in the Mishnah speaks of God’s presence resting on two who study the Law together; Jesus says this of himself.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the office of binding and loosing given to Peter was also given to the college of the apostles united with its head (CCC 1444), and it links this power to reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445). Among the ways Christ is present to his Church, it names the gathering in his name, and above all the Eucharistic species (CCC 1373; Sacrosanctum Concilium 7).

qa: Why does the English say “sins against you” while the Malayalam only says “does wrong”?

Some important old manuscripts of Matthew do not have the words “against you” (the NRSV notes this), and the POC follows that shorter wording. With them, the passage is about a personal injury. Without them, it is about any serious sin we notice in a fellow believer. In both, the first step is the same: go quietly, in love.
study: Is there someone I have talked about to others, when I should have gone to speak to that person alone?
Whom in my family or parish could I pray with this week, trusting the promise of Matthew 18:20?

lead: Two images about what is empty and what is fruitful. 2 Peter describes false teachers as springs with no water, who promise and do not give. John the Baptist asks for fruit, and when the crowds ask what that means, he speaks about coats and food. Near the end of the Great Fast, both readings ask whether anything has actually changed in the way we live and give.

set: The letter continues its warning about false teachers. Much of this passage runs closely parallel to Jude 8–13, and many scholars think the author of 2 Peter used Jude. The language is sharp, in the style of ancient polemic. Its concern is the harm done to “unsteady souls” (v. 14), who were being drawn away by teachers who shared the community’s table while living in greed and license. The authorship of the letter is discussed by scholars, and the Church receives it as inspired.
str: vv. 11–12: they slander what they do not understand, where even angels hold back.
vv. 13–14: their life: feasting, adultery, greed, and leading others astray.
vv. 15–16: the road of Balaam.
v. 17: the two images and the end they come to.
kw: These same two ideas, turned to the negative, describe what Christians should be at the Lord’s coming: “without spot or blemish” (3:14). 1 Peter 1:19 uses them for Christ the Lamb.

The word comes from the training of athletes, as in our “gymnasium”. Their hearts have been “trained in greed” (v. 14). A vice is learned through repeated practice, and so is a virtue (compare Hebrews 5:14).
In a dry land a spring means life. A traveller walks to it and finds dust. Compare Jeremiah 2:13, the people who forsook “the fountain of living water”.
vv: They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their dissipation while they feast with you.

A note on the text: some manuscripts have a word meaning “dissipation” or “deceptions” (apatais), and others have “love-feasts” (agapais), as in Jude 12. Either way, the wrongdoers were sitting at the table of the community.
They have hearts trained in greed.
The Catechism says that the tenth commandment forbids greed and the desire to amass earthly goods without limit (CCC 2536). The Great Fast is a training too, in the opposite direction.
following the road of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of doing wrong,

The story is in Numbers 22–24, with the donkey that sees what the prophet cannot. A note on the text: most manuscripts of this verse read “Bosor”, while the Old Testament and the Malayalam POC have “Beor”. A few manuscripts here also have Beor. The man is the same.
These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm;
Both images are about a promise that is not kept. The mist looks like rain and blows away. The warning reaches anyone who teaches or leads: the form of religion, with nothing to give to the thirsty.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church’s shepherds have the task of guarding God’s people from deviations and defections, so that they may profess the true faith without error (CCC 890). Christ is the true spring: “let anyone who is thirsty come to me” (John 7:37).

set: John the Baptist preaches a baptism of repentance in the region of the Jordan (3:3). Luke says that crowds came out to be baptized by him (3:7). He is a Jewish prophet speaking to his own people, in the manner of Amos and Isaiah, and his warning is for all who trust in a religious label. Luke alone gives the practical answers that follow, in vv. 10–14.
str: v. 8: bear fruit, and do not rely on descent from Abraham.
v. 9: the axe at the root.
v. 10: the crowds’ question.
v. 11: the first answer: share clothes and food.
kw: A change of mind and direction. John shows it must appear in action. Without fruit it is only a feeling.
In Hebrew “stones” (’ăbānîm) and “sons” (bānîm) sound alike, and many think a play on words may lie behind John’s saying. God can make his people from anything: only his grace makes us children.
The garment worn next to the skin. John does not ask for the outer cloak. A person with two of these has one more than he needs.
vv: Bear fruits worthy of repentance.
John does not reject the baptism people came for. He says what it must lead to. No one can merit the first grace (CCC 2010); the tree that has received it bears fruit by that same grace.
God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham.

This is no word against Abraham or his descendants, for God’s promises to them stand. The warning fits any Christian who says, “I am baptized, I am from an old family of the faith,” and leaves it at that.
What then should we do?
The same question returns in 3:12 and 3:14, and again at Pentecost (Acts 2:37). It is the right question after hearing God’s word.
Whoever has two coats must share with anyone who has none; and whoever has food must do likewise.
John asks for nothing spectacular. He asks that no one keep what another needs. The answer is simple enough for a child, and hard enough for a lifetime.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it speaks of the works of mercy (CCC 2447), and it teaches that interior repentance shows itself above all in fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434). St Basil the Great, preaching on the rich fool, says that the coat stored in your closet belongs to the one who has none (in substance). So the fast and the sharing belong together.

qa: Is it unkind for Christians to use language as harsh as 2 Peter’s?

The letter is using the strong conventions of ancient warning, to protect vulnerable people from real harm. It does not give us licence to insult those we disagree with; the same letter praises the angels for holding back from slander (2:11). We may be firm about error, and we are still called to love the person.
study: When someone thirsty comes to me (a lonely neighbour, a child with questions), do they find water?
What do I have two of? Whom could I share one with before Easter?

lead: This year the Fortieth Friday, Nalpatham Velli, meets the feast of St Joseph. The readings belong to the Friday, and they stand at the door of the Week of the Passion. Abraham looks out at the smoke of Sodom, and we learn that God remembered his prayer and brought Lot out. Israel nearly goes to war over an altar by the Jordan, and sends envoys first. Paul asks Christians to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them, and names the root of Jesse, the royal line in which Joseph, son of David, gave Jesus his place. At Bethany Jesus calls a dead man out of the tomb, days before his own burial. The key words are remember, one altar, welcome and come out. Over all of them stands the quiet man who guarded the Lord’s childhood, whose prayers the Church seeks for the grace of a good death.

set: This short passage follows the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. In chapter 18 Abraham stood before the Lord and pleaded for the city, bringing the number of the righteous down from fifty to ten (18:22–33). In chapter 19 not even ten are found, and Lot and his family are led out by the two messengers. Now Abraham, who has heard nothing since, comes back in the morning to the place of his prayer.
str: v. 27: Abraham returns early to the place where he prayed.
v. 28: what he sees: smoke rising.
v. 29: the narrator’s explanation: God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out.
v. 30: Lot, afraid to stay in Zoar, goes to live in a cave.
¶ The reading stops at the cave and does not go on to the sad story of Lot’s family that follows. It wants us to stay with v. 29.
kw: In the Bible God’s remembering is never a mere recollection. It leads to action. “God remembered Noah” and the waters went down (8:1); he remembered Rachel, and she conceived (30:22); he remembered his covenant, and the Exodus began (Exodus 2:24).
Kiln or furnace. The same word describes the smoke on Sinai (Exodus 19:18). The fire that destroys and the fire of God’s presence look alike from a distance.
The word for God’s overturning of Sodom. Words from the same root became a standing phrase for divine judgment in the prophets (Amos 4:11; Isaiah 13:19).
vv: Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the Lord;
He goes back to where he prayed, without knowing the answer. Prayer here includes the courage to come back and look.
God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow,

Notice the wording: the rescue of Lot is credited to the memory of Abraham’s prayer. Abraham had asked for the city and was given his nephew. He saw only smoke. The reader knows what he did not know: his prayer was heard, in a way he could not see.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham’s heart is attuned to the Lord’s compassion and that he dares to intercede for others with bold confidence (CCC 2571); intercession belongs to a heart in tune with God’s mercy (CCC 2635). For anyone praying for a child or a spouse far from God, this verse is a comfort: we do not always see what our prayer has done.

set: Two and a half tribes (Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh) had received land east of the Jordan on condition that they fight beside the others (Numbers 32). They kept their word (Joshua 1:12–18) and have just been sent home with a blessing (22:1–9). On the way they build a huge altar near the river. The law asks for one place of worship (Deuteronomy 12:5–14), and the tabernacle now stands at Shiloh (18:1). To the western tribes the new altar looks like a breakaway.
str: vv. 10–11: the altar, and the report.
v. 12: the assembly gathers at Shiloh for war.
vv. 13–15: Phinehas and ten chiefs are sent.
vv. 16–18: the charge, recalling the sin at Peor.
v. 19: a generous offer: come and share our land.
v. 20: the warning from Achan.

¶ The reading stops before the answer. In vv. 21–29 the eastern tribes explain that the altar is no place of sacrifice. It is a witness for their children that they too belong to the Lord. War is avoided (vv. 30–34).
kw: A strong word for unfaithfulness to God, used in vv. 16 and 20, and of Achan (7:1). The fear is not about a building but about a whole people drifting away.
Used repeatedly in vv. 16–19. The envoys see a rebellion, and they see the danger to everyone: the sin of one group brings harm on “the whole congregation” (v. 18).
The priest whose zeal at Peor stopped a plague (Numbers 25:7–13). The priest best known for zeal is the one sent, and he comes to talk.
vv: the whole assembly of the Israelites gathered at Shiloh, to make war against them.
Their anger comes from a real love of God’s law. Good zeal can still act on a wrong reading of the facts.
Then the Israelites sent the priest Phinehas son of Eleazar
This is the turning point. Before anyone draws a sword, someone goes to ask. The Great Fast may ask the same of our families and parishes.
take for yourselves a possession among us;
Under the anger there is real generosity. If your land seems unclean, come and live with us. They would rather give up some of their own land than lose their brothers.
Did not Achan son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things,
Sin is never wholly private in the Bible. It wounds the whole body.
ch: St Paul says, “there is one body” (Ephesians 4:4) and calls Christ “our peace” who broke down the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14). St Ignatius of Antioch urges Christians to keep one Eucharist, for there is one flesh of the Lord, one cup and one altar, as there is one bishop (To the Philadelphians 4; in substance). The Catechism speaks of the altar of the New Covenant as the Lord’s Cross, from which the sacraments flow (CCC 1182), and of the wounds to the Church’s unity as something we must pray and work to heal (CCC 817–822).

set: Paul writes to Rome around AD 57. Chapters 14–15 deal with a real tension in the community between the “strong” and the “weak” over food and days. Many scholars think this tension ran largely, though not wholly, between believers of Gentile and of Jewish background. This passage rounds off the discussion, and with it the main body of the letter. Christ himself is the model, and Scripture is the proof.
str: v. 7: the command: welcome one another, as Christ welcomed you.
vv. 8–9a: Christ served the Jews for God’s faithfulness, and the Gentiles for God’s mercy.
vv. 9b–12: four quotations from Scripture.
v. 13: a blessing of hope.

¶ The quotations are from Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1 and Isaiah 11:10. So the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms all give the same witness: the nations will praise God together with his people.
kw: To take someone to oneself, as into a home or friendship. The same verb opens the discussion (14:1).
A remarkable title for Christ. He came as a servant to his own Jewish people, to confirm God’s promises to them (compare Matthew 15:24). God’s word to Israel stands.

From Isaiah 11. The POC has “a shoot from Jesse”. Jesse was David’s father, and the title means the Messiah of the royal house. “The one who rises” (ho anistamenos) may also suggest to Paul’s readers the Resurrection.
vv: Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
The measure of our welcome is the welcome we received: while we were sinners (5:8). The goal is God’s glory, which shines when people who differ sit at one table.
Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of the truth of God
“Truth” here includes God’s faithfulness to his promises. Because God keeps faith with Israel, the Gentile believer can trust him as well.
The root of Jesse shall come,

Today this line turns our minds to St Joseph. Matthew and Luke trace Jesus’ legal descent through Joseph, “son of David” (Matthew 1:20). The Catechism says that God called him so that Jesus should be born into the messianic lineage of David (CCC 437).
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
Paul’s title for God is unusual and beautiful. Hope is the last word of the main body of the letter, and it is above all a gift of the Spirit.
ch: The Catechism defines hope as the virtue by which we desire the kingdom and eternal life, relying on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). The Second Vatican Council adds that the Church awaits the day, known to God alone, when all peoples will address the Lord with one voice (Nostra Aetate 4). On St Joseph’s day it is fitting to remember that Christian hope reached its goal through a family, and that God’s promises to Israel came through the patient obedience of one man of David’s house.

set: This is the last and greatest of the signs in John’s Gospel before the Passion. Lazarus of Bethany has died, and Jesus delayed his coming on purpose (11:6, 15). He has told Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25), and he has wept (11:35). Bethany is near Jerusalem (11:18). This sign leads the council to plan his death (11:47–53), so the giving of life to Lazarus will cost Jesus his own.
str: vv. 38–39: at the tomb: “Take away the stone”, and Martha’s objection.
v. 40: “you would see the glory of God”.
vv. 41–42: Jesus’ prayer of thanks to the Father.
vv. 43–44: the call, and Lazarus comes out still bound.
v. 45: many believe.
kw: A strong word (vv. 33, 38), used elsewhere of a stern warning or an indignant snort. Jesus is deeply moved: with grief, and many think with anger at death itself. The POC has “sighing”, which is gentler than the Greek.
The goal of the whole sign (11:4, 40). In John the glory of God is seen in Jesus’ works and above all on the Cross (12:23–24).

Lazarus comes out bound in grave cloths and will need them again one day. On Easter morning the wrappings of Jesus are left behind in the tomb, and the same word for the face cloth is used (20:6–7). He rises never to die again.
vv: Jesus said, “Take away the stone.”

Jesus could move the stone himself. He asks people to do what they can. The objection comes from a woman of faith, and it is honest: “already there is a stench”. A later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days. The four days make plain that Lazarus is truly dead.
Father, I thank you for having heard me.

He gives thanks before anything has happened. The Catechism notes that thanksgiving comes first here, and that the Father always hears his Son (CCC 2604). He prays aloud so that the crowd may know that he comes from the Father (v. 42).
When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”

It is a call by name, as the shepherd calls his own (10:3), and it fulfils his own word about the dead hearing his voice (5:28–29). John uses the same strong verb for the shouts at the entry into Jerusalem (12:13) and before Pilate (19:6). Here it is Jesus who cries out, and the cry gives life.
Unbind him, and let him go.
He gives life, and asks others to do the rest. St Augustine sees here the ministry of the Church, which looses the penitent whom Christ has called to life (in substance).
Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what Jesus did, believed in him.

All the people in this scene are Jews: Jesus, Martha, Mary, Lazarus, and the mourners who came to comfort the sisters. Many believe. When John goes on to speak of opposition, he means certain authorities (11:47), not the people as a whole.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person (CCC 994), and that the raising of Lazarus was a return to ordinary earthly life, unlike Christ’s Resurrection, which passes beyond death (CCC 646). St Augustine reads the four days as a soul long buried in the habit of sin, and he finds hope for such a soul in Christ’s loud cry (in substance). So a sinner who feels too long in the tomb can hear this Gospel as his own.

qa: Abraham prayed for Sodom and it was still destroyed. Did his prayer fail?

Not ten righteous people were found, so the city fell. And yet “God remembered Abraham” and rescued Lot. Abraham’s prayer did more than he could see. God’s answer to our prayer is often larger or different than what we can see from where we stand.
Why does the Church honour St Joseph so greatly, when Scripture gives him no spoken word?

Because of what he was given to do. He was the husband of Mary and, in the place of a father, guarded and raised the Son of God. Matthew calls him “a righteous man” (Matthew 1:19). Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870, and St John Paul II wrote about him in Redemptoris Custos (1989), as Pope Francis did in Patris Corde (2020). In the Gospels he speaks by what he does. The Church also entrusts the dying to him as patron of a happy death (CCC 1014).
Lazarus died again. So what was the point?

The sign points beyond itself. It shows that Jesus has power over death, and that those who believe in him will live even though they die (11:25–26). Lazarus returned to this life. Christ opens the way to a life where death has no more power (CCC 646).
rite: Nalpatham Velli marks the completing of the first stage of the Great Fast and the turn toward the Passion of the Lord. In many Syro-Malabar parishes the Way of the Cross is made with special devotion, and some climb a hill shrine on foot. Where the feast of St Joseph is kept today, many places also hold the meal for the poor (oottu) in honour of the Holy Family. How fast and feast are kept together on this day follows the direction of one’s own eparchy. It is a fitting meeting. The man who took the Child and his Mother and rose in the night to obey is the patron of families and of the dying. As Lazarus is called out of the tomb, we may ask St Joseph to walk with us through the coming days, and to stay with us at the hour of our own death.
study: Abraham went back to the place of prayer without knowing the answer. For whom do I keep praying while seeing only smoke?
The tribes sent Phinehas to talk before they went to war. What quarrel in my family or parish needs someone to go and ask first?
“Welcome one another.” Whom do I find hard to welcome in my own Church, and how has Christ welcomed me?
Jesus asked others to unbind Lazarus. Who around me has come back to faith but is still bound, and needs my help? What can I learn from St Joseph’s quiet way of serving?

lead: On the eve of Hosanna Sunday, two farewells. Paul, on his way to Jerusalem and expecting chains, says goodbye to the elders of Ephesus with tears and tells them to care for the flock. At Bethany Mary pours out costly perfume on the feet of Jesus, who says it is for his burial. Both Paul and Mary know that a road is ending in Jerusalem, and both spend without counting.

set: Paul is ending his third missionary journey, probably around AD 57, and hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (20:16). He does not go back to Ephesus, where he had spent about three years, but sends for its elders to come to Miletus, a port some 50 km to the south (20:17). This is the only speech in Acts that Paul addresses to Christian leaders, and it reads like a last testament.
str: vv. 22–24: where he is going: bound by the Spirit, ready to give his life.
vv. 25–27: none of them “will ever see my face again”; he has kept nothing back.
vv. 28–31: keep watch over the flock; wolves will come.
v. 32: he commends them to God.
vv. 33–35: his own example: he worked with his hands and helped the weak.
vv. 36–38: prayer and tears at the ship.
kw: In v. 17 these men are called elders (presbyteroi), and in v. 28 overseers. At this early stage the two words overlap. The offices of bishop and presbyter became distinct as the Church’s ministry took its settled form, already clear in St Ignatius of Antioch.
To feed and to guard. The elders share the work of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11; 1 Peter 5:2–4).
The word of v. 32. It is the verb Jesus uses on the Cross in Luke: “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Paul gives his people to God, because they were never his own.
vv: But I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course
The image of a runner, as in 1 Corinthians 9:24–27 and 2 Timothy 4:7. His life is worth something only as the means of finishing what he has been given to do.
Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he obtained with the blood of his own Son.

First “yourselves”: a shepherd who does not watch himself cannot watch others. A note on the text: the Greek at the end can mean “with the blood of his own” (that is, his own Son) or “with his own blood”, and some manuscripts read “the church of the Lord”. The NRSV and the POC take it differently. All agree on the price.
remembering the words of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’
This saying of Jesus is not in any of the four Gospels. Acts has preserved it for us. Paul has just shown what it means: he worked with his hands so as to give.
When he had finished speaking, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
Grown men weep and embrace (v. 37). The Church’s leaders are also friends. This warmth is part of what ministry should be.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse when it speaks of the apostles entrusting the flock to those who would follow them (Lumen Gentium 20; see also CCC 861). The same teaching stands behind every bishop and priest in the Church today. For the rest of us, the passage is a mirror: a good shepherd tells the whole truth (v. 27), does not love money (v. 33), and cares for the weak (v. 35).

r.h: The house was filled with fragrance
set: “Six days before the Passover” begins the countdown in John to the Lord’s death. Bethany is close to Jerusalem (11:18). In the house, the people of the last chapter are together: Martha serving, Lazarus at table, and Mary. John’s readers know the leaders have already resolved to kill Jesus (11:53).

This Mary is the sister of Martha and Lazarus. The Gospels do not identify her with Mary Magdalene or with the sinful woman of Luke 7; that merger became common in the West after St Gregory the Great, and the Churches of the East have generally kept them distinct.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: a dinner at Bethany.
v. 3: Mary’s act.
vv. 4–6: Judas’s objection, and John’s comment.
vv. 7–8: Jesus’ reply.
kw: Nard is a fragrant oil from a plant of the Himalayan region, carried to the Mediterranean at great cost. The exact meaning of pistikē is uncertain; it is usually taken as “genuine, pure”. The word is found only here and in Mark 14:3.
A Roman pound, about a third of a kilogram. That is a large amount of perfume to pour out at one time. The POC has “a bottle”.
A denarius was a day’s pay for a labourer (Matthew 20:2), so this was close to a year’s wages. Judas has done the sum correctly.
vv: The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.

Washing feet was a servant’s task. Mary anoints them with perfume and wipes them with her hair. In a few days Jesus will wash the feet of his disciples (13:5). St Augustine says that the whole world has since been filled with the good odour of Christ (in substance; compare 2 Corinthians 2:15).
Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?
A good argument used for a bad reason, as John notes (v. 6). The disciple who looks most concerned for the poor is the one stealing from them. John does not let us use the poor as a pretext.
She bought it so that she might keep it for the day of my burial.

A note on the text: this verse is hard. The older Greek manuscripts read “let her keep it for the day of my burial”, and the NRSV expands this. Some later manuscripts read “she has kept it”. The POC puts it differently again, “let her consider that she has done this for the day of my burial”. In every reading Jesus receives the act as an anointing for his burial.
You always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.

Jesus echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, which goes on to command an open hand to the poor. So this is no excuse for neglecting them. It is a statement about this moment. The Catechism uses the verse to teach that Jesus’ presence is to be recognized in the poor themselves (CCC 2449).
ch: In the same way, the Church has always held together costly beauty in the worship of Christ and generous care for the poor. The Catechism’s teaching on the poor (CCC 2443–2449) sits beside its teaching on sacred art and worship, and neither cancels the other. St John Chrysostom could praise gifts for the altar and in the same breath tell his people not to neglect Christ in the poor (in substance). The perfume and the alms come from one love.

qa: Is Mary of Bethany the same person as Mary Magdalene?

The Gospels treat them as different women: Mary of Bethany lives near Jerusalem with Martha and Lazarus, and Mary Magdalene comes from Galilee (Luke 8:2). The Western tradition for some centuries joined them. Today the Roman calendar itself keeps separate days for them (22 and 29 July), and the Eastern traditions did not join them.
study: What would it mean for me to give something costly to the Lord this coming Week of the Passion, without counting?
Who is the “weak” person I am called to help (Acts 20:35), and what is the work of my own hands that could help them?

lead: Today the Great Fast opens into the Week of the Passion, and the Church walks with her King into Jerusalem. The four readings follow one question: what kind of king? Jacob promises that the scepter will stay with Judah, and pictures a donkey’s colt tied to a vine. Zechariah sees the king come, humble, on that very animal, and bringing peace in place of chariots. Paul reminds the Gentile believers that they live from Israel’s root, grafted in by grace, and must not boast. Matthew shows Jesus riding into the city to the cry of Hosanna, going straight to the Temple, and healing the blind and the lame. The key words are scepter, humble, root and Hosanna.

set: Jacob is about to die in Egypt. He gathers his twelve sons and tells them “what will happen to you in days to come” (49:1). This is the Testament of Jacob, a poem that many scholars consider very old, in which each son stands for a future tribe. Some of the words are hard to understand, and translations differ. The reading takes the two longest blessings: Judah, who will rule, and Joseph, who suffered and was upheld.
str: v. 8: Judah praised by his brothers.
v. 9: the lion.
v. 10: the scepter.
vv. 11–12: a picture of plenty: vines, wine and milk.
vv. 22–24: Joseph, fruitful and attacked, made strong by the Mighty One of Jacob.
vv. 25–26: the blessings on the head of Joseph.
kw: A play on the name Judah (yᵉhûdâ), which Genesis has linked with praise (29:35). The tribe’s very name is a promise.

The ruler’s staff, a sign of royal authority. David came from Judah, and Israel looked to a future king from his line. The Letter to the Hebrews notes that “our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14).
An ancient title of God (v. 24), found again in Isaiah 49:26 and Psalm 132:2. Joseph’s strength was never his own.
vv: Judah is a lion’s whelp;

The Book of Revelation takes up this picture: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered”. When John turns to look, he sees a Lamb, standing as if slaughtered (Revelation 5:5–6). That is the surprise of today’s Gospel as well.
The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him;

A note on the text: the Hebrew here is famously difficult (literally “until Shiloh comes”). The NRSV reads it, by a small change, as “until tribute comes to him”. The ancient Greek and Syriac versions read “until he comes to whom it belongs”, and the POC is close to that: “until its heir comes”. Ancient Jewish tradition, in the Targums, also read the verse of the King Messiah. So do the Fathers.
Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey’s colt to the choice vine,
