Only a very rich man could tie an animal to a vine and let it eat. It is a picture of overflowing plenty in the days of this king. Christian readers could not miss the colt today, nor the robe washed “in the blood of grapes”.
Yet his bow remained taut, and his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,

The archers suggest the hatred of Joseph’s brothers and all that followed. God stood behind his arms. Joseph was the one “set apart from his brothers” (v. 26), and the one who was rejected became the saviour of his family.
ch: St Justin Martyr, writing to the Roman emperor, reads this prophecy of Jesus: the colt, and the robe washed in the blood of the grape, which points to the blood by which he cleanses those who believe (First Apology 32; in substance). St Augustine sees in the lion who lies down the Christ who laid down his life by his own power, and took it up again (City of God XVI, 41; in substance). Of Joseph, the Catechism recalls his words to his brothers, “it was not you who sent me here, but God”, as an example of God’s providence working through evil (CCC 312). St Ambrose reads him as a figure of Christ (On Joseph; in substance).

r.h: Your king comes to you, humble
set: Chapters 9–14 of Zechariah differ in style from chapters 1–8, and many scholars think they come from a later hand in the years after the return from exile. Israel has no king. Foreign armies pass through the land, and the chapter even names Greece (9:13). Into that situation comes this oracle. It has just described God coming to defend his house (9:8). Now the daughter of Zion is told to shout, because her king is on his way.
str: v. 9: the call to rejoice, and the king.
v. 10: the end of war, and peace to the nations.
v. 11: the blood of the covenant and the prisoners released.
v. 12: “prisoners of hope”, and the promise of double.
kw: The word also means poor, afflicted. This king is on the side of the lowly because he is one of them.
Literally “just and saved” or “just and having victory”. His victory is something God gives him. Matthew’s quotation leaves these two words out and goes straight to “humble”.
the blood of my covenant with you
It recalls Sinai, where Moses sprinkled “the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). At the supper Jesus will speak of “my blood of the covenant” (Matthew 26:28).
vv: Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

A donkey was no shameful animal for a ruler in old Israel; Solomon rode David’s mule to his anointing (1 Kings 1:33). But it is not a warhorse, as the next verse makes clear. In Hebrew verse the second line repeats the first: “on a donkey, on a colt” means one animal.
and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall command peace to the nations;
This king disarms his own people, Ephraim in the north and Jerusalem in the south. His rule reaches “from sea to sea”, as in Psalm 72:8, and he wins it by no war.
Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope;

A lovely phrase. They are bound, and what binds them is hope. “The waterless pit” (v. 11) recalls the pit into which Joseph was thrown: “the pit was empty; there was no water in it” (Genesis 37:24). In v. 11 the POC calls the prisoners “exiles”.
ch: The Catechism says that the King of glory enters his city riding on a donkey, and that he does not conquer the daughter of Zion, a figure of his Church, by ruse or violence, but by the humility that bears witness to the truth (CCC 559). St Matthew and St John both quote this oracle at the entry (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). The Church hears in v. 11 the blood of the new covenant, which she receives in the Holy Qurbana (CCC 610–611).

set: Romans 9–11 is Paul’s long wrestling with a question that hurt him deeply: why have most of his own people not accepted Jesus as Messiah? He begins with “great sorrow” (9:2). He has already asked, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (11:1). He ends by saying that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26), “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Today’s passage lies between. It is addressed to Gentile Christians in Rome, who may have been tempted to look down on Jews.
str: vv. 13–15: Paul’s mission to the Gentiles is also for the sake of his own people.
v. 16: dough and root.
vv. 17–18: the wild shoot grafted in: do not boast.
vv. 19–22: “stand in awe”: kindness and severity.
vv. 23–24: God can graft them back.
kw: Paul’s hope (v. 14) comes from Deuteronomy 32:21. He wants his people to see in the Gentile Churches what God has promised, and to desire it.
Israel is the cultivated tree of God (compare Jeremiah 11:16). The Gentile is the wild shoot. Paul himself says the grafting is “contrary to nature” (v. 24). It is all grace.
Paul sets both together in v. 22. Apotomia is a cutting off, a word that suits the pruning image. Neither can be used as a claim against anyone else; both are a call to stay in God’s kindness.
vv: If the part of the dough offered as first fruits is holy, then the whole batch is holy; and if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.
The first image comes from Numbers 15:17–21. The root is most probably the patriarchs, “for the sake of their ancestors” (11:28). The holiness of the root has not been cancelled.
remember that it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.
This is the sentence of the passage for Christians. All we have from Abraham, Moses and the prophets, and from Jesus, a son of Israel, we have received through this root.
They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand only through faith. So do not become proud, but stand in awe.

Paul is writing to warn the Gentile believer, and he says “some of the branches” (v. 17). He himself is one of the natural branches (11:1). This verse has been misused against the Jewish people, and that misuse is a sin against the text and against them. The tree stands, and they are still its own.
Note then the kindness and the severity of God:
The warning is addressed to the Christian: “otherwise you also will be cut off”. Baptism is a gift to be lived in. Perseverance is itself a grace, for which we ask and in which we must walk.
for God has the power to graft them in again.
The passage ends in hope: “how much more” (v. 24) these natural branches will be grafted into “their own olive tree”.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this image directly: the Church draws sustenance from the root of that well-cultivated olive tree onto which the wild shoots of the Gentiles have been grafted, and the Jews remain most dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism says the same (CCC 60, 755, 839). St John Paul II, visiting the synagogue of Rome in 1986, called the Jewish people our dearly beloved and, in a certain way, elder brothers. So Israel is not replaced. As the Church enters the Week of the Passion, she reads this page to learn humility before the root from which her Lord came.

r.h: Hosanna to the Son of David
set: Jesus has come up from Jericho with the pilgrims going to Jerusalem for Passover (20:17, 29). All four Gospels tell of the entry. The Mount of Olives, east of the city, was linked with the coming of the Lord (Zechariah 14:4). Matthew stresses that this is planned and fulfils Scripture. Unlike the earlier times when Jesus told people to keep silent about who he was (16:20), he now accepts a public acclamation.

Passover brought great crowds to Jerusalem, with memories of liberation and hopes of a king. In the Temple’s outer court, pilgrims bought animals for sacrifice and changed money into the coin accepted for the Temple tax. Doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7), the one that Joseph and Mary brought for the child Jesus (Luke 2:24).
str: vv. 1–3: the disciples are sent for the animals.
vv. 4–5: the fulfilment of Scripture.
vv. 6–9: cloaks, branches and the Hosanna.
vv. 10–11: “Who is this?”
vv. 12–13: Jesus clears the Temple.
vv. 14–16: healing, the children, and the anger of the authorities.
v. 17: to Bethany for the night.
kw: Hebrew for “Save, we pray” (Psalm 118:25). By Jesus’ time it was also a cry of joyful greeting. Our Malayalam “Oshana” comes through the Syriac form of the word. The psalm was sung at the great feasts, and it gives the next line as well, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”.
Jesus uses this word of himself: “I am gentle and humble in heart” (11:29), and of the blessed: “the meek” (5:5). It is the key to the entry.
“The whole city was in turmoil” is literally “was shaken”. Matthew uses the same verb when the earth shakes at the Cross (27:51) and when the guards shake at the tomb (28:4).
vv: Look, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

Matthew begins the quotation with words from Isaiah 62:11 and goes on with Zechariah. Only he mentions two animals. He may be following the wording of the Hebrew closely, and wanting to show that every word was fulfilled.
Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heaven!
Cloaks on the road greeted a new king (2 Kings 9:13). The people are naming Jesus as David’s heir. They are right, though the throne they have in mind may not be the one he is going to.
It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a den of robbers.

He joins Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. In Jeremiah a den is where robbers go to feel safe between raids: it warns against thinking that worship protects a life of injustice. Jesus loved the Temple, and he acts here as prophets had, out of zeal for his Father’s house (CCC 583–584). This is not an attack on Judaism.
The blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he cured them.

This verse is found only in Matthew. A saying in 2 Samuel 5:8 had kept the blind and the lame out of “the house”, in connection with David. The Son of David now brings them in and heals them. The Temple is being made what it was meant to be.
Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself
The words are from Psalm 8:2, in the Greek version. The children carry on the cry after the adults have gone, and Jesus defends them. The Church sees here how the small ones know the King.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus entered Jerusalem as the Messiah, acclaimed by children and by God’s poor, and that the Church takes up their Hosanna in the Sanctus (CCC 559); this entry shows the coming of the kingdom that the King-Messiah will bring about by his death and Resurrection (CCC 560). St Andrew of Crete invites us to spread before Christ’s feet not branches but ourselves (in substance). St Augustine says it was no promotion for the Lord of the ages to become King of Israel, but condescension: he came to rule souls (On John 51; in substance).

qa: Did Jesus really ride on two animals?

Mark, Luke and John speak only of the colt. “He sat on them” (v. 7) may refer to the cloaks. Matthew seems to read Zechariah’s words closely and to show them being met in full. St Justin Martyr saw in the two animals a picture of the two peoples called together: Israel, already used to the yoke of the Law, and the Gentiles (Dialogue with Trypho 53; in substance).
Did the same people who shouted Hosanna shout “Crucify him” a few days later?

Preachers often say so, but the Gospel does not. Matthew’s crowd on the road knows Jesus as the prophet “from Nazareth in Galilee” (v. 11), and many think they were pilgrims travelling with him. At the trial he says that “the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds” (27:20). The Church teaches that the Jews as a whole cannot be held responsible for his death, and that all sinners were the authors of his Passion (CCC 597–598). The better question is how quickly my own Hosanna can change.
Does Romans 11 mean that God has replaced Israel with the Church?

No. Paul is writing precisely against that idea. God’s gifts and call to Israel are irrevocable (11:29). The Gentile is grafted into Israel’s tree and does not uproot it. The Church lives from that root and awaits the day when all peoples will call on the Lord with one voice (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: Hosanna Sunday is among the most loved days of the Syro-Malabar year. The people gather with tender coconut leaves, the kuruthola. The palms are blessed, the Gospel of the entry is proclaimed, and the procession moves to the church with the cross going before and the Hosanna hymns on every lip. The King we have welcomed with palms then comes to us truly on the altar in the Holy Qurbana. Families take the blessed palm home to the prayer corner, and a cross folded from it is pressed into the Pesaha appam. So the leaf that greeted the King will be on the table of the Lord’s Supper. Today begins Hasha Week, the Week of the Passion. We enter it with our children crying out in front of us, as they did in the Temple, asking only to remain with him when the shouting stops.
study: Zechariah’s king has no warhorse. Where do I still expect God to win by force and not by humility?
“It is not you that support the root.” What have I received from Israel’s Scripture and faith? How should this shape the way I speak of the Jewish people?
When Jesus enters my “temple”, what tables would he overturn? Who are the blind and lame he would bring in?
How can my family walk through Hasha Week together, so that the Hosanna of today is still on our lips on Friday?

lead: Hasha is the Syriac word for suffering, and from today the Church walks with the Lord toward his Passion. Two plots stand side by side: Joseph’s brothers plan to kill the beloved son whom their father sends to them, and the council in Jerusalem resolves that Jesus must die. In both, people intend one thing and God is working another. The second reading (Joshua 22:21–29) tells of an altar built as a witness, which was mistaken for rebellion and nearly caused a war. The epistle (Hebrews 1:5–14) tells us who it is that is being plotted against: the Son, above all the angels. The words to watch are dream, sent and gather.

set: The story of Joseph fills most of Genesis 37–50. Jacob, also called Israel, loves Joseph more than his other sons and has given him a long robe, and the brothers “could not speak peaceably to him” (37:4). Today’s reading begins there. It leaves out vv. 14–17, where Joseph searches for his brothers and a stranger points him from Shechem to Dothan.
str: vv. 5–8: the first dream: the sheaves bow down.
vv. 9–11: the second dream: sun, moon and eleven stars. Jacob rebukes Joseph, yet keeps the matter in mind.
vv. 12–13: the father sends him, and Joseph answers, “Here I am.”
vv. 18–20: the brothers plot to kill him.
vv. 21–22: Reuben tries to save him.
kw: In the Joseph story dreams come in pairs: Joseph’s two, the two prisoners’, and Pharaoh’s two. Joseph himself says that a doubled dream means the thing is fixed by God (41:32). The brothers think they are fighting a boy, but they are fighting what God has said.
Literally “master of dreams” (v. 19). It is a sneer, and the story will prove it true: in Egypt Joseph becomes the one who can explain dreams.
The answer of Abraham (22:1) and Moses (Exodus 3:4), and here of a young man sent into danger, though he does not yet know it.
vv: So his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
The same event produces envy in some and pondering in another. Readers often think of Mary, who “treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).
He answered, “Here I am.”
Joseph knows that his brothers hate him, and still he goes when his father sends him.
Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits; then we shall say that a wild animal has devoured him, and we shall see what will become of his dreams.

This is the irony of the whole story: the plot meant to end the dreams becomes the road by which they come true. In the Greek Old Testament “come, let us kill him” is the very phrase of the wicked tenants when they see the son in Jesus’ parable (Matthew 21:38).
ch: St Stephen tells this story before the council: “The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9). The Persian sage Aphrahat, a Father of the Syriac tradition, sets Joseph and Jesus side by side in his Demonstration on Persecution, and St Ambrose wrote a whole work on Joseph in which he sees Christ in him (in substance). A figure is not an accusation: the brothers do not stand for any one people, but for every sinner, since sinners themselves were the authors of Christ’s sufferings (CCC 598).

set: Jesus has just raised Lazarus. Many believed, and some went to report it to the Pharisees (11:45–46). The greatest sign in John’s Gospel leads straight to the decision that Jesus must die: he gives life, and it costs him his own. The Passover draws near.

Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, so “that year” does not mean a yearly office, but that decisive year. The men of this council feared Rome, which had the power to destroy Temple and nation. John names the chief priests and the Pharisees of the council. The Catechism recalls that the authorities in Jerusalem were not unanimous about Jesus (CCC 596). Where v. 54 says “the Jews”, John means the authorities in Judea who opposed him; Jesus and his disciples were themselves Jews.
str: vv. 47–48: the council’s fear: “What are we to do?”
vv. 49–50: Caiaphas’s advice.
vv. 51–52: John explains what Caiaphas said without knowing it.
vv. 53–54: the decision; Jesus withdraws to Ephraim.
vv. 55–57: pilgrims look for him as the Passover nears; orders are given for his arrest.
kw: The ruling assembly in Jerusalem, called the Sanhedrin. John says only that the chief priests and Pharisees called it together.
John does not say that Caiaphas was a prophet in his life, but that his words as high priest said more than he intended (v. 51).
The purpose of the Cross as John sees it. It looks back to God’s promise to gather scattered Israel and forward to “one flock, one shepherd” (10:16).
vv: You do not understand that it is better for you to have one man die for the people than to have the whole nation destroyed.
As political advice it is cold calculation. In God’s plan it is the Gospel in one line.
and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.
John corrects and widens the sentence. Jesus dies for his own nation and for more than his nation; the Church in Kerala is among those gathered.
What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival, will he?
The crowd’s question leads into Hosanna, already behind us in the liturgy. He does come, and he comes for this.
ch: St Augustine says that Caiaphas spoke the truth without knowing it: a wicked man uttered a prophecy because of the office he held, not because of any holiness of his own (in substance). The Second Vatican Council takes up v. 52 when it says that the one People of God is to gather the scattered children into one (Lumen Gentium 13). The Catechism’s teaching on responsibility for the Passion is the frame for reading this passage (CCC 596–598; Nostra Aetate 4).

qa: Did God make Joseph’s brothers and Caiaphas sin?

No. God is in no way the cause of moral evil. But in his power he can bring good out of the evil his creatures do, and the Catechism gives Joseph’s words to his brothers as its example (CCC 312). The same is true of the Passion, where human sin served a plan of love without ceasing to be sin (CCC 600).
study: When has God’s plan moved forward through something meant to harm me or someone I know?
John says that Jesus died “to gather into one”. Whom am I keeping apart from me this Hasha week, and what step could I take before Pesaha?

lead: Joseph’s story moves from plot to deed: he is stripped, thrown into a pit and sold, and his father is left in grief. In John, some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he answers that the hour has come and speaks of a grain of wheat that must die. Both readings say that what looks like an end is the way God brings fruit. Between them, Joshua 22:30–23:1 shows brothers who listen before they fight, and peace is restored, the very thing Joseph’s brothers would not do. Hebrews 5:1–10 names the Son who “learned obedience through what he suffered” (5:8).

r.h: Sold for twenty pieces of silver
set: The plan of vv. 18–22 is carried out, but not as anyone intended. Reuben meant to rescue Joseph; Judah proposes the sale; Jacob is deceived with a robe dipped in blood, as he once deceived his own father with goatskin (27:16).

The chapter speaks of both Ishmaelites and Midianites as the traders (vv. 25, 28, 36). Many scholars think two forms of the story have been joined here. What the text says clearly is that Joseph’s own brothers bear the guilt: Joseph later says to them, “whom you sold into Egypt” (45:4).
str: vv. 23–24: the robe and the pit.
vv. 25–28: the brothers eat; a caravan passes; Judah’s proposal; the sale.
vv. 29–30: Reuben finds the pit empty.
vv. 31–35: the robe in goat’s blood; Jacob’s mourning.
v. 36: Joseph is sold on to Potiphar. God has not been named once, yet the story is moving.
kw: The exact meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The old “coat of many colours” comes from the Greek and Latin translations. It is a garment of honour, and 2 Samuel 13:18 uses the same words for a king’s daughter’s robe.
An empty cistern cut in rock for rainwater. The same word is used for the grave in the Psalms (for example Psalm 88:4). Joseph goes down, as if alive into the place of the dead.
The brothers’ words to Jacob over the robe (v. 32). Tamar will use the same words to Judah in the next chapter (38:25). The man who deceived is himself brought to the truth.
vv: The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
A small detail that means slow death. Zechariah speaks of prisoners in a “waterless pit” (9:11), a passage read on Hosanna Sunday.
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not lay our hands on him, for he is our brother, our own flesh.
Judah’s words sound like mercy, but they make a profit out of a brother. Judah and Judas are the same name, and Christian readers have noticed the link between this sale and the one Judas makes.
sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver.
Twenty shekels is the value Leviticus 27:5 sets on a male between five and twenty years old. Thirty was the compensation for a slave (Exodus 21:32), the sum paid to Judas (Matthew 26:15).
All his sons and all his daughters sought to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted,
Those comforting him know what he does not know. Genesis does not hurry past a father’s grief, and this week neither should we.
ch: Psalm 105 sings: “he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave” (105:17). Nothing in the sale was good, and yet God was “sending” him. Joseph says it himself at the end: “Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good” (50:20). The Catechism uses this as its example of providence (CCC 312). The Fathers saw Christ here: St Ambrose, among others, sees in Joseph the one who was stripped and sold and who became the saviour of those who sold him (in substance).

set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem to the crowd’s cry of Hosanna (12:12–19). Now some “Greeks” come to worship at the festival. They are probably people of Gentile birth drawn to the God of Israel. They approach Philip, who has a Greek name and comes from Bethsaida, a town on the edge of Greek-speaking territory. That the nations are now coming is the signal Jesus has been waiting for.
Up to now the hour has “not yet come” (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now he says it has come.
str: vv. 20–22: the request passes from the Greeks to Philip, to Andrew, to Jesus.
v. 23: “The hour has come.”
v. 24: the grain of wheat.
vv. 25–26: what this means for the disciple.
kw: In John, the hour is the time of the Cross and of the return to the Father together. For John, the Cross is already glory.
A single seed. The POC says it must decay in the ground (അഴിയുക), where the Greek says “die”. Either way it is the only road to harvest.

Semitic speech uses “love” and “hate” to mean “put first” and “put second” (compare Luke 14:26 with Matthew 10:37). Jesus is not teaching contempt for the life God has given; he is teaching what comes first.
vv: Sir, we wish to see Jesus.
It is a good prayer for anyone. They are not told that they saw him. Jesus’ answer tells them where he will be seen: lifted up.
Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Jesus says this first about himself. The Greeks and all the nations will come to him through his death and not around it.
Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.
Where he is this week is the Cross. And where he is after that is with the Father. The promise covers both.
ch: St Augustine reads the grain as Christ himself, who dies and is multiplied in the faith of the nations (in substance). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom, applied the image to himself: he called himself God’s wheat, to be ground by the teeth of beasts so as to become the pure bread of Christ (Letter to the Romans 4, in substance). The grain is thus also a word about the Holy Qurbana, where wheat becomes the bread of life.

study: Joseph’s brothers sat down to eat beside the pit. Where do I sit comfortably near someone else’s suffering?
What in my life is the Lord asking me to let “fall into the earth” this week, so that it may bear fruit?

lead: Joseph is in prison, forgotten by the man he helped. Jesus says that his soul is troubled, and does not turn back from the hour. Both readings stand at the low point just before God acts. In the second reading (Joshua 23:1–11) the aged Joshua asks Israel to hold fast to the Lord, and in the epistle (Hebrews 9:15–28) Christ enters heaven by his own blood, once for all. The words to watch are remember and lifted up.

set: Between yesterday’s story and today’s lie chapters 38 and 39. Joseph has served Potiphar faithfully, been falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife, and been put in the royal prison, where “the Lord was with Joseph” (39:21). Now two high officials of Pharaoh are placed in his care. The chief cupbearer and the chief baker held positions of trust at court, since they handled what the king ate and drank.
str: vv. 1–4: the two officers in prison, under Joseph’s care.
vv. 5–8: two dreams; “Why are your faces downcast today?”
vv. 9–15: the cupbearer’s dream and Joseph’s request.
vv. 16–19: the baker’s dream.
vv. 20–23: the third day: all happens as Joseph said, and he is forgotten.
kw: The word comes again and again in this chapter. Joseph’s claim is that interpretation is not a skill he owns, but something that belongs to God.
A play on words. To the cupbearer it means restoration (v. 13), to the baker it means “from you!”, being beheaded or hanged (v. 19), and in v. 20 the same phrase covers both.
In the Bible, to remember is to act on someone’s behalf. Joseph asks it of a man (v. 14) and is forgotten (v. 23); God will not forget.
vv: Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me.
In a prison, in a foreign land, with no one to help him, Joseph still speaks of God first. He also notices the sadness in others’ faces (v. 7), though his own situation is worse than theirs.
But remember me when it is well with you;

Here Joseph asks for help for himself, and he tells the truth about his case: he was stolen, and he has done nothing wrong (v. 15). The words will sound again from a cross: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).
Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
The chapter ends here. Two full years will pass (41:1). God’s silence, in Hasha week, is not God’s absence.
ch: Christian preachers since early times have compared Joseph, placed between two prisoners of whom one is raised up and one is put to death, with the Lord crucified between two criminals. The cup and the bread in the hands of these two servants may also turn our minds toward Pesaha; this is a devout association, and the author of Genesis need not have intended it. The Catechism holds up Joseph’s story as a lesson in how God’s providence works through what seems lost (CCC 312).

set: This follows directly on the grain of wheat. John does not narrate the agony in the garden as the other Gospels do; this passage carries much of its weight. “Now my soul is troubled” corresponds to “I am deeply grieved” in Mark 14:34, and Hebrews 5:7 speaks of “loud cries and tears”.
The voice from heaven answers a prayer that has just been made, and the crowd can hear only noise.
str: v. 27: “Now my soul is troubled”: the temptation and its refusal.
v. 28: “Father, glorify your name”; the voice.
vv. 29–30: the crowd’s confusion: thunder or an angel?
v. 31: the judgment of this world.
vv. 32–33: lifted up, and drawing all.
kw: The same verb is used at the death of Lazarus (11:33) and before Jesus names his betrayer (13:21). The Son of God has a true human soul and truly feels dread.
It means both to raise physically and to exalt. It is John’s third saying of this kind (3:14; 8:28). The Cross is the throne.
The same verb as “No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father” (6:44). No one is compelled; love draws.
vv: Now my soul is troubled. … No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour.
Jesus names his dread, and then weighs a prayer for rescue, and sets it aside. Courage here is not an absence of fear.
Then a voice came from heaven, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
God’s name has been glorified in the signs; it will be glorified again in the Cross and Resurrection.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.

A note on the text: Greek manuscripts differ here. Some read pantas, “all people”, and others read panta, “all things”; the Latin Vulgate has “all things”. The NRSV and the POC both have “all people”. The two readings do not contradict each other, and both are true to the faith. John adds in v. 33 that “lifted up” means the kind of death he would die.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 27 and 32 in two important places: the Son’s embrace of the Father’s plan in his own human heart (CCC 607), and the lifting up on the Cross that points to his Ascension (CCC 662). St Leo the Great, preaching on the Passion, marvels at this verse: from the Cross, the Lord drew all things to himself (in substance).

qa: If Jesus is God, how could he be afraid?

Jesus is true God and true man, and he has a true human soul and a true human will. His dread at death is real, and it is part of how fully he shares our life. His human will is at one with the Father’s (CCC 612), and this is what makes his “No” to rescue an act of love.
study: Joseph was forgotten by the man he helped. How do I act when kindness is not returned?
When I am afraid, can I say both things that Jesus says: “my soul is troubled” and “Father, glorify your name”?

lead: On this night the Church reads four passages about one table. In Exodus a household eats the lamb, ready to leave, with blood on the door. In Malachi God rejects careless offerings at his altar and speaks of a pure offering among the nations. Paul hands on the words of the Lord over the bread and the cup, the oldest written account we have. In John and Matthew the Lord kneels with a towel and then gives his body and blood.
Pesaha is the Syriac and Aramaic form of the Hebrew pesaḥ, Passover. The key words of the night are remembrance, offering and to the end.

set: Nine plagues have not moved Pharaoh. Before the last, God gives Israel instructions for a meal. The story of liberation stops, in the middle, to teach a liturgy: before Israel leaves Egypt, it is told how it will remember leaving. Chapter 12 looks at that first night and at every later year together.

Many scholars think that two older spring customs lie behind this chapter, a shepherds’ offering of a lamb and a farmers’ feast of new unleavened bread, and that Israel’s faith gathered them into the memory of the Exodus. The Jewish people still keep this night at the Seder, and the Church honours it as the root of her own Pesaha.
str: vv. 1–2: a new calendar: this month is the first of the year.
vv. 3–6: the lamb is chosen and kept until the fourteenth day.
vv. 7–11: the blood on the door, the meal, and how to eat it.
vv. 12–13: the meaning: God passes through in judgment and passes over.
v. 14: the command to remember for all generations.
vv. 15–20: seven days of unleavened bread.
kw: The verb pāsaḥ in v. 13 is usually translated “pass over”. Isaiah 31:5 uses it for God’s protecting Jerusalem, so some scholars also hear “stand guard over” in it. Both senses fit a blood-marked door.
Whole, complete. The word for what is offered to God is the word used of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and asked of Abraham (Genesis 17:1). Peter calls Christ a lamb “without defect or blemish” (1 Peter 1:19).
A memorial is more than a thought about the past. Each generation stands inside the event. The Catechism uses this sense to explain the Holy Qurbana (CCC 1363).
Bread made in haste, without yeast. Paul turns it into a picture of a clean life: “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8).
vv: Your lamb shall be without blemish, a year-old male; you may take it from the sheep or from the goats.
The Hebrew word covers a young sheep or goat. The best of the flock is given, and it is not to be a castoff. Today’s second reading will return to this point.
They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.
Those eating are the same people who are protected by the blood. In the Bible blood means life given (Leviticus 17:11). Salvation comes to the household through a death.
your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it hurriedly. It is the passover of the Lord.
It is a meal for people on the road. The Christian table is the same: food for those who have not arrived.
when I see the blood, I will pass over you,
The blood is a sign “for you”, says the verse, though God is the one who sees it. It teaches trust: Israel stays behind a marked door and does not fight.
This day shall be a day of remembrance for you.
Not a date in a history book, but a day that comes round again in every generation.
ch: “For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). John the Baptist points to “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), and John’s Passion notes that none of his bones was broken (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46). St Melito of Sardis, in his On Pascha, reads the whole Egyptian night as a figure of Christ (in substance), and St Justin Martyr points out that the lamb was roasted on a form like a cross (Dialogue with Trypho 40, in substance). The Catechism says that by celebrating the Last Supper during the Passover meal, Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340). Israel’s memorial is not cancelled by this; God’s gifts and call are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).

r.h: From the rising of the sun
set: Malachi is the last book in the order of the prophets. The name means “my messenger”, and we know nothing else of him. The book is usually dated in the fifth century BC, after the return from exile and the rebuilding of the Temple. The first excitement had passed, the priests had grown bored, and they offered God what they would never have offered a governor (1:8).

This is a rebuke from inside Israel, by a prophet who loves the Temple, and he wants worship to be honest, not abolished. The Bible’s harshest words about careless worship are always a warning to the people of God in every age, the Church included.
str: v. 10: God would rather have the doors shut than have such offerings.
v. 11: in contrast, his name is great among the nations and a pure offering is made everywhere.
vv. 12–13: the priests’ contempt: “What a weariness this is.”
v. 14: the cheat who vows the good animal and offers the bad; “I am a great King.”
kw: Literally a gift or tribute, and in the Law especially the grain offering (Leviticus 2). The Fathers were struck that the pure offering of v. 11 is named with this word.
The word for ritual cleanness, used here of an offering made outside Jerusalem, which is surprising. The Greek has thysia kathara, “pure sacrifice”, the phrase the first Christians picked up.
Israel’s law gives one sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12). So “in every place” was a startling thing to say.
vv: Oh, that someone among you would shut the temple doors, so that you would not kindle fire on my altar in vain!
God would prefer no worship to false worship. A hard word for anyone who comes to the altar with no heart in it.
For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering;

The Hebrew has no verb tense here, so it is debated whether the prophet means something happening in his own day (perhaps among Jews scattered abroad, or among those who honoured the one God) or something still to come. The NRSV and POC read it as present. The Fathers read it as a promise.
You bring what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick,
The best lamb of Exodus has become the worst animal in the flock. What do I bring to God: the first of my time and strength, or what is left?
ch: The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings, quotes this passage when it teaches about the Sunday Eucharist (Didache 14). St Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 41) and St Irenaeus (Against Heresies IV, 17) apply it to the Eucharist too. The Council of Trent sees in the Eucharistic sacrifice the pure offering foretold by Malachi (Session 22, chapter 1), and the Catechism calls the Eucharist “the pure offering” of the whole Body of Christ (CCC 2643). So on Pesaha night this reading is more than a rebuke. It promises that the sun will never set on this offering.

r.h: What I also handed on to you
set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8) in the mid-50s. This is earlier than any of the written Gospels, so these verses are our oldest written account of the Lord’s Supper. Paul says he has already taught it to them, which takes the tradition further back still, to the first years of the Church.

He mentions it because of a scandal. In Corinth the Lord’s Supper was joined to a shared meal, and the wealthy ate and drank well while the poor, who many scholars think came late from work, went hungry: “one goes hungry and another becomes drunk” (11:21). Paul’s answer is to remind them what the supper is.
str: v. 23a: the chain of tradition: received, handed on.
vv. 23b–24: the bread.
v. 25: the cup.
v. 26: Paul’s comment: to eat and drink is to proclaim.
vv. 27–29: the warning: examine yourself, discern the body.
kw: The technical words of Jewish teachers for passing on a tradition. Paul uses the same pair for the Resurrection (15:3). The second verb is also used in v. 23 for “betrayed”: on the night he was handed over, he handed himself over.
Our word Eucharist comes from this word. The Jewish thanksgiving prayer at table stands behind it.
Greek for the Hebrew zikkārôn of Exodus 12:14. This is the memorial in which the event is made present (CCC 1363–1364). The Church does this as Christ commanded.

It means recognising the Lord’s body in the Sacrament. In this chapter it also means recognising the body which is the community, which the wealthy were despising. Paul has joined them already (10:16–17). The Church does not need to choose between them.
vv: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread,
Paul fixes it in time. In the darkest hour, when one of his own was handing him over, the Lord gave himself.
This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.
“Do this” is a command to the apostles and through them to the Church. The Catechism says that here the Lord made his apostles priests of the New Covenant (CCC 611, 1337).
This cup is the new covenant in my blood.
This recalls Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant (31:31) and the blood of the covenant in Exodus 24:8.
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
The Holy Qurbana looks both ways, to the Cross and to the Lord’s return. It is itself a proclamation, even before the homily.
For all who eat and drink without discerning the body, eat and drink judgment against themselves.

Paul’s warning would make no sense if the bread were only a symbol. The Catechism applies this passage to our preparation for Communion: anyone conscious of grave sin must receive the sacrament of Reconciliation first (CCC 1385).
ch: Paul’s account stands behind the Church’s faith that this is a true memorial and a true sacrifice: the Eucharist makes present the sacrifice of the Cross, and it is one single sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367). The Catechism quotes St John Chrysostom: it is not man who makes the gifts become the Body and Blood of Christ, but Christ himself; the priest pronounces the words, and the power and grace are God’s (CCC 1375; in substance). The Lord’s presence in the Eucharist is true, real and substantial (CCC 1374).

r.h: He loved them to the end
set: The reading joins two moments of the same night. John, who tells of the washing of the feet at length, gives no account of the words over the bread and cup. He has given that teaching already in chapter 6. Matthew, like Mark and Luke, tells of the bread and cup and gives no account of the washing. Heard together, they interpret each other: the one who gives his body is the one who kneels.
Washing a guest’s feet was a task for a servant; a host would not do it (compare 1 Samuel 25:41). Guests reclined at a low table on couches, feet stretched behind them.
str: John 13:1–3: the great introduction: he knew, he loved.
John 13:4–5: the action, step by step.
John 13:6–11: Peter’s protest: “Unless I wash you…”
John 13:12–14: the meaning: “you also ought”.
Matthew 26:26: the bread.
Matthew 26:27–28: the cup.
Matthew 26:29–30: the promise of the Kingdom; the hymn; out into the night.
kw: Both “to the last moment” and “to the utmost”. On the Cross Jesus will say tetelestai, “It is finished” (19:30), from the same root.
The verbs for his garment in vv. 4 and 12 are the verbs for his life in 10:17–18: “I lay down my life in order to take it up again”. Many commentators see the whole Passion acted out in a small sign.
“You have no share with me” (v. 8). The word for a portion in an inheritance. To be washed by Christ is to belong to him.
A solemn bond. “My blood of the covenant” takes up Moses’ words at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).
A Semitic way of speaking in which “the many” is not a limit. See the question below.
vv: Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
John 13:1
The whole Passion is summed up here. The Catechism opens its teaching on the institution of the Eucharist with these words (CCC 1337).
got up from the table, took off his outer robe, and tied a towel around himself.
John 13:4
He knows that all things are in his hands (v. 3), and what those hands now hold is a towel. Knowing who he is sets him at the feet of others.
Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.
John 13:8
Peter would rather serve than be served. The first step in discipleship is to let the Lord do this.
One who has bathed does not need to wash, except for the feet, but is entirely clean.
John 13:10

A note on the text: Some ancient witnesses, among them Codex Sinaiticus, lack “except for the feet”. Both forms are old. St Augustine takes the bath as Baptism and the washing of feet as the daily forgiveness of those already baptized (in substance).
So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
John 13:14
He gives a command at the table, as he does with “Do this”. The Holy Qurbana and service belong together.
Take, eat; this is my body.
Matthew 26:26
Spoken by one who is about to die. The Church has taken the words as they stand (CCC 1374–1376).
for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
Matthew 26:28
Only Matthew adds “for the forgiveness of sins”. The words recall the Servant of Isaiah, who “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12), a chapter the Church reads tomorrow.
When they had sung the hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Matthew 26:30
At Passover the psalms of the Hallel (Psalms 113–118) were sung. Knowing where he was going, he sang.
ch: The Catechism teaches that on this night the Lord, in loving his own to the end, instituted the Eucharist as the memorial of his death and Resurrection and commanded his apostles to celebrate it until his return (CCC 1337). He included them in his own offering and made them priests of the New Covenant (CCC 611). The washing of feet shows what kind of priesthood this is. St Augustine urges Christians to wash one another’s feet both in action and in the heart, by forgiving one another (in substance).

qa: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?

Matthew, Mark and Luke present it as one. John says the meal was “before the festival” and that Jesus was condemned on the day of Preparation, as the Passover lambs were being made ready (13:1; 18:28; 19:14). Scholars have proposed several ways of relating the two. The Catechism speaks of the Last Supper “in the course of the Passover meal” (CCC 1340). Pope Benedict XVI, in his book Jesus of Nazareth, inclined to John’s dating and held that the supper was Jesus’ own new Passover. On any view, its meaning is Passover: Jesus is the Lamb.
Does “for many” mean that Jesus did not die for all?

No. The Catechism says that this term “is not restrictive”, but contrasts the whole of humanity with the one person of the Redeemer who hands himself over to save us (CCC 605). Jesus died for every human being without exception.
Why does John not tell the institution of the Eucharist?

We do not know for certain. John has given the teaching on the bread of life in chapter 6, and he may be assuming that his readers already know and celebrate the Supper. In its place he gives a sign that shows what it means to receive it.
rite: For the St Thomas Christians this is the night of two tables. In the parish, the Pesaha Holy Qurbana with the washing of feet; at home, the Pesaha appam, marked with a cross from the kuruthola kept from Hosanna Sunday, and the paal, shared by the head of the family after prayer and the reading of Scripture. Exodus 12:3 asks for “a lamb for each family”, and our home Pesaha hears something of that. It is a domestic echo and does not take the place of the Holy Qurbana, which is the one sacrifice of the Lord. Keep the home table as a school for the altar: this is how a Kerala child first learns what the Pesaha is.
study: Exodus says to eat ready for the road. In what ways have I become too settled to follow where the Lord leads?
Malachi speaks of offerings that are lame or sick. What do I give God: my best hour or what is left over?
“Discerning the body” includes recognising the poor at the table. Who goes hungry while I am well fed?
Whose feet is the Lord asking me to wash before this night ends?

lead: On this day there is no Holy Qurbana, and the Church reads and looks at the Cross. A father climbs a mountain with his only son, and the question is asked: “where is the lamb?” Isaiah sees the Servant led like a lamb to the slaughter and confesses, “by his bruises we are healed.” Paul explains the love behind it: Christ died for us while we were still sinners. The Gospel then tells the Passion in two parts, the first woven from Luke, Matthew and John, the second from John alone, ending in a garden and a new tomb.
The key words of the day are only son, for us and finished.

r.h: God himself will provide the lamb
set: God has promised Abraham descendants through Isaac (21:12), and now he asks for Isaac. The narrator tells us at once what Abraham does not know: “God tested Abraham” (v. 1). Jewish tradition treasures this chapter as the Akedah, the binding of Isaac, and reads it at the New Year. Christians have long read it in the days of the Passion and Resurrection.

Moriah is named here, and 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mount Moriah with the place where Solomon built the Temple. Sacrifice of children was known among Israel’s neighbours, and Israel’s Law and prophets condemned it (Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31). Many scholars hear in this chapter a refusal of that practice as well: the God of Israel stops the knife.
str: vv. 1–2: the test and the command.
vv. 3–5: the journey; on the third day; “we will come back to you”.
vv. 6–8: father and son: the wood, the fire, the question.
vv. 9–10: the altar and the knife.
vv. 11–14: the angel’s call; the ram; “The Lord will provide”.
vv. 15–19: the oath and blessing for all nations.
kw: Literally “only one”. The piling up in v. 2 slows down the terrible command: your son, your only son, whom you love. The Greek Old Testament has agapētos, “beloved”, the very word the Father uses at Jesus’ baptism (Mark 1:11).
Abraham says it three times: to God (v. 1), to Isaac (v. 7) and to the angel (v. 11). He is fully present to each of them, in the hardest hour of his life.
The Hebrew verb is “to see”. God “sees to” it. Abraham’s answer in v. 8 and the name of the place in v. 14 both use it.
The ram is offered “instead of his son” (v. 13). The whole Bible’s thought about substitution finds an early root here.
vv: Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah,
The same command, lek-lekā, “go”, opens Abraham’s story (12:1). Then he left his past behind, and now he is asked for his future.
Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac,
Isaac is old enough to carry the wood up a mountain, and he goes with his father. “So the two of them walked on together” is said twice (vv. 6, 8). It is the most tender line in the chapter.
The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?
Isaac’s only words in this story. The whole Old Testament leaves this question open until the Baptist says, “Here is the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).
God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.
Abraham does not know how, and he speaks more truly than he knows. Hebrews says that he trusted God “to raise someone from the dead” (11:19), and in v. 5 he had said that “we” would come back.
for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.
Paul takes up this word for God’s own act: “He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32). On Moriah the hand is stopped; on Calvary it is not.
Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.
In Christian reading, Isaac is spared and the Lamb is not.
ch: The Catechism sees in Abraham’s offering a final purification of his faith and a likeness to the Father who did not spare his own Son (CCC 2572). Origen, preaching on this chapter, sees in Isaac carrying the wood a figure of Christ carrying his Cross (Homilies on Genesis 8, in substance), and St Melito of Sardis draws the same figure. Reading it this way does not mean that Isaac was killed or that Abraham was only acting. It means that what God did not ask in the end of Abraham, he has done himself.

r.h: By his bruises we are healed
set: This is the fourth of the “Servant Songs” in the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 40–55), addressed to Israel in exile. The song runs to 53:12; today’s reading stops at the Servant’s grave. A startled “we” is speaking, who once looked away from him and now confess what they had not understood.

The prophet does not name the Servant. Jewish readers have often understood him as Israel or its faithful remnant, and the Pontifical Biblical Commission asks Christians to respect that reading (The Jewish People and Their Sacred Scriptures, 2001). The New Testament recognizes its fulfilment in Jesus (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25), and the Church reads it so today.
str: 52:13–15: God speaks: “my servant shall prosper”; kings are struck silent.
53:1–3: the speakers recall how he looked: no beauty, despised.
53:4–6: the turn: “Surely he has borne our infirmities.”
53:7–9: his silence, his unjust death and his grave.
kw: A title of honour in the Old Testament, used of Moses and David. The honour here is hidden: the servant of God looks like one rejected by God.
the punishment that made us whole
Literally “the discipline of our shalom”. What he bore became our peace and wholeness.
A single word in Hebrew, “his bruise”, the mark left by a blow. “By his bruises” is quoted by Peter (1 Peter 2:24). The wound becomes the medicine.
vv: See, my servant shall prosper; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
The song begins with the end. Before we see his disfigured face, we are told that he will be lifted up. John’s “lifted up” (12:32) stands in this line.
He was despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity;
Isaiah describes someone from whom people turn their faces. Many in every age have been treated so, and the Lord stands among them.
Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our diseases;
Matthew quotes this of Jesus’ healings (Matthew 8:17). The first step in understanding is to see that the burden was ours.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.
The heart of the song. Four times in one verse “he” and “our” stand against each other.
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have all turned to our own way, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
The verse begins and ends with “all”. No one stands outside it, including the one who is reading it.
like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he did not open his mouth.
The Ethiopian official was reading this very verse when Philip came to him (Acts 8:32). At his trial before Herod Jesus “gave him no answer” (Luke 23:9), in today’s Gospel.
ch: St Jerome said that Isaiah should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet, so clearly does he speak of Christ (in substance). The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ redemptive death fulfils this prophecy of the Suffering Servant (CCC 601) and that he willingly made it his own, turning his death into the supreme act of obedience and love (CCC 615–616). The song does not glorify suffering for its own sake; it says that love carried what we could not.

set: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, probably from Corinth, about AD 57. In chapters 1–4 he has shown that all, Jew and Gentile, need the grace of God and receive it through faith. Now he turns to what this means. Today’s reading has two parts: God’s love shown on the Cross, and a contrast between Adam and Christ.
str: vv. 6–8: the proof of love: Christ died for the ungodly.
vv. 9–11: “much more”: what the reconciled can hope for.
vv. 12–14: Adam: sin and death came in through one man.
vv. 15–16: the gift is not like the trespass.
kw: Not ordinary time, but the moment appointed by God.
A word for the ending of a quarrel. In the New Testament it is above all Paul who uses it for God’s work. God takes the first step; he is the one reconciling (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).
Adam is “a type of the one who was to come” (v. 14). A type is an imprint that shows the shape of what made it. Here the likeness is mostly a contrast.
The word Paul uses in vv. 15–16. Salvation is a pure gift of God’s grace.
vv: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
Christ did not wait for us to improve. It happened in God’s time, and in our weakness.
But God proves his love for us in that while we still were sinners Christ died for us.
Paul says “God proves his love”, not “Christ changes God’s mind”. The Cross comes from the Father’s love. The Catechism builds its teaching on this verse (CCC 604).
For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more surely, having been reconciled, will we be saved by his life.
If this was done for enemies, what will he not do for friends? St John Chrysostom presses this argument on his hearers (in substance). This is hope, and hope is not presumption.
Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death came through sin, and so death spread to all because all have sinned

A note on the language: The Greek eph’ hō is usually translated “because”; the Latin has in quo, “in whom”, the form St Augustine knew. The Church’s doctrine of original sin (Council of Trent, Session 5; CCC 402–404) does not rest on one phrase but on Paul’s whole contrast between Adam and Christ.
But the free gift is not like the trespass.
The two are not equal. Paul repeats “much more”. The first Adam’s harm is real, but Christ’s grace is greater.
ch: Paul’s line about love is the Church’s answer on this day to the question “Why the Cross?” God’s plan is one of benevolent love that comes before any merit of ours (CCC 604). By his obedience, Christ the new Adam makes up for the disobedience of the first (CCC 411, 615). By his loving obedience Christ made satisfaction for our sins to the Father (CCC 615–616). The Cross is no anger appeased by violence; it is God’s love reaching those who had turned away.

set: This Gospel is woven from three Evangelists, following Luke’s order and adding what only Matthew and John tell. Weaving the Gospels together is an old custom in our family of Churches: Tatian’s Diatessaron, a single harmony of the four Gospels, was long used by Syriac-speaking Christians, and St Ephrem wrote a commentary on it.

Crucifixion was a Roman punishment and only the Roman governor could order it. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, and other ancient writers (Philo and Josephus) show a harsh ruler. The Creed names him. The Gospels name the chief priests, some leaders and a crowd in Jerusalem on that morning; they do not condemn a people. Sin is what crucified the Lord, and the Passion shows its many faces: unbelief, hatred, mockery, cowardice, cruelty, betrayal, denial (CCC 1851).
str: Luke 22:63–71: mocking; the council at daybreak.
Luke 23:1–12: Pilate; then Herod (told only by Luke).
Matthew 27:19: Pilate’s wife.
Luke 23:13–23: Pilate says three times that he finds no guilt; Barabbas.
Matthew 27:24–25: the washing of hands; the cry of the crowd.
Luke 23:24–45: Simon of Cyrene; the daughters of Jerusalem; the Crucifixion; “Father, forgive them”; the good thief; darkness.
Matthew 27:51–54: the curtain, the earthquake, the centurion.
John 19:23–30: the tunic; his mother and the beloved disciple; “It is finished.”
kw: A Persian word for a walled garden, used in the Greek Old Testament for Eden. What was closed is opened by a word to a criminal.
Luke’s favourite word for salvation arriving (2:11; 4:21; 19:9). The last “today” of salvation in his Gospel is spoken from a cross (23:43).
Used only here in the New Testament (John 19:23). Many commentators recall the high priest’s robe, which Josephus describes as woven in one piece.
From telos, the end or goal (13:1). It is a cry of completion and not of defeat: the work is accomplished.
vv: Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.”
Luke 23:34

A note on the text: Some ancient manuscripts lack this sentence, which is why the NRSV prints it in double brackets. The Church has always received and prayed it. The Catechism sets it at the heart of her teaching on responsibility for the Passion (CCC 597).
Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”
Luke 23:42

It is often noted that no one else in the Gospels calls him simply “Jesus”. This man has read the inscription and heard the mockery, and he sees a King. On Wednesday we heard Joseph ask the same in prison, and be forgotten.
He replied, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
Luke 23:43
“With me” is the whole of the promise. The Catechism cites this word in its teaching on what follows death (CCC 1021).
Then the people as a whole answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!”
Matthew 27:25

Only Matthew has this. See the question below. No Christian may use it against the Jewish people, then or now. Pope Benedict XVI recalled that the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): it does not cry for vengeance, and it was poured out for many (in substance).
At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
Matthew 27:51

Torn from above. Hebrews speaks of a new way opened into the sanctuary “through the curtain (that is, through his flesh)” (10:20). The tombs opening in vv. 52–53 is Matthew’s way of saying that this death breaks the power of death; the text itself places the appearances “after his resurrection”.
Truly this man was God’s Son!
Matthew 27:54
The soldiers of Rome say what the disciples had not dared to say in that hour. In Matthew the Gentiles are coming.
Woman, here is your son.
John 19:26

He calls her “Woman”, as at Cana (2:4). Then to the disciple: “Here is your mother.” The Church sees here more than the care of a son. Mary is given as mother to the disciples (Lumen Gentium 58; CCC 964).
When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
John 19:30

The wine came on a branch of hyssop (v. 29), the plant used for the blood on the door in Egypt (Exodus 12:22). The Greek for “gave up” is “handed over”, and many commentators see a hint here of the gift of the Spirit.
ch: St Cyprian saw in the seamless tunic the unity of the Church that must not be torn (On the Unity of the Church 7, in substance), a word for all of us. The Catechism reads the Cross as the one sacrifice that completes and surpasses all sacrifices, the source of our salvation (CCC 613–614), and says that it is love to the end that gives it its value (CCC 616). Above all, it teaches that responsibility for the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (CCC 597; Nostra Aetate 4), and that sinners were the authors of his sufferings (CCC 598).

r.h: The pierced side and the burial
set: Jesus has died. John, alone among the Evangelists, stays at the Cross for what follows. It is the day of Preparation, and the Law asks that a body hanged not remain overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23), all the more on so great a sabbath. “The Jews” in v. 31 means the authorities, as elsewhere in John; v. 38 says that Joseph, himself a Jew, feared them. Their request to Pilate rests on their care for the Law.
Soldiers broke the legs of the crucified to hasten death, it is commonly explained, since a man could then no longer lift himself to breathe. It was not needed for Jesus.
str: vv. 31–33: the request; the legs of the two are broken, not his.
vv. 34–35: the spear; blood and water; the witness.
vv. 36–37: two Scriptures are fulfilled.
vv. 38–40: Joseph and Nicodemus and the body.
vv. 41–42: the garden and the new tomb.
kw: The same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the “rib” taken from Adam (Genesis 2:21–22). It is the basis for the Fathers’ image of the Church born from the side of Christ.
Physically this confirms a true death. John, the only one to tell it, gives it special weight. The Church has long seen in it the Holy Qurbana and Baptism.
John alone mentions the garden, at the arrest (18:1) and at the tomb. Many readers think of Eden. The first Easter morning will happen here.
vv: Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
The last blow of violence becomes a spring. The heart of Christ, opened by our sins, is the sign of his love for all (CCC 478).
He who saw this has testified so that you also may believe.
This is the disciple who stood at the Cross. The whole purpose of the Gospel is in this one sentence (compare 20:31): he saw, and he writes so that you may believe.
None of his bones shall be broken.
Spoken of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12) and of the just man (Psalm 34:20). On the day of Preparation, Jesus is the true Lamb.
They will look on the one whom they have pierced.
Zechariah 12:10. In the prophet, those who look mourn as for an only child, and God pours out on them a spirit of compassion. This verse is a promise of grace for all who look on the Crucified.
Nicodemus, who had at first come to Jesus by night, also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, weighing about a hundred pounds.

The Roman pound was about a third of a kilogram, so this is a very great amount, spices fit for a king (compare 2 Chronicles 16:14). Two members of the council who had been afraid (3:2; 7:50; 19:38) come out into the open at the moment when it seems too late. Their love is real. The Lord’s Passion has begun to draw them.
Now there was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden there was a new tomb in which no one had ever been laid.
He is laid where no one had been laid, as he came from a womb that had borne no other (St Augustine, in substance). The story of the first Easter begins in this garden.
ch: St John Chrysostom, teaching those about to be baptized, says that the blood and water are signs of the Holy Mysteries and of Baptism, and that the Church was formed from Christ’s side as Eve from the side of Adam (in substance). St Ephrem sings of the same mystery, and it is a treasured image of the Syriac tradition. The Second Vatican Council and the Catechism take this up: the Church is born from the pierced side of Christ (Lumen Gentium 3; CCC 766, 1225). His burial shows that his was a real death; his body did not see corruption (CCC 627).

qa: Does “His blood be on us and on our children” lay guilt on the Jewish people?

No. This cry has been terribly misused, and the Church has rejected that misuse. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and that they should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Many scholars think Matthew wrote at a time of painful conflict between Church and synagogue, which colours his telling. Sinners, and so all of us, are the authors of the Lord’s sufferings (CCC 598), and the blood of Jesus is poured out for forgiveness.
Did the Father punish Jesus in our place?

Isaiah says “the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all”, and the same song says, “we accounted him stricken, struck down by God”, as a mistake that the speakers later see through. Jesus never ceased to be the beloved Son. The Catechism teaches that he did not experience reprobation as if he himself had sinned, but in the redeeming love that always united him to the Father, he took us up in the state of our sin (CCC 603). The Cross is the act of the Father and the Son together, in love (CCC 604, 606).
Did God really want Abraham to kill his son?

The chapter says from the first line that this is a test, and at the decisive moment God stops the knife (vv. 1, 12). The Law and the prophets condemn child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31). What God sought was Abraham’s complete trust, and it pleased him. It is not a pattern for anyone to imitate. It is told so that we may see what God alone will do in giving his own Son.
rite: Passion Friday in the Syro-Malabar Church is a day of bare altars, fasting and abstinence, with the reading of the Passion and the veneration of the Cross, when the faithful come forward to kiss the wood. Many Kerala parishes also keep the way of the Cross and give a sip of the bitter drink, kaippuneer, as a share in the Lord’s thirst. In homes, the Puthen Pana of Arnos Paathiri is read, and its verses have shaped how generations of our people have wept over the Lord’s Passion and with his Mother. Keep the evening quiet and pray for those who suffer in many lands, for those who have wronged them, and for your own enemies, in the words the Lord used: Father, forgive them.
study: Abraham and Isaac “walked on together”. With whom do I walk this day, and how can I help them carry what they carry?
Read Isaiah 53:4–6 slowly, putting your own name in place of “our” and “us”. What changes?
Which of the figures in the Passion am I nearest to today: Pilate, the crowd, Simon of Cyrene, the thief, Joseph of Arimathea?
Who is the person I find hardest to forgive? Can I pray for that person today in the Lord’s words?

lead: Great Saturday is the day of the closed tomb, and the Church spends it listening. Each reading goes down into death and comes up again. Isaac climbs Moriah carrying the wood and walks down alive. Jonah sinks to the roots of the mountains and is given back to the dry land. Paul tells the baptized that they were buried with Christ so that they might walk in newness of life. Matthew then opens the tomb and sends the disciples out to all nations. The line runs from a father's obedience on a mountain to the Son's command on a mountain, and its key words are third day, buried and raised.

set: This is the hardest test in the story of Abraham. God had promised him descendants as many as the stars (15:5), and after long years of waiting that whole promise rested on one boy, Isaac (21:12). Ishmael has already gone away with Hagar (21:14). Now God asks for Isaac too. The narrator tells us at once that this is a test, so we know what Abraham does not know.

Jewish tradition calls this chapter the Akedah, “the binding”, from the verb used in v. 9. It is read in the synagogue at the New Year and holds a great place in Jewish prayer. Christians and Jews alike receive it as a sacred text, and we read it with respect. 2 Chronicles 3:1 places the Temple on “Mount Moriah”, so later readers saw this mountain as the place of Israel's worship.
str: vv. 1–2: the test and the command.
vv. 3–8: the journey of three days. Twice we hear that “the two of them walked on together”.
vv. 9–10: the altar, the wood, the knife.
vv. 11–14: the angel's call, the ram, the name of the place.
vv. 15–18: God's oath: all nations will gain blessing through Abraham's offspring.
v. 19: the return to Beer-sheba.
kw: The verb means to put to the proof. The same verb is used of Israel in the desert (Deuteronomy 8:2). God does not test in order to learn something or to trap a person; the test brings faith into the open and makes it strong.
Abraham says it three times: to God (v. 1), to his son (v. 7) and to the angel (v. 11). The word is one of total readiness, and he gives it equally to God and to the child walking beside him.

God's words pile up: “your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love”. The Greek Old Testament renders this word agapētos, “beloved”. It is the word the Father uses of Jesus at his baptism (Matthew 3:17).
Literally, “the Lord will see”. To see a need and to provide for it are one act in God. The same verb stands in Abraham's answer to Isaac (v. 8).
vv: So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac;
The same Abraham who argued with God over Sodom (18:22–33) now says nothing. The narrator gives us only his hands at work: the saddle, the wood, the road. Everything he feels is left unsaid.
Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac, and he himself carried the fire and the knife. So the two of them walked on together.
The father keeps the dangerous things, and the son bears the wood. Origen, preaching on this verse, sees here a figure of Christ carrying his own cross (in substance).
Abraham said, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.”

Isaac's question in v. 7 is the most painful line in the chapter. Abraham's answer is an act of faith spoken in the dark. When the moment comes, the animal in the thicket is a ram. The question about the lamb stays open until John the Baptist says, “Here is the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).
for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.
Paul seems to echo these words when he writes of the Father: “He who did not withhold his own Son” (Romans 8:32). What God stopped Abraham from doing, he did not spare himself.
ch: The Catechism sees here the last stage in the purifying of Abraham's faith: the father of believers is “conformed to the likeness of the Father who will not spare his own Son” (CCC 2572). The Letter to the Hebrews says that Abraham “considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead” and, figuratively speaking, received Isaac back (Hebrews 11:19). That is why this chapter belongs to this day. Abraham had told his servants, “we will worship, and then we will come back to you” (22:5). He had more hope than he knew.

r.h: Out of the belly of Sheol
set: The Book of Jonah tells of a prophet who ran from God's command to preach at Nineveh, and who was thrown into the sea. Just before this reading comes the verse that Jesus will take up: “Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” (1:17). In the Hebrew Bible that verse is numbered 2:1, so the numbers in chapter 2 differ by one between Hebrew and English.
The prayer is a psalm of thanksgiving, full of the language of the Psalter. What is striking is its place: Jonah gives thanks while he is still inside the fish, before he has seen the shore.
str: v. 1: the setting of the prayer.
v. 2: the whole story in one line: I called, he answered.
vv. 3–4: thrown into the deep, far from the Temple.
vv. 5–6: going down, to the roots of the mountains, then the turn: “yet you brought up my life”.
vv. 7–9: remembering God; the vow and thanksgiving.
v. 10: God speaks to the fish.
kw: The realm of the dead in the Old Testament, a place of silence, not yet the hell of the damned. “The belly of Sheol” joins the belly of the fish to the grave. The Greek word is Hades, and the Creed's “descended into hell” stands on this ground (CCC 633).
Another name for the grave. In v. 6 the movement stops and reverses: the man who went down to the land “whose bars closed upon me forever” is brought up by God.
“Deliverance belongs to the Lord” (v. 9) is the summit of the prayer. The word comes from the same root as the name Yeshua, Jesus.
vv: I called to the Lord out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.
Prayer can reach God from a place that seems beyond every prayer. No depth is too far for him to hear.
I went down to the land whose bars closed upon me forever; yet you brought up my life from the Pit, O Lord my God.
Read on Great Saturday, this verse goes far beyond Jonah. The Church thinks of Christ among the dead, breaking those bars from within.
But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Deliverance belongs to the Lord!
Then the Lord spoke to the fish, and it spewed Jonah out upon the dry land.
The word is blunt and a little comic. The sea monster that seemed to be Jonah's end was God's way of saving him all along. Jonah did not rescue himself; God spoke.
ch: Jesus takes this story as a sign of himself: “so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). The Catechism names “the sign of Jonah” when it speaks of the Lord announcing his Resurrection (CCC 994). On the descent to the dead it teaches that Christ went down as Saviour, proclaiming the good news to the spirits imprisoned there (CCC 632), and it quotes the ancient homily for this day: “Today a great silence reigns on earth” (CCC 635). Mar Aprem, in his Nisibene Hymns, lets Death itself complain of the one who came down to Sheol and emptied it (in substance).

set: Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, a Church he did not found, probably from Corinth around AD 57. He has just said that “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (5:20), and someone might conclude that sin does no harm. His answer does not begin with a rule. It begins with a memory: “Do you not know?” What happened to you at the font settles the question.
str: vv. 3–4: baptized into his death, buried with him, raised to walk in new life.
vv. 5–7: united with him; the old self crucified.
vv. 8–10: Christ will never die again.
v. 11: the conclusion: consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God.
kw: To plunge or immerse. The one baptized goes under the water as into a grave and comes up as from it (CCC 1214).

One of a chain of Greek words beginning with syn, “with”: buried with, grown together with (v. 5), crucified with (v. 6), living with (v. 8). The whole of Paul's teaching on baptism is in that small word.
The word can mean grown together, as a graft grows into a tree. Baptism is more than a sign placed on us from outside; we grow into Christ's own death and life.
Christ's death will not be repeated, and death will not return to claim him (vv. 9–10).
vv: Therefore we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

Burial is the sign that a death is real. Paul calls the font a tomb, and today of all days the Church knows what a tomb is. The purpose clause matters: all of this is “so that” we might walk in a new way.
We know that our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and we might no longer be enslaved to sin.
“The body of sin” does not mean that our flesh is evil. It means the whole person as held in the grip of sin.
We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.
Lazarus came back to a life that would end again. Christ's rising is of another order (CCC 646).
So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
This is the first command in the chapter, and it is a command about how to see ourselves. Grace comes first, and then the call to live what grace has done.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it explains that the believer enters through Baptism into communion with Christ's death, is buried with him and rises with him (CCC 1227). The instruction given to the newly baptized at Jerusalem, handed down under the name of St Cyril, compares the three immersions to the three days of the Lord in the tomb (in substance). In the Church's earliest centuries the great night of baptism was the night of Easter, so that the candidates could go down into the water at the very hour of the Lord's rising.

set: Matthew has prepared this chapter. An earthquake shook the ground at the death of Jesus (27:51), and another now shakes it at the tomb. The chief priests and Pharisees had asked Pilate for a guard (27:62–66), and those guards now shake with fear. The Gospel that opened with the name Emmanuel, “God is with us” (1:23), will close on “I am with you always”. The whole of the chapter is read today: the Church hears the end of the story before she keeps the night of the Resurrection.
str: vv. 1–4: dawn, earthquake, the angel on the stone.
vv. 5–7: the angel's message to the women.
vv. 8–10: Jesus meets the women on the road.
vv. 11–15: the guards are paid to tell another story.
vv. 16–20: the mountain in Galilee and the great commission.
kw: The women at his feet (v. 9) and the eleven on the mountain (v. 17) do the same thing. In Matthew's temptation story Jesus said that worship belongs to God alone (4:10). This is faith in who he is.
