The verb appears in the New Testament only here and in 14:31, when Peter sank in the water. Matthew does not hide that the first worshipers were not all at peace. Jesus comes nearer to them anyway.
The one command in vv. 19–20 is this verb; “go”, “baptizing” and “teaching” all serve it. A disciple is one who keeps learning from Jesus and obeying him.
vv: So they left the tomb quickly with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
Fear and joy go together. Matthew does not separate them, and Easter faith often begins this way.
Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me.”
My brothers: these are the men who ran away. The first word he sends them is a word of family. He sends them back to Galilee, where it all began.
When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.
And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.
These words recall the son of man of Daniel 7:14, to whom dominion was given. The authority for the mission comes from him, not from the disciples.
Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

One “name” and three Persons. Christians are baptized in the name, not the names, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (CCC 233). The nations now come within the blessing promised to Abraham's offspring (Genesis 22:18).
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
Matthew tells of no ascension. The book ends with Jesus present and staying.
ch: The Catechism places the Church's missionary mandate on these verses (CCC 849). It also notes that the women were “the first messengers of Christ's Resurrection for the apostles themselves” (CCC 641). The presence promised in v. 20 is what the Church lives on: Christ is present in his word, in the sacraments and above all in the Holy Qurbana, and in the Church when she prays (Sacrosanctum Concilium 7).

qa: Did God really want Abraham to kill his son?

No. The narrator says from the first line that this is a test, and God stops the knife. Scripture condemns child sacrifice as abhorrent (Deuteronomy 12:31), and of such offerings God says through Jeremiah, “which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). The chapter teaches total trust in God and shows that God provides. It gives no one any permission to harm a child in God's name.
What did Christ do in “hell”?

Here the word means the abode of the dead, Sheol or Hades, where the just of old were waiting. The Catechism says that Jesus did not go there to deliver the damned or to destroy the hell of damnation, but to set at liberty the just who had gone before him (CCC 633). The Saviour went to the lowest place of human loss, so that the good news might reach every age.
Matthew 28:15 says the story is “told among the Jews to this day”. How should we read it?

Matthew records a rumour current where he wrote, and he names who began it: some leaders and some soldiers, on one morning. He does not blame the Jewish people, then or now, and neither may we (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The first witnesses of the Resurrection, the women and the apostles, were themselves Jews.
rite: In many Syro-Malabar parishes this day brings the blessing of new fire and new water and the renewal of baptismal promises, while the service of the Resurrection is held late tonight or before dawn; follow your own parish timetable. Today's epistle gives the meaning of those promises: we renew what happened at the font, when we were buried with Christ. Jonah is close to our people as well. Our tradition keeps the three-day Rogation of the Ninevites, the Moonnu Nombu, before the Great Fast, and the prophet who was given back from the depths now stands beside the tomb of the Lord as his sign.
study: Abraham says “here I am” to God and to his son in the same way. To whom in my life do I find it hardest to say it?
Jonah gives thanks while he is still inside the fish. What would it mean for me to thank God before the rescue has come?
Paul asks, “Do you not know?” What do I actually remember and believe about my own Baptism, and how does it change how I live today?
The risen Lord calls those who ran away “my brothers”. Whom do I need to send that word to?

lead: The tomb is open, and the Church answers with light. Isaiah calls a darkened city to rise and shine. Hannah sings of the Lord who “brings down to Sheol and raises up”. Paul asks how those who died to sin can go on living in it. Two Gospel passages are listed for this day: Matthew's angel on the stone, “He is not here”, and John's morning in the garden, where a weeping woman hears her own name. The readings move from a promise of light, through a song of reversal, to a new way of living, and end with a person who has seen the Lord. The key words are rise, light and I have seen.

set: Many scholars think that chapters 56–66 of Isaiah come from the years after the return from Babylon, when Jerusalem was poor, half rebuilt and disappointed. Chapters 60–62 are the bright centre of this section. The prophet speaks to the city as to a woman sitting on the ground in the dark, and calls her to stand. These words are God's promise to Zion, and the Church reads them with Israel, seeing their fullness in the risen Christ.
str: vv. 1–3: the light has come; the nations walk toward it.
vv. 4–5: her children come home, and the wealth of the sea with them.
vv. 6–7: caravans, gold and frankincense, flocks for the altar, and the house made glorious.
kw: A command spoken to a woman: stand up. The word comes from the Semitic root meaning to rise, and the name of this season in Syriac, Qyamta, Resurrection, comes from the same root. So does the koum of Jesus to the little girl in Mark 5:41.
The verb used of the sunrise. It returns in vv. 2 and 3, where the “brightness of your dawn” is built on the same root. The glory of God comes up on Zion as the sun comes up.
The root means weight. God's glory is his real and heavy presence, not a passing glow.
vv: Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.
The order matters. The city does not shine in order to earn the light. The light has come first, and that is the reason she is told to rise. Easter has the same order.
For darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the Lord will arise upon you, and his glory will appear over you.
The darkness is still there when the promise is spoken. The Resurrection also happened “while it was still dark” (John 20:1).
Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn.
They shall bring gold and frankincense, and shall proclaim the praise of the Lord.
Matthew surely has this verse in mind when the wise men from the East bring gold and frankincense to a child (Matthew 2:11). The gifts lead to praise.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its teaching on the Church with these words: Christ is the light of the nations (Lumen Gentium 1). The Catechism adds that the Church has no other light than Christ's, and repeats the image favoured by the Fathers: the Church is like the moon, all of whose light is reflected from the sun (CCC 748). The promise was given to Zion and has not been taken from her (CCC 839–840). In the risen Lord, the Church sees how far that promised light reaches.

r.h: He brings down to Sheol and raises up
set: Hannah had no child. Her husband's other wife, Peninnah, had children and taunted her year after year. At the shrine of Shiloh she prayed so silently that the priest Eli thought she was drunk (1:13). God gave her a son, Samuel, and she brought him back to serve the Lord. This song is her prayer on that day. It stands at the head of the story of Israel's kings, and it is far larger than one mother's joy.
str: v. 1: the heart rejoices.
vv. 2–3: no one is holy like the Lord; a warning to the proud.
vv. 4–8: a list of reversals: the mighty and the feeble, the full and the hungry, the barren and the mother of many, death and life, poor and rich.
vv. 9–10: God guards his faithful, and gives strength to his king.
kw: In v. 1 the NRSV says “my strength is exalted”, and in v. 10 “the power of his anointed”. Behind both stands the Hebrew word for horn, the sign of an animal's strength. The song begins with Hannah's horn lifted and ends with the horn of God's anointed lifted. The POC renders it “head” (ശിരസ്സ്).
“There is no Rock like our God” (v. 2). A woman whose whole life has been unstable names God with the most stable word she knows.
In the story Israel has no king yet, and still the song ends with God's king and his anointed. The word gives us Messiah; in Syriac it is Mshiha, the word we say for the Lord.
vv: My heart exults in the Lord; my strength is exalted in my God.
The source of her joy is the Lord, even before Samuel. The son is not named once in the song.
The Lord kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.

This is the verse that makes the song an Easter song. All life and all death are in God's hand, and Sheol is no border to him. Later Israel would come to believe more clearly in the resurrection of the dead, and on this morning the Church hears these words fulfilled.
He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.
“Dust” is the word of Genesis and of the grave. God's habit of lifting the lowly is the same habit that lifted his Son from the tomb.
he will give strength to his king, and exalt the power of his anointed.
ch: Mary's Magnificat is clearly built on this song: “lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52) is the same movement. The Catechism names Hannah among the women through whom God showed his faithfulness to his promises, choosing those considered powerless and weak (CCC 489). St Augustine, in The City of God, reads the song as a prophecy of Christ and the Church (in substance).

set: The question of v. 1 is one that any preacher of grace will meet: if God's mercy is greater than sin, why stop sinning? Paul answers with baptism. On this Easter morning the reading goes on past the verses on the burial and lets us hear what follows: the risen life has to be lived, in the body, on an ordinary day.
str: vv. 1–2: the question, and “By no means!”
vv. 3–10: baptized into his death and into his life.
v. 11: consider yourselves alive to God.
vv. 12–13: so do not let sin reign; offer your members to God.
v. 14: the promise: sin will have no dominion over you.
kw: Paul does not call this a better version of the old life. It is a life of a new kind, and it shares in the life of the risen Christ.
A common biblical way to speak of daily conduct. Easter faith is measured on the road, in how one walks.

The same verb appears in v. 9, “death no longer has dominion over him”, and in v. 14, “sin will have no dominion over you”. Paul puts the freedom of the baptized on the same line as the victory of the risen Lord.
The word also means weapons. A hand or a tongue is taken up on one side or the other in a real struggle. The POC uses both ideas in v. 13 (ഉപകരണങ്ങൾ, ആയുധങ്ങൾ).
vv: What then are we to say? Should we continue in sin in order that grace may abound?
By no means! How can we who died to sin go on living in it?
Paul's answer is a question about what is even possible. A dead person does not return to the old address. Mercy does not make sin small; it ends sin's claim on us.
but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and present your members to God as instruments of righteousness.
The word “present” is the language of offering. The baptized bring their eyes, hands and tongues to God day by day. The Holy Qurbana is where we learn this offering.
For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.

This is a promise. Paul does not mean that God's law is bad or that commandments have ended: “the law is holy” (7:12). He means that the power to obey does not come from the commandment alone. It comes from grace, which changes us from within and makes our works truly good.
ch: At the start of its teaching on life in Christ the Catechism takes up v. 11: incorporated into Christ by Baptism, Christians are “dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (CCC 1694). It also says honestly that the inclination to sin remains in the baptized, as a struggle in which they can prevail by the grace of Christ (CCC 1264). So v. 12 is still needed after the font. The Catechism adds that justification consists in both victory over the death caused by sin and a new share in grace (CCC 654).

set: In Matthew two women go to the tomb, and they go to see it, having sat opposite it when he was buried (27:61). No one expects anything. A guard has been posted and the stone sealed (27:66). What happens next happens without any human help. Matthew does not describe the moment of the rising itself, and no Gospel does.
str: v. 1: the first day of the week, at dawn.
vv. 2–4: earthquake and angel; the guards fall as dead.
vv. 5–6: “Do not be afraid”; he is not here.
kw: Matthew's word also for the storm on the lake (8:24). When God acts, the ground under the world moves.
A perfect participle: the crucified one, as if this name stays with him. The risen Lord remains the one who was crucified and still bears the marks.
A passive, which points to God as the one who raises. Scripture speaks of the Father raising him, and of Jesus himself rising; both are true (CCC 648–649).
vv: And suddenly there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord, descending from heaven, came and rolled back the stone and sat on it.
The angel sits on the stone as on a throne. The stone is not moved to let the Lord out, for no one sees him leave. It is moved to let the witnesses look in.
For fear of him the guards shook and became like dead men.
A striking turn: the living guards look dead, and the dead man is alive.
But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid; I know that you are looking for Jesus who was crucified.
He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.

Two small words carry much: as he said. The Resurrection does not surprise his own word. And the first thing the angel does with these frightened women is invite them to look, because faith has a place on the map and the tomb is empty. The POC places “come and see” in v. 7.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Resurrection is a real event, with manifestations that were historically verified (CCC 639), and that the empty tomb, though not a direct proof by itself, “was still an essential sign for all” (CCC 640). In every Holy Qurbana we announce what the angel announced: he who was crucified is alive.

set: John alone tells us that the place of the crucifixion had a garden with a new tomb in it (19:41), and he alone tells this meeting in full. Here it is “still dark”, and darkness in John is never only a matter of the clock. Mary Magdalene comes, finds the stone removed and draws the only conclusion anyone would draw: someone has taken the body. The first response to the empty tomb is grief.
str: vv. 1–2: Mary at the tomb; she runs to the disciples.
vv. 3–10: Peter and the other disciple run; the wrappings; “he saw and believed”.
vv. 11–13: Mary stays and weeps; two angels.
vv. 14–17: the gardener, her name, “Rabbouni”, “go to my brothers”.
v. 18: “I have seen the Lord.”
kw: The cloth on the head, found “rolled up in a place by itself” (v. 7). Lazarus came out still wrapped, with a cloth on his face, because he would need them again (11:44). This body has left its wrappings behind for good. Thieves do not stop to roll up a cloth.
Mary's mistake is a true one. Many Christian readers have seen in this garden and this gardener an echo of Eden: the new creation has begun on the first day of the week.
John says “in Hebrew”, meaning the language spoken by the Jews of Palestine, usually taken to be Aramaic. It is a warm and reverent form of address, and it is all she can say.
do not hold on to me

The form of the Greek means “stop clinging”. It is not a ban on touching (compare Matthew 28:9), and the POC renders it “do not hold me back”. He is not going back to life as it was, and a new way of being with him has begun.
vv: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.
The first day: creation began with light on a first day, and now the same day opens again.
Then the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

He does not see the Lord. He sees cloths lying in order and an absence, and love reads the signs. The next verse says that they did not yet understand the scripture: faith came first, and understanding followed.
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!”
The whole Gospel has been saying this: “the sheep hear his voice. He calls his own sheep by name” (10:3). She did not recognize his face, but she recognized the voice saying her name.
But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’

For the first time in John he calls the disciples his brothers. After the Cross, his Father has become their Father. St Augustine notes that he does not say “our Father”: he is Father by nature to the Son and by grace to us (in substance).
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”;
The first Easter sermon has five words in English. Every witness since has only repeated them.
ch: St Gregory the Great says that Mary stayed and kept seeking when the others left, and so she was the one who found (in substance). St Thomas Aquinas calls her “apostle of the apostles”, a title the Holy See took up in 2016 when it raised her memorial to a feast. The Catechism explains the strangeness of the meeting: the risen body is the same body, and yet it has new properties, no longer bound by earthly life as before (CCC 645–646). It also rejects the idea that the disciples' faith produced the Resurrection: they were discouraged and doubting, and it was the Resurrection that produced their faith (CCC 643–644).

qa: Why do the Gospels differ in their accounts of Easter morning?

The number of women and angels and the order of events differ from one Gospel to the next. The evangelists each selected and arranged what they received from the witnesses, always telling us the honest truth about Jesus (Dei Verbum 19). They all agree on the heart of it: the first day of the week, women at the tomb, the tomb empty, the Lord alive and seen. Independent witnesses often differ in details like these, and such differences do not touch that heart.
Why did Mary not recognize him at once?
She saw the same Jesus, but his body was now glorified (CCC 645). The same thing happens on the road to Emmaus and at the lake. Recognition comes when he gives it: here, by a word.
Could the Resurrection be a way of saying that the disciples' faith came alive again?

No. These accounts show people who did not expect it: Mary looks for a stolen body, and some doubt on the mountain. The Catechism teaches that it is impossible to read the Resurrection as a product of the apostles' faith; their faith, under grace, came from the direct experience of the risen Jesus (CCC 644).
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church celebrates the Uyirppu in the night or before dawn, so that the darkness of the church can be broken by light, as Isaiah says. The season of the Resurrection, Qyamta, now runs seven weeks until Pentecost, and the first word of today's first reading comes from the same root as the name of the season. The Great Fast is over. In many of our homes, from today until Pentecost, the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) takes the place of the Angelus, and with it we greet Mary, whose faith kept watch through the dark. Let every home hear the words of Mary Magdalene: I have seen the Lord.
study: Isaiah says, “your light has come”, before he says the city is shining. How does it change my prayer to begin with what God has already done?
Hannah's song lists God's reversals. Where in my life or in my family do I most need to hear “he raises up”?
Paul says that my members are instruments in a real struggle. What is one thing I will offer to God today with my hands or my tongue?
Mary recognized the Lord when he said her name. When have I known that God was speaking to me, and whom can I tell this Easter?

lead: This first week of the Resurrection was traditionally the week of the newly baptized, who came to hear what had happened to them. Isaiah promises a forsaken city a light that will never set. Peter, in Acts, reasons from David's tomb to the risen Messiah, and Paul in Romans shows that Abraham was reckoned righteous as a gift, through faith, by God's grace. In John, on the night before he died, Jesus promises his friends that they will not be left as orphans. The key words are light, home and peace.

set: The chapter that began with “Arise, shine” now reaches its end. Zion had been “forsaken and hated”. God replaces each mark of her ruin with a gift. These are promises to the Jerusalem of the prophet's own people, and Revelation takes up the same language for the city at the end of time.
str: vv. 15–16: from forsaken to majestic.
vv. 17–18: gold for bronze; peace in place of violence.
vv. 19–20: the Lord himself will be the light.
vv. 21–22: a righteous people, God's own planting.
kw: The next of kin who buys back a relative from slavery or debt. God calls himself Zion's closest relative, the one who pays to bring her home (v. 16).

The word used of the Egyptian slave-drivers in Exodus 3:7. In v. 17 God says, “I will appoint Peace as your overseer and Righteousness as your taskmaster.” The only drivers left in the city will be peace and justice.
Used in both vv. 19 and 20. The sun and moon were the greatest lights anyone knew, and God promises a light that does not depend on them.
vv: you shall call your walls Salvation, and your gates Praise.
A city's walls and gates are its defence. Here defence is God's saving act, and the way in is praise.
The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give light to you by night; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory.
Your sun shall no more go down, or your moon withdraw itself; for the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall be ended.
The newly baptized carried lit candles from the font. This verse tells them what those candles mean, and it says to all who grieve that mourning has an end.
ch: Revelation sees the new Jerusalem: “the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). The Catechism describes this hope of the new heaven and the new earth (CCC 1042–1045). Israel keeps her place in this promise (CCC 839–840), and the Church waits for its fulfilment with her.

r.h: I will not leave you orphaned
set: These words were spoken at the Last Supper, on the night before the Passion, and the Church reads them after Easter because only now can they be understood. Jesus is preparing the disciples for a new way of being with him. Their question, the same as ours, is how he can be present when they no longer see him.
str: vv. 18–20: not orphans; “because I live, you also will live”.
vv. 21–24: love and keeping his word; Judas's question; the Father and the Son make their home with the believer.
vv. 25–26: the Advocate will teach and remind.
vv. 27–28: peace, and his going to the Father.
kw: He has just called them “little children” (13:33). Their fear is that of children losing a father, and he answers it directly: “I am coming to you.”
Literally, one called to one's side: a helper or defender (CCC 692). The POC says സഹായകൻ, helper.
The same word as the “dwelling places” of 14:2. He spoke there of rooms in the Father's house; here the believer becomes the house.
vv: In a little while the world will no longer see me, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.
The whole of Easter is in the last clause. Our life rests on his, and we live because he lives now.
Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.

The Catechism quotes this verse when it says that the goal of all God's work is our entry into the life of the Trinity (CCC 260). Heaven is promised for later, and God's home in the believer is promised for now.
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives.
The world's peace often means that the trouble has gone away. His peace comes with wounded hands (20:19–20), and it can hold firm in the middle of trouble.
ch: The Church has always read v. 26 as the promise that the Spirit keeps the words of Jesus alive in her; he is “the Spirit of truth” who leads the disciples into all the truth (CCC 729). The Holy Qurbana lives by this: at the epiclesis the Church calls on the Spirit whom the Father sends in the Son's name, and in every Qurbana we are given the peace he left us.

qa: Jesus says, “the Father is greater than I” (14:28). Does this make the Son less than God?

No. The Church confesses that the Son is one in being with the Father (CCC 242, 253). St Augustine reads the verse of the Son in the form of a servant, in the humanity he took for us (in substance). Other Fathers add that the Son eternally receives everything from the Father, who is the source; this is an order of origin, not a lesser Godhead.
study: Where do I feel most like an orphan, and how does “I am coming to you” speak to that place?
Isaiah says that God will be my light when sun and moon are gone. What would it change if I really believed this about my own days of mourning?

lead: Isaiah hears an anointed one sent with good news to the poor and broken. In Acts the crowd at Pentecost asks, “what should we do?”, and a community of teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer is born. In the epistle Paul says plainly, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile”. On the road to Emmaus, two sad disciples walk with the risen Lord and do not know him. The reading stops before they reach the table. The key words are anointed, we had hoped and interpreted.

set: A voice in the first person speaks, and we are not told whose it is: the prophet, or a figure God has chosen. The audience is a poor community back from exile, among ruins. Jesus will open this passage in the synagogue at Nazareth and say, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).
str: vv. 1–3: the anointed one and his mission.
vv. 4–7: ruins rebuilt, a priestly people, a double portion.
vv. 8–9: God's everlasting covenant and his blessed people.
kw: The verb behind Messiah, in Syriac Mshiha. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; here the anointing comes from the Spirit (CCC 436, 714).
The word of the Jubilee year in Leviticus 25:10, when debts ended and slaves went home. The “year of the Lord's favor” (v. 2) uses this picture of a great release.
People once as weak as ash will be trees that stand for generations, planted by God (v. 3).
vv: The spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me;
to give them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the mantle of praise instead of a faint spirit.
Ashes were put on the head in mourning, and the Hebrew words for “garland” and “ashes” sound alike (pe’ēr, ’ēper). God turns one into the other, and this week the Church sees that turning done.
but you shall be called priests of the Lord, you shall be named ministers of our God;
What Exodus 19:6 said of Israel is said again here. Peter applies the same words to the baptized as “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9) without taking them away from Israel.
ch: In Nazareth Jesus stops reading after “the year of the Lord's favor” (Luke 4:19) and does not go on to “the day of vengeance”. The Catechism uses this reading to show the Spirit at work in the Messiah (CCC 714). It teaches also that all the baptized share in Christ's priesthood, the common priesthood of the faithful (CCC 1546). This week the newly baptized learned that they had been anointed too, and the same is true of each of us.

set: Only Luke tells this story. It is still the day of the Resurrection. Two disciples, one named Cleopas, walk to Emmaus, about seven miles away. The exact site is not known with certainty. They have heard the women's report and they are leaving anyway. The story has the shape of the Holy Qurbana, but today's reading stops at v. 27, in the middle of the journey.
str: vv. 13–16: the walk; he joins them; their eyes are kept from recognizing him.
vv. 17–24: “What things?” Their story of hope and disappointment.
vv. 25–27: his rebuke, and the whole of Scripture opened.
kw: The saddest verb in the chapter. They have the facts right, and even the empty tomb; what they lack is the meaning.
Luke's word for God's plan (compare 9:22). The Cross was no accident that defeated the Messiah.
From the same family as our word hermeneutics. The risen Lord himself is the first interpreter of the Old Testament as speaking of him.
vv: While they were talking and discussing, Jesus himself came near and went with them,

He comes to them as they walk away, and on their own road. Their eyes “were kept” from knowing him (v. 16), and the passive suggests that God is the one who holds them, until the moment “their eyes were opened” (v. 31).
But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel.

Jesus lets them tell the whole of it first. Notice who is named in v. 20: “our chief priests and leaders”, the authorities of the moment, as the disciples themselves say, and not a people. The disciples are Jews, speaking of the hope of Israel.
Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things and then enter into his glory?
Then beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things about himself in all the scriptures.
Moses and the prophets are not left behind at Easter. We would give much to have heard this sermon, and the Church has spent her life trying to hear it again.
ch: The Second Vatican Council, following St Augustine, says that the New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old made manifest in the New (Dei Verbum 16; CCC 129). The Catechism sees in Emmaus the movement of the Eucharist itself: walking with them he explained the Scriptures, and sitting with them at table he took bread, blessed and broke it (CCC 1346–1347). That is why, in the Holy Qurbana, the readings and the homily come first, and then the altar.

qa: Why were they unable to recognize him?

Luke says only that their eyes “were kept”. The risen body is the same body in a new state (CCC 645), and faith is also at work here: they could not see what they had stopped hoping for, until he opened the Scriptures and broke the bread.
study: Where in my life am I saying “we had hoped”? Can I tell him the whole of it, as these two did?
How do I listen to the Old Testament readings at the Holy Qurbana? What would change if I heard them as Jesus explained them on this road?

lead: Today the Church hears two great images of union. Isaiah speaks of the Lord rejoicing over Zion as a bridegroom over his bride, and John gives us the vine and its branches. In between, Acts shows the threatened community at prayer until the place shakes, and the epistle calls believers to “one Lord, one faith, one baptism”. The risen life means being joined to someone. The key words are new name, abide and fruit.

r.h: You shall be called My Delight
set: The voice of 61:10 rejoices, dressed like a bride or a bridegroom; many readers hear in it the voice of Zion herself. Chapter 62 then has the prophet or God refusing to stay silent until her salvation shines. A people who heard the names “Forsaken” and “Desolate” from all around now receive a new name. It is a promise to Jerusalem, and the Church hears in it also her own calling.
str: 61:10–11: thanksgiving for garments of salvation; the garden of righteousness.
62:1–2: God will not be silent; the new name.
62:3–5: crown, royal diadem, and marriage.
kw: A name that describes what others see. God ends its use (62:4).
Hephzibah in the Hebrew. God's name for Zion expresses how he feels about her, and it is the opposite of what her enemies said.
Beulah. In the Bible's thought, a land belongs with her God as a wife with her husband (see Hosea 2:16–20).
vv: he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness,
Salvation is something God puts on us, as Paul tells the baptized that they “have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27). The newly baptized wore white this week.
and you shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the Lord will give.
In the Bible a new name means a new vocation, as with Abraham and Peter.
You shall no more be termed Forsaken, and your land shall no more be termed Desolate; but you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married;
For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your builder marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.

A note on the text: the traditional Hebrew vowels read “your sons shall marry you”. The NRSV reads “your builder”, changing only the vowels, and the POC also follows this sense. The line ends with a God who rejoices. God is not merely patient with his people; he delights in them.
ch: The covenant of God with Israel as a marriage prepared the way for the new covenant (CCC 1612). Revelation sees the new Jerusalem “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2), and the Church calls herself the bride of Christ (CCC 796). She reads these promises with gratitude, knowing that they were first given to Zion, whom God has not forsaken.

set: Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, as in the chapter before. Israel knew the vine as a picture of herself: the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5, and Psalm 80. Jesus says, “I am the true vine”. He takes that image onto himself, as the one in whom Israel's calling is fulfilled and in whom all may be joined to God. This does not mean that Israel has been cast aside; Paul says that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
str: vv. 1–3: the vine, the vinegrower, the pruning.
vv. 4–6: abide, or wither.
vv. 7–8: prayer and fruit.
vv. 9–10: abide in my love by keeping my commandments.
kw: To stay, to remain, to make one's home. John's great word for the relation of Jesus and the believer. It says nothing of a single burst of feeling; it speaks of staying.

A play on words in vv. 2–3: airei takes away, kathairei prunes or cleanses, and the disciples are already katharoi, “cleansed”, by the word. The pruning knife and the word of Jesus are doing the same work.
The Catechism says that the fruit in this saying is the holiness of a life made fruitful by union with Christ (CCC 2074).
vv: Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
The healthy branch is the one that gets cut. Our hard seasons are not always punishment; a vine-grower cuts where he hopes for fruit.
I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
“Nothing” means nothing that counts toward eternal life. This is not a word against our effort; by his grace our effort becomes true fruit.
As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
The sap of the vine is the love between the Father and the Son. To keep his commandments (v. 10) is the way we stay in it.
ch: St Augustine comments that a branch has one of two places, the vine or the fire (in substance). The Catechism says that here Jesus speaks of a still more intimate communion between himself and those who follow him (CCC 787). Christian readers have long seen the vine and the cup together: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them” (John 6:56). We come to the Holy Qurbana in order to stay in him.

qa: Does v. 6 mean that God throws people into hell?

It is a real warning: to refuse him for good is a real and terrible possibility. But God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). A branch that is still alive in this world can come back through repentance; the warning is given so that we will abide.
study: What in my life might be God's pruning instead of God's punishment?
God says, “My Delight Is in Her”. Do I think of God as delighting in me, or only as putting up with me? How would that change my prayer?
